A rationalisation investment is meant to make work cheaper or faster. The state invests in roads, railway lines, schools and hospitals; this is called public investment.

abschnitte.titel: When has it paid for itself?
abschnitte.text: With the **payback calculation** you check how long it takes until the money is back. If a machine costs 60,000 francs and brings in a surplus of 15,000 francs every year, it has paid for itself after 4 years. The shorter this time, the lower the risk usually is. However, this calculation does not take into account what is earned after the payback period.

abschnitte.titel: Net present value and rate of return
abschnitte.text: The **net present value method** is more precise. Here future income is converted back to today’s value, because a franc today is worth more than a franc in a year’s time. If 1000 francs bring in 1100 francs after one year, at 5 per cent interest that is worth around 1047.62 francs today, so the net present value is around 47.62 francs. The **internal rate of return** is the interest rate at which the net present value would be exactly zero.

Machines and vehicles lose value over time. This loss in value is called **depreciation**. If equipment worth 50,000 francs is depreciated in equal amounts over 5 years, that is 10,000 francs a year. In economics, depreciation is subtracted from gross investment to give net investment, the real increase in capital.

One of the largest investments in Swiss history was the **New Rail Link through the Alps** (NEAT) with the Gotthard Base Tunnel, which opened in 2016. Companies such as Roche or Novartis invest billions in research every year. Farms invest too, for example in a new cowshed or a milking robot. Investments create jobs and make a country fit for the future.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time until the money invested has come back in.
The loss in value of a machine or a building, spread over years.
How much more an investment brings in than it costs, converted to today’s value.
The earnings from an investment, usually as a percentage per year.

gewusst: You can invest time too, for example in practising an instrument.
At 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
An investment can be worthwhile on paper and still fail if the future turns out differently than expected.

teile.einleitung: A referral is an instruction from a doctor to another expert. In the health insurer’s family doctor model, the family doctor sends you to a specialist in this way.
wichtigste: In the family doctor model, the family doctor issues a referral.
With the referral you go to a specialist, for example the skin doctor.
This keeps the treatment coordinated.
Duplicate examinations are avoided.
In a real emergency, you do not need a referral.

abschnitte.text: Sometimes an illness needs special expertise. Then the **family doctor** sends you to a **specialist**, for example a skin doctor or an eye doctor. This instruction is called a **referral**. In it, the family doctor writes why you are coming and what has already been examined. The specialist then sends a report back.

Anyone who has chosen the **family doctor model** with their health insurer always goes to their own family doctor first. She decides whether a specialist is needed and then issues the referral. Without a referral, the insurer may not pay for the treatment by the specialist. In return, the **premium** is lower than in the standard model. In a real **emergency**, however, you may get help directly.

The family doctor knows the whole **medical history** of her patients. She keeps an overview of all treatments and medicines. In this way the treatment is **coordinated**, in other words everything fits together well. Examinations are not done twice. This saves costs for everyone who pays premiums.

gewusst: There is also a kind of referral in the Telmed model: the telephone advice service tells you which expert to go to.

teile.einleitung: Lindt & Sprüngli is one of the best-known chocolate makers in the world and is based in Kilchberg on Lake Zurich. The Lindor balls and the golden Easter bunny with the red ribbon are famous. The company’s history goes back almost 200 years.
wichtigste: Lindt & Sprüngli has its headquarters in Kilchberg in the canton of Zurich.
Its roots lie in the Zurich confectioner’s Sprüngli, founded in 1836.
In 1879 in Bern, Rodolphe Lindt invented conching.
In 1899 the Sprüngli family bought the company from Rodolphe Lindt.
At Easter Lindt sells the famous Gold Bunny.
Lindt & Sprüngli also owns foreign brands such as Ghirardelli in the USA.
The chocolate museum Lindt Home of Chocolate is in Kilchberg.

abschnitte.text: In 1836 David Sprüngli and his son bought a confectioner’s shop in Zurich’s old town. Soon they were also making **chocolate** there. Later the company was split. The confectioner’s with its famous Luxemburgerli is still a separate company today, and the chocolate factory became Lindt & Sprüngli.

Rodolphe Lindt had a small chocolate factory in Bern. In 1879 he invented **conching**, in which the chocolate mass is stirred and warmed in a machine for many hours. This made the chocolate melt smoothly and less grainy. This invention changed the whole world of chocolate. In 1899 Johann Rudolf Sprüngli bought the company from Lindt and combined the two names.

The **Gold Bunny** in gold foil with a red ribbon and a little bell has been made since 1952. Many millions of them are sold every year at Easter. The round **Lindor** balls with their soft filling are just as well known. At Christmas there are matching reindeer and teddy bears made of chocolate.

abschnitte.titel: Kilchberg and the Home of Chocolate
abschnitte.text: The factory and the headquarters are in **Kilchberg** on the left bank of Lake Zurich. There, in 2020, Lindt opened the museum Lindt Home of Chocolate. At the entrance stands a huge chocolate fountain more than nine metres high. Visitors learn everything about cocoa and chocolate there.

Lindt & Sprüngli sells its chocolate in over a hundred countries. The group also includes the US brands **Ghirardelli** and Russell Stover and the Italian brand Caffarel. The company has factories in Switzerland, Germany, France, Italy and the USA. The Lindt share is one of the most expensive on the Swiss stock exchange.

begriffe.erklaerung: Stirring and warming the chocolate mass for a long time so that it melts smoothly.
A shop that makes pralines, gateaux and other sweets.
Powder or paste made from the beans of the cocoa tree.
A name or sign by which you recognise a company’s products.

gewusst: Before conching was invented, chocolate was rather rough and crumbly.
The chocolate fountain in the Lindt Home of Chocolate contains around 1500 litres of liquid chocolate.

teile.einleitung: After a visit to the doctor, a letter with an amount often arrives: the bill. It shows what the treatment cost. It is worth checking every bill, keeping it and sending it to the health insurer.
wichtigste: The bill shows how much a treatment costs.
You check every bill and keep it.
Sometimes you pay the bill yourself and then send it to the insurer.
Sometimes the pharmacy or hospital bills the insurer directly.
You also send small bills below the deductible to the insurer.
If something is not right, you ask the surgery or the insurer.

abschnitte.text: A **bill** shows how much a treatment costs. You can see the date, the name of the surgery and which services were charged. Often each service is listed separately. For children, the parents receive the bill. They then check what the **health insurer** pays.

There are two systems. In the first, you pay the bill **yourself** and then send it to the insurer. The insurer then pays you back its share. In the second, the **pharmacy** or hospital, for example, bills the insurer **directly**. This is called **tiers payant**. It is still not free, though: the insurer later sends a statement for your own share, in other words the deductible and excess.

It is worth sending **all bills** to the insurer, including small ones. The insurer adds up the amounts. That way it knows when the **deductible** has been reached and it starts to pay. Many insurers offer an **app** for this, which lets you photograph and submit bills. That way nothing gets forgotten.

Read every bill carefully. Are the date and name correct? Does it list a treatment that you never received? Then ask at the **doctor’s surgery** or the **health insurer**. Bills can contain mistakes. Anyone who checks them helps to save costs. Keep bills, because they can be important for the **tax return**, for example.

gewusst: Even if the insurer pays a bill directly, you have the right to a copy of it.
Medical costs that you pay yourself can be deducted in the tax return under certain conditions.

teile.einleitung: Rega is the Swiss Air Rescue. It helps with helicopters and planes when people need medical help quickly. Its emergency number is 1414.
wichtigste: In Switzerland you can reach Rega on the number 1414.
Rega stands for Swiss Air Rescue.
It flies rescue helicopters to accidents and emergencies.
With air ambulance jets it brings sick or injured people back from abroad.
Rega is a non-profit foundation and is supported by many patrons.
It was founded in 1952.

abschnitte.text: Rega helps where an ambulance can only get through with difficulty or slowly. That might be in the **mountains**, on a lake or at a serious road accident. In the helicopter there is a pilot, an emergency doctor and a rescue specialist. They treat the injured person on the spot and then fly them to the right **hospital**.

Anyone who dials **1414** reaches Rega’s operations centre. There, experts ask what has happened and where you are. With the **Rega app** you can raise an alarm that sends your exact location at the same time. This helps a lot if you do not know exactly where you are out in the open. From abroad you can reach Rega on a separate number with the Swiss dialling code.

If someone from Switzerland falls seriously ill or is seriously injured abroad, Rega can help with an **air ambulance jet**. This is a plane that is equipped like a small intensive care unit. Rega also gives telephone advice to people abroad who have medical questions. This way patients get home safely.

Rega is a **foundation** and receives no money from the state for its operations. It is largely financed by **patron contributions**. Millions of people in Switzerland pay a small amount every year. As a thank you, Rega can waive the costs of a mission for them if no insurance pays. But the rescue itself never depends on whether someone is a patron.

In Switzerland there are several important numbers. **144** is the ambulance service, **117** the police and **118** the fire brigade. **112** is the European emergency number. If in doubt, the important thing is to call at all: the control centres send each other the right help.

gewusst: Rega has bases all over Switzerland so that a helicopter can reach any place as quickly as possible.
Rega also flies sick people between hospitals, for example babies who need special treatment.

teile.einleitung: Manor is the largest department store chain in Switzerland. In a Manor store you find clothes, toys, cosmetics, household goods and often a supermarket too, on several floors. The name is made up of the surnames of the founders.
wichtigste: Manor is the largest department store chain in Switzerland.
The name Manor is made up of the surnames Maus and Nordmann.
Its history began in 1902 with a department store in Lucerne.
Its headquarters is in Basel.
Manor belongs to the family holding company Maus Frères, based in Geneva.
There are around 60 Manor department stores, as well as supermarkets called Manor Food and restaurants called Manora.

abschnitte.text: A **department store** is a large shop with many different goods on several floors. At Manor there are departments for fashion, shoes, perfumes, toys, sport and household goods. Many stores also have a food shop, **Manor Food**. So you can buy many things under one roof.

In 1902 Léon Nordmann, together with the brothers Ernest and Henri Maus, opened a department store on the Weggisgasse in **Lucerne**. The Maus family had already had a wholesale business in Geneva since 1901. Bit by bit, more department stores in other cities were added. For a long time many of them had different regional names.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the name come from?
abschnitte.text: The name **Manor** is formed from the first letters of **Maus** and **Nordmann**. It has been used since 1965. Only from 2000 did all the branches throughout Switzerland have the same name, Manor. Before that there were, for example, stores with names such as Rheinbrücke in Basel or Placette in western Switzerland.

Manor has department stores in all parts of the country, in German-speaking Switzerland, French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino. The group also includes the **Manora** restaurants, where you put your own meal together. Manor employs several thousand people. Because the company is private, it traditionally does not publish profit figures.

Since online shops appeared, many people shop less in department stores. Manor’s turnover has also fallen considerably in recent years. That is why Manor is expanding its own **online shop** and redesigning its stores. Some branches have been closed, others modernised.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large shop with many departments on several floors.
A single shop of a company that has many shops.
A company that owns and controls other companies.
All the money a company takes in from selling its goods.

gewusst: From 1933 to 1945 it was forbidden in Switzerland to open new department store branches, which also held Manor back.
The name Manor sounds English, but it comes from two surnames.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who has paid a doctor’s bill themselves gets part of the money back from the health insurer. This is called reimbursement. To get it, you have to submit the bill to the insurer.
wichtigste: Reimbursement means: the insurer pays back money for a bill that has been paid.
This mainly happens with the tiers garant system.
The insurer deducts the deductible and excess.
You can submit bills by app or by post.
Afterwards the insurer sends a benefits statement.
You should submit every bill, including small ones.

abschnitte.text: With the **tiers garant** system, the doctor’s surgery sends the bill to your home. The insured person first pays it themselves. Then they submit the bill to the **health insurer**. The insurer checks what basic insurance covers. Then it transfers its share to your account.

The insurer does not always pay everything back. First the **deductible** applies: you pay this amount yourself every year. For adults it is at least 300 francs, and for children it can be zero. After that there is the **excess**, usually ten per cent. It is limited to a maximum amount per year.

Many health insurers have an **app**. With it you photograph the bill and send it off in a few seconds. Anyone who prefers paper sends the bill by **post**. It is important that the name and insurance number are correct. That way the insurer can match up the bill quickly.

After checking, the insurer sends a **benefits statement**. It shows how much the bill cost and how much the insurer pays. You can also see how much of the deductible has already been used. It is worth checking this statement briefly. If you have questions, you can call the insurer.

gewusst: You should also submit bills below the deductible so that the insurer keeps an accurate count.
For children, the yearly maximum excess is only half as high as for adults.

teile.einleitung: The health insurer helps to pay the costs of the doctor, hospital and medicines. In Switzerland, every person who lives here must have basic insurance with a health insurer. Anyone who knows how the premium, deductible and excess work can save a lot of money.
wichtigste: The health insurer helps to pay the costs of the doctor, hospital and medicines.
Basic insurance is compulsory for everyone who lives in Switzerland.
The premium is the amount you pay to the health insurer every month.
You pay the deductible yourself each year before the health insurer covers costs.
The excess is a share of the costs after the deductible, up to a yearly maximum.
Supplementary insurance is voluntary, and the health insurer may turn down an application.
Alternative models such as the family doctor model or Telmed lower the premium.
You can change health insurer for basic insurance every year.

abschnitte.text: Health can become expensive, because an operation quickly costs many thousands of francs. The **health insurer** spreads these costs over many shoulders. All insured people pay premiums, and the bills of those who are ill are paid from them. That way nobody is alone if something happens. In Switzerland this has been governed by the Health Insurance Act, KVG for short, since 1996.

**Basic insurance** is compulsory and offers the same services at all health insurers. It pays for the most important treatment for illness, maternity and accidents. Every health insurer must accept everyone into basic insurance, including people who are ill or old. Normal visits to the dentist are not included. Health insurers are supervised by the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH).

You pay the **premium** every month, whether you are ill or not. The **deductible** is the amount you pay yourself each year before the insurer steps in. For adults it is between 300 and 2500 francs, and for children it is 0 francs as standard. After that you pay a 10 per cent **excess**, for adults at most 700 francs a year. For a hospital stay, adults also pay 15 francs a day.

Anyone who wants more can take out voluntary **supplementary insurance**. It pays, for example, for braces, glasses or a two-bed room in hospital. Here the health insurer may turn down an application or exclude certain illnesses. That is why many parents take out supplementary insurance for their children early on. Here the premiums depend heavily on age and health.

With an **alternative insurance model** you can save on premiums. In the family doctor model, you always go to the family doctor first. In the Telmed model, you first call a medical advice line. A higher deductible also lowers the premium. People who earn little can get a **premium reduction** from the canton.

Every autumn the new premiums are announced. Anyone who wants to change usually has to cancel their basic insurance by the end of November. You can compare premiums on the Confederation’s official website **priminfo.admin.ch**. Because the services in basic insurance are the same everywhere, comparing is worth it. But you should only cancel supplementary insurance once the new one has definitely been taken out.

begriffe.erklaerung: Amount you pay to the health insurer every month.
Amount you pay yourself each year before the health insurer pays.
Share of 10 per cent that you still pay yourself after the deductible.
Compulsory health insurance with the same services at all insurers.
Voluntary insurance for extra services.

gewusst: From the age of 26 you pay the full adult premium in Switzerland.
Premiums differ from canton to canton, and they are particularly high in Geneva and Basel-Stadt, for example.
In Switzerland there are about 40 health insurers, which all offer the same basic insurance.

teile.einleitung: Money is a means of payment that you can use to pay for goods and services. Money exists as coins and banknotes, but more and more of it is only digital, in an account, on a card or in a mobile phone.
wichtigste: You need money to pay.
Before there was money, people swapped goods for goods.
Coins and banknotes that you hold in your hand are called cash.
You can also pay without cash, with a card or your mobile phone.
If you give too much, you get change back.
A country’s money is called its currency; in Switzerland it is the franc.
In many European countries people pay in euros, in the USA in dollars.

abschnitte.text: In the past there was no money; people **swapped** goods for goods. A farmer, for example, gave grain and got a pair of shoes in return. This was difficult, because the shoemaker might not want any grain at all. So people began to use things that everyone valued as a means of payment, such as shells, salt, cattle or metal.

The first **coins** were minted about 2600 years ago in the Kingdom of Lydia in what is now Turkey. Later, paper money was invented in **China**. Coins and banknotes together are called **cash**. In Switzerland there are coins from 5 centimes to 5 francs and banknotes from 10 to 1000 francs.

Today many people pay without cash, for example with a **card**, with their watch or with their mobile phone. In Switzerland the payment app TWINT is very popular. The money is moved directly from one account to another. You cannot see it, but it is still real money that you can only spend once.

A country’s money is called its **currency**. Switzerland and Liechtenstein have the **Swiss franc**, which has been in use since 1850 and is made up of 100 centimes (Rappen). In many European countries people pay with the euro, which has been in circulation as cash since 2002. In the USA people pay in dollars, in Japan in yen and in Great Britain in pounds. If you travel to another country, you often have to change money.

Money has three important jobs. It is a **means of payment** that you can use to go shopping. It is a measure of value, because prices let you compare what is expensive and what is cheap. And you can use money to store value, that is, to save. For money to work, everyone must trust that it will keep its value.

If an ice cream costs 3 francs and you pay with a 5-franc coin, you get 2 francs **change** back. It is worth quickly counting your change. In Switzerland the National Bank makes sure that there is enough money in circulation and that prices stay stable. When prices rise in general, money loses value; this is called inflation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Coins and banknotes that you can touch.
The official money of a country.
The money you get back when you have paid too much.
Trade in which goods are swapped directly for other goods.
When prices rise and money is therefore worth less.

gewusst: On the island of Yap in the Pacific, huge stone wheels used to be used as money; some were over three metres across.
The word salary comes from the Latin word for salt, because salt used to be very valuable.
The Swiss franc is one of the most stable currencies in the world and is considered a safe haven in crises.

teile.einleitung: The premium reduction is money from the state that helps people on a low income to pay their health insurance premiums. The cantons are responsible for it, and the Confederation makes a large contribution. The aim is that nobody should get into money trouble because of health insurance.
wichtigste: With the premium reduction, the cantons support people on a low income with their health insurance premiums.
Each canton sets its own rules on who gets how much.
The Confederation pays the cantons a contribution towards it.
The money usually goes directly to the health insurer, and the premium bill becomes smaller.
More than a million people in Switzerland receive a premium reduction.
For children from families on low and middle incomes, the premium must be reduced by at least 80 per cent.
In many cantons, entitlement is checked using the tax return.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, all adults with the same insurer in the same place pay the same **per-person premium**, whether they earn a lot or a little. For families on a small income, premiums are therefore a heavy burden. The **premium reduction** is meant to balance this out. It was introduced in 1996 with the Health Insurance Act. It is an important part of social balance in the health system.

Each canton has its own rules on who gets how much money. That is why there are big differences between the 26 cantons. Every year, the **Confederation** pays the cantons a contribution that is based on health costs. The cantons also contribute their own money. Together, the Confederation and the cantons spend several billion francs on it every year.

In many cantons, the **tax return** is used to check automatically who is entitled. In other cantons you have to submit an application, for example to the cantonal compensation office. The money is usually transferred directly to the health insurer. The premium bill then shows a lower amount. People who receive social assistance or supplementary benefits usually have all or most of their premiums paid.

For **children**, federal law requires the cantons to reduce their premiums by at least 80 per cent for low and middle incomes. For young adults in education or training it is at least 50 per cent. This is meant to ease the burden on families. Young adults with a small income of their own can sometimes be entitled themselves. It is worth asking the canton.

Because premiums are rising sharply, there is a lot of debate about the premium reduction. In June 2024, voters rejected the **premium relief initiative**. It wanted nobody to have to pay more than 10 per cent of their income on premiums. Instead, a **counter-proposal** applies, which obliges the cantons to spend more money on the premium reduction. But the debate about affordable premiums continues.

begriffe.erklaerung: Contribution from the canton and the Confederation that makes the health insurance premium smaller.
Premium that is the same for each person, regardless of income.
Money that someone earns, for example through work.
Form in which you report your income and wealth to the state.

gewusst: The premium reduction is often abbreviated to IPV, which stands for “individual premium reduction” in German.
In French-speaking Switzerland, the premium reduction is called “subsides”.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, municipalities and schools look after children’s teeth. A school dental hygienist shows the classes how to brush properly. There is also a regular check-up with the school dentist.
wichtigste: School dental care in Switzerland is regulated by the cantons.
A school dental hygienist visits the classes and practises toothbrushing with them.
Many municipalities organise a yearly dental check-up for schoolchildren.
This means holes in the teeth are spotted early.
Basic insurance usually does not pay for dental treatment.
Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste protects your teeth.

abschnitte.text: In many Swiss schools, a **school dental hygienist** comes by regularly. She explains how tooth decay develops and how to prevent it. She practises **brushing teeth** properly with the children. Children often learn the **KAI rule**: first the chewing surfaces, then the outer surfaces, then the inner surfaces (in German: Kauflächen, Aussenflächen, Innenflächen). She also talks about healthy mid-morning snacks and sugary drinks.

Many **municipalities** offer a yearly **dental check-up** for schoolchildren. A school dentist looks into the children’s mouths. This way, small holes are discovered before they become big and painful. Crooked teeth are also noticed. Afterwards the parents are told whether treatment is needed.

In most cases, **basic insurance** does not pay for dental treatment. That is why it is important to spot problems early. A small filling costs much less than major treatment. Many municipalities contribute to the costs for children, depending on the family’s income. The rules differ from canton to canton.

**Tooth decay** happens when bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid. The acid attacks the tooth enamel. Brushing your teeth in the morning and evening helps against this. **Fluoride** in toothpaste makes tooth enamel harder. Anyone who eats sweet things less often protects their teeth even more.

gewusst: In Switzerland there has been table salt with added fluoride since the 1950s, which is meant to strengthen teeth.
Thanks to school dental care, Swiss children today have much less tooth decay than a few decades ago.

teile.einleitung: Saving means keeping money instead of spending it straight away. This way you can make a big wish come true later or have a reserve for difficult times. Many children start with a piggy bank, and later a savings account at the bank often comes along too.
wichtigste: Saving means keeping money instead of spending it.
A typical money box is shaped like a pig.
You can keep your savings safe at the bank.
An account on which you save money is called a savings account.
The bank sometimes pays interest on money in a savings account.
If you save 2 francs every week, you have 8 francs after 4 weeks.
When shopping, you save money by comparing prices.

abschnitte.text: **Saving** means not spending part of your money, but keeping it for later. You save, for example, for a bike, a game or a holiday. Adults also save for a flat, for their children’s education or for old age. If you save, you sometimes have to do without something, but you are all the happier later.

The best-known container for savings is the **piggy bank**. In many countries the pig is considered a symbol of luck and a sign of wealth. In the past you had to smash a clay piggy bank to get at the money. Today many money boxes have a stopper underneath.

Larger amounts are best kept in a **savings account** at the bank. There the money is protected from theft and fire. Many banks offer special youth savings accounts for children and young people. Sometimes the bank pays **interest** on them, a small reward for letting the bank have the money.

If you save regularly, you see your money grow. If you save 2 francs every week, you have 8 francs after 4 weeks and 104 francs after a year. With a **budget** you plan how much you spend and how much you save. If you get interest and leave it in the account, the money grows faster and faster thanks to **compound interest**.

When shopping, you save by **comparing prices** and not buying everything straight away. One trick is to wait a few days when you want something; often you then notice that you do not need it that much after all. You can also write down or draw a savings goal and follow your progress. Buying or swapping second-hand things also saves money.

Compared with many other countries, people in Switzerland save a lot. For old age there is the **three-pillar system** with the AVS, the pension fund and private saving in pillar 3a. At the end of October many banks celebrate **World Savings Day**; in the past, children brought their money boxes to the bank on this day. The Confederation and the municipalities must also manage their money well so that they do not take on too much debt.

begriffe.erklaerung: An account at the bank on which you save money.
Money the bank pays when you let it have your money.
Interest that is also paid on interest received earlier.
A plan of how much money you take in, spend and save.
Something you put money aside for on purpose.

gewusst: The first piggy banks probably existed several hundred years ago.
In Switzerland a money box is also called a Kässeli or Sparkässeli.
Thanks to compound interest, someone who starts saving a little every month at 20 often has much more in old age than someone who only starts at 40.

teile.einleitung: Geberit is a Swiss company that makes technology for bathrooms. It is especially well known for cisterns hidden in the wall. When someone in Europe presses a toilet flush, they are very often using a Geberit product.
wichtigste: Geberit is known for cisterns and sanitary technology.
The name Geberit comes from the surname of the founder, Gebert.
The company was founded in Rapperswil in 1874.
Geberit’s headquarters is in Rapperswil-Jona in the canton of St Gallen.
Geberit is a leader in sanitary products in Europe.
Geberit shares are traded on the Swiss stock exchange.

abschnitte.text: **Geberit** makes products that are needed in the bathroom, many of them hidden behind the wall. These include **cisterns**, pipes for water and waste water, and flush plates. Since taking over the company Sanitec in 2015, Geberit has also made ceramic toilets and washbasins. There are also shower toilets, which clean with water after using the toilet.

In 1874 **Caspar Melchior Albert Gebert** opened a workshop for sheet-metal work in Rapperswil. Later the company made wooden cisterns lined with lead on the inside. From the 1950s the cisterns were made of plastic. The company name Geberit was later formed from the surname Gebert.

In 1964 Geberit brought a **concealed cistern** onto the market, which is built into the wall. In the past the cistern hung visibly above the toilet. The hidden cistern saves space and makes the bathroom look tidier. Today it is standard in many new buildings.

A toilet flush uses a lot of drinking water. Modern Geberit cisterns therefore have a **dual flush** with a large and a small button. The small flush needs only about 3 litres instead of 6 litres. In this way households can save many thousands of litres of water every year.

Geberit employs about 11,000 people worldwide (as of 2024) and has factories in many European countries as well as in Asia and America. The company is one of the largest in Switzerland and is listed on the **SIX** stock exchange. Most products are installed by plumbers and not bought directly in shops. Geberit also trains many plumbers in its own training centres.

begriffe.erklaerung: Everything to do with water pipes, toilets, showers and washbasins.
A container of water that flushes the toilet when you press the button.
Built into the wall and therefore not visible.
A craftsman who works with sheet metal, for example on gutters.

gewusst: Geberit’s first cisterns were made of wood.
A concealed cistern is meant to last for decades, so spare parts are available even for very old models.
Many people use Geberit products every day without ever having seen the company’s name.

teile.einleitung: In basic insurance you can choose between different models. The standard model offers the most freedom: you may go directly to any approved doctor. In return, the premium is usually the highest.
wichtigste: In the standard model, you have a free choice of doctor.
You can go directly to a specialist without calling anyone first.
The premium is usually higher than with other models.
Alternative models include, for example, family doctor, HMO and Telmed.
The services of basic insurance are the same in all models.

abschnitte.text: In the **standard model**, you may go to any approved doctor in Switzerland. You do not have to ask anyone first. Anyone with skin problems, for example, can go straight to the **skin doctor**. This **free choice of doctor** is convenient. But it comes at a price.

As well as the standard model, there are **alternative models**. In the **family doctor model**, you always go to your own family doctor first. In the **HMO model**, the first point of contact is a group practice. In the **Telmed model**, you first call a medical advice line. In emergencies, you may go straight to hospital in all models.

abschnitte.titel: Why the standard model costs more
abschnitte.text: In the alternative models, points of contact help to avoid unnecessary examinations. This saves costs. That is why insurers give a **discount** on the premium there. There is no such discount in the standard model. That is why the **premium** is usually the highest. But the services of basic insurance are the same in all models.

Anyone who often goes to different specialists and wants to stay free may choose the standard model. Anyone who wants to save money and has a regular family doctor often chooses an alternative model. You can usually change the model at the start of a new year. Many people in Switzerland today have an alternative model.

gewusst: Changing model can save several hundred francs in premiums every year.
Emergencies are exempt in all models: you may always get help straight away.

teile.einleitung: The excess is the part of the doctor’s and medicine costs that you still pay yourself in basic insurance after the deductible. As a rule, it is 10 per cent of the bill. So that the costs do not get too high, there is an upper limit each year.
wichtigste: The excess comes after the deductible.
As a rule, it is 10 per cent of the costs.
For adults, the excess is limited to at most 700 francs a year.
For children, the upper limit is 350 francs a year.
For certain expensive original medicines, the excess can be higher.
No excess has to be paid for maternity services.
Together, the deductible and excess are called cost sharing.

abschnitte.text: The **excess** is a percentage share of the costs. Once you have paid your whole **deductible** for the year, the health insurer covers 90 per cent of further bills. You pay the remaining 10 per cent yourself. This continues until you have reached the yearly limit. After that, the health insurer covers everything that is insured in basic insurance for the rest of the year.

Tom has a deductible of 300 francs and needs an operation costing 20,300 francs. First he pays the 300-franc deductible. Of the remaining 20,000 francs, 10 per cent would actually be 2000 francs. But because the excess is limited to 700 francs, Tom only pays 700 francs. So altogether he bears 1000 francs, and the **hospital contribution** is added for the days in hospital.

If there is a cheaper **generic** with the same active ingredient for a medicine, the excess for the more expensive original can be higher. Since 2024 it has usually been 40 per cent in such cases. This is meant to encourage patients to choose cheaper medicines. If the doctor prescribes the original for medical reasons, the normal excess applies again. It is worth asking about generics at the pharmacy.

For **children** up to 18, the yearly excess is limited to 350 francs. With **maternity** you do not have to pay any excess, from the 13th week of pregnancy until eight weeks after the birth. Special rules also apply to certain check-ups. The exact cost sharing is always shown on the health insurer’s statement. You should keep this statement safe.

The excess is meant to make sure that people use health services sensibly. Anyone who pays part themselves is more likely to think about whether a visit to the doctor is really necessary. At the same time, the **upper limit** protects people who are ill from having to pay too much. An adult with a deductible of 300 therefore pays at most 1000 francs a year themselves, not counting premiums and the hospital contribution. With a deductible of 2500 francs it is at most 3200 francs.

begriffe.erklaerung: Share, usually 10 per cent, that you pay yourself after the deductible.
Cheap copy of a medicine with the same active ingredient.
Deductible and excess together, in other words the part you bear yourself.
Highest amount you have to pay.

gewusst: Without an upper limit, for an operation costing 100,000 francs you would have to pay up to 10,000 francs in excess.
After a treatment, the health insurer sends a statement listing the deductible and excess exactly.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who leaves Switzerland for good has a lot to arrange, including health insurance. The obligation to have basic insurance depends on living in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Basic insurance is compulsory for all people who live in Switzerland.
Anyone who emigrates deregisters with their municipality.
Basic insurance ends when you move away.
The health insurer needs confirmation of the deregistration.
In the new country you need your own health insurance.

abschnitte.text: Ines is moving to **Canada** for good. In Switzerland, the obligation to have basic insurance applies to everyone whose **residence** is here. Anyone who emigrates no longer has their residence in Switzerland. That is why **basic insurance** ends when you move away. So Ines has to take care of new cover.

Before moving away, you deregister with the municipality’s **residents’ registration office**. The municipality gives you a **confirmation of deregistration**. You send this to the health insurer so that it can end the basic insurance. Supplementary insurance is a separate contract, and the rules in the contract apply to it. That is why it is best to find out early what will happen to it.

In the new country, different rules apply to health insurance. That is why you find out before leaving how to get insured there. For the time in between, there is private **international health insurance**. For certain countries, for example in the EU, there are special rules, for example for pensioners. Anyone who comes back later and lives in Switzerland again has to take out insurance again.

gewusst: Anyone who only goes on holiday stays insured in Switzerland, and basic insurance pays part of the costs of emergencies abroad.

teile.einleitung: A burn happens when heat injures the skin, for example from a hot hob, boiling water or the sun. Small burns can be treated yourself, but large ones need medical help immediately.
wichtigste: A mild burn is cooled straight away under cool, running water.
The water should be cool, but not ice-cold.
Never put ice directly on a burn.
Do not burst blisters on the skin.
For large or deep burns, call the number 144.
Sunburn is also a burn of the skin.

abschnitte.text: In a **burn**, the skin is damaged by heat. This can happen through fire, hot objects, steam or hot liquids. Scalding with hot water or tea is also a kind of burn. The skin turns red, hurts and can swell. The longer and stronger the heat, the deeper the injury goes.

Doctors divide burns into **degrees**. In the first degree, the skin is only red and painful, as with sunburn. In the second degree, **blisters** also form. In the third degree, the skin is deeply destroyed and can look white or dark. Severe burns always need to be treated in hospital.

With a small burn, hold the spot under **cool water** for a few minutes straight away. This relieves the pain and stops the heat in the skin. Ice-cold water or ice can damage the skin even more. Leave blisters intact, because they protect the wound from dirt. Afterwards you can loosely cover the spot with a clean dressing.

If the burn is bigger than the palm of your own hand, on the face or very deep, get help straight away. In Switzerland you can reach the ambulance service on the **emergency number 144**. Take special care with small children, because their skin is thinner. A burn counts as an **accident**, so the treatment is paid for by accident insurance or, for children, by the health insurer’s accident cover.

Many burns happen in the kitchen. Turn pan handles inwards so that nobody gets caught on them. Do not put hot drinks at the edge of the table. Be careful with candles and fire. **Sun cream**, a hat and shade around midday help against sunburn.

gewusst: The skin is the largest organ of the human body.
Very severe cold can also injure the skin in a similar way to heat, and this is called frostbite.

teile.einleitung: As well as the standard model, health insurers offer alternative insurance models: family doctor, HMO and Telmed. In all of them you give up the free choice of doctor and get a lower premium in return.
wichtigste: The family doctor, HMO and Telmed models have a fixed first point of contact.
You give up the free choice of doctor and pay lower premiums in return.
The services paid for are the same as in the standard model.
In a real emergency you may go straight to A&E.
The emergency number for the ambulance service is 144.
Anyone who repeatedly does not keep to the rules risks reduced payments or being moved to the standard model.

abschnitte.text: In the **family doctor model**, you choose a family doctor from a list provided by the health insurer. When you have health problems, you always go to her first. She knows you well and keeps an overview. If a specialist is needed, she issues a **referral**. This way duplicate examinations are avoided.

In the **HMO model**, the first point of contact is a **group practice**, also called a health centre. Several doctors and often other experts work together there. When you have symptoms, you go to this centre first. The experts there decide whether treatment elsewhere is necessary. This model is found mainly in larger towns.

In the **Telmed model**, you call a telephone **health advice service** before every visit to the doctor. Medical experts listen and give advice. Sometimes a tip for home is enough, sometimes they send you to the doctor. The advice line can usually be reached around the clock. You then have to follow the advice so that the insurer pays.

In a real **emergency**, the obligation to use the first point of contact does not apply. Then you get help straight away, for example on the number **144**. In everyday life, however, the rule is: you only get the lower premium if you keep to the **agreements**. Anyone who repeatedly ignores them risks the insurer reducing payments or moving them into the standard model. Some exceptions, for example for certain specialists, are set out in each insurer’s conditions.

gewusst: The services of basic insurance are the same at all health insurers in Switzerland, no matter which model you choose.
You can change the model with effect from the start of each new year.

teile.einleitung: In online shopping you buy goods over the internet, for example with a computer or a mobile phone. The goods are then usually delivered to your home by post. This is convenient, but you should know a few rules so as not to be cheated.
wichtigste: In online shopping you order goods over the internet.
You can recognise a secure connection by “https” and a padlock symbol in the address bar.
Phishing means fake messages that fraudsters use to try to get passwords.
Before ordering from an unknown shop, you check the legal notice and other customers’ reviews.
In Switzerland there is no general right of return; what the shop sets out in its terms and conditions applies.
When buying on invoice, you get the goods first and pay afterwards.
When comparing prices, you must also include delivery costs.

abschnitte.text: In **online shopping** you visit a shop on the internet, a so-called **online shop**. You put items into a virtual shopping basket, enter your address and pay. Well-known shops in Switzerland are, for example, Galaxus and Digitec, but Migros and Coop also sell online. Worldwide, Amazon, founded in the USA in 1994, is one of the largest online retailers.

You can pay online in various ways, for example by credit card, debit card, **TWINT** or on invoice. When **buying on invoice**, you get the goods first and pay afterwards, usually within 30 days. Many banks require confirmation in an app for card payments, so that nobody can shop with stolen details. Children and young people should always discuss bigger purchases with their parents.

You can recognise a secure connection by the address beginning with **https** and a padlock being shown. Before ordering from an unknown shop, check the **legal notice** (Impressum) with the company name and address. Reviews from other customers also help. If an offer is far too cheap, there is often a fake shop behind it.

In **phishing**, fraudsters send fake emails or text messages that look as if they come from the Post, a bank or a shop. They want you to click on a link and enter passwords or card details. Real companies never ask for your password by email. If in doubt, type the shop’s address in yourself and do not click on the link.

In Switzerland there is **no legal right to return** faultless goods bought online. What the shop sets out in its general terms and conditions applies, although many shops still allow returns within 14 or 30 days. If the goods are broken or faulty, however, you are entitled to a **guarantee**. With orders from abroad, VAT and fees may also have to be paid.

Online you can compare prices easily, for example with comparison websites. What matters is the total price including **delivery costs**. If headphones cost 49 francs plus 7 francs delivery in shop A, that is 56 francs, and 54 francs with no delivery charge in shop B, you save 2 francs at shop B. If you order several things together, you often save on delivery costs and help the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shop on the internet.
A sign of an encrypted, secure connection.
Fraud with fake messages to get hold of passwords.
Information on who is behind a website, with name and address.
The general terms and conditions, the shop’s rules.

gewusst: The word phishing is a variation of the English “fishing”, because fraudsters fish for data.
Parcel deliveries in Switzerland have increased greatly because of online shopping, especially before Christmas.
Many returned items are not sold again but thrown away, so it is worth thinking carefully before you order.

teile.einleitung: Supply and demand are the two forces that set prices in a market. If many people want to buy something that is scarce, it becomes expensive, but if there is a lot of it, it becomes cheap.
wichtigste: Supply is the amount of a product that sellers want to sell at a particular price.
Demand is the amount that buyers want to buy at a particular price.
If demand rises while supply stays the same, the price normally rises.
If there is a great deal of a product, for example strawberries in summer, the price falls.
At the equilibrium price, the amount supplied and the amount demanded are the same.
In a monopoly there is only one single supplier.
Strong competition usually brings customers lower prices and more choice.

abschnitte.text: A **market** is any place where buyers and sellers come together. It can be a weekly market on the village square, a supermarket or an online shop. The sellers make up the **supply**, the buyers the **demand**. In the market, people work out at what price how much is sold.

If a price is high, many suppliers want to sell, but few customers want to buy. If the price is low, many want to buy, but few want to sell. Somewhere in between lies the **equilibrium price**, at which both amounts are the same. In diagrams, this is drawn as a rising **supply curve** and a falling demand curve, which cross at one point.

In June there are lots of local **strawberries** at Swiss markets, which is why they are cheap then. In winter, strawberries have to come from far away and cost more. At a concert by a global star, many more fans want tickets than there are seats, so they sell out quickly and are expensive. Hotel rooms during the ski holidays also cost more, because many people want to go away at the same time.

When many companies sell the same thing, there is **competition**. Each company then tries to win customers with low prices or better quality. If there is only one single supplier, this is called a **monopoly**. A monopolist can keep prices high more easily, because customers cannot go elsewhere. When a few large companies share a market, this is called an **oligopoly**.

In Switzerland, the **Competition Commission** makes sure that companies do not make illegal agreements on prices. The **Price Supervisor** checks prices in areas with little competition, for example electricity, water or public transport. The state also sets or influences some prices itself. This is meant to prevent customers from paying too much.

In 1776, the Scottish thinker **Adam Smith** described how markets work in his book “The Wealth of Nations”. He spoke of an “invisible hand” that balances supply and demand. Later, the British economist Alfred Marshall drew the well-known curves that cross like a pair of scissors. To this day, supply and demand are among the most important ideas in **economics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where goods are bought and sold.
The price at which the amount supplied equals the amount demanded.
A market with only one single supplier.
Rivalry between several suppliers for customers.

gewusst: On the stock exchange, prices sometimes change several times a second because of supply and demand.
With trading cards or rare trainers, scarce items can cost many times their original price.
Adam Smith’s term “invisible hand” is over 250 years old and is still often quoted.

teile.einleitung: A stock exchange is a marketplace where shares, bonds and other securities are traded. The Swiss stock exchange is called SIX Swiss Exchange and is in Zurich.
wichtigste: Securities such as shares and bonds are bought and sold on the stock exchange.
The Swiss stock exchange SIX Swiss Exchange is in Zurich.
The Swiss Market Index (SMI) includes 20 large Swiss companies (as of 2026).
The Dow Jones Industrial Average in the USA contains 30 companies.
A bull market is a period of prices rising steadily.
In an IPO, a company goes on the stock exchange for the first time.
From 1602, shares of the Dutch East India Company were traded in Amsterdam.

abschnitte.text: A **stock exchange** is an organised market for securities, raw materials or currencies. Buyers and sellers meet here so that trading happens quickly and fairly. The price of a security is called its **share price** and comes about through supply and demand. Private individuals do not trade directly on the stock exchange, but give their order to a bank or an online broker.

Exchanges already existed in the Middle Ages in trading cities such as Bruges and Antwerp. From 1602, shares of the **Dutch East India Company**, VOC for short, were traded in Amsterdam; it is considered one of the first public companies. In the past, traders shouted prices to each other on the trading floor. Today trading happens almost entirely electronically by computer.

The **SIX Swiss Exchange** in Zurich is the most important stock exchange in Switzerland. In the 1990s it was one of the first exchanges in the world to switch completely to electronic trading. The best-known Swiss share index is the **SMI**, the Swiss Market Index. It contains the 20 largest and most traded Swiss companies, including Nestlé, Novartis, Roche and UBS.

An **index** shows how a group of shares develops on average. The Dow Jones Industrial Average from the USA contains 30 large American companies and is one of the oldest indices in the world. Other well-known indices are the German DAX and the S&P 500. If an index rises, most of the shares in it have become more expensive.

When prices rise over a long time, people speak of a **bull market**, because a bull thrusts upwards with its horns. When prices keep falling, it is called a **bear market**, because a bear strikes downwards with its paw. That is why there are statues of a bull and a bear in front of the Frankfurt stock exchange. Sharp falls in prices are called a stock market crash, as in 1929 or 2008.

If you want to buy a share, you place an instruction, a so-called **order**. With a limit order you set a maximum price, and the order is only carried out up to this price. When a company goes on the stock exchange for the first time, this is called an **IPO**, an Initial Public Offering. The company sells new shares to investors and in this way gets money for its growth.

begriffe.erklaerung: The current price of a security on the stock exchange.
A figure that shows how a group of shares is developing.
A period of prices rising for a long time.
A company’s first listing on the stock exchange.

gewusst: The German word for stock exchange, Börse, is said to come from the van der Beurse merchant family in Bruges, in front of whose house traders met.
The Dow Jones was first calculated in 1896 and at that time contained only 12 companies.
Today computers at large stock exchanges carry out thousands of trades per second.

teile.einleitung: An occupation is the work a person has learned and earns their money with. In Switzerland there are hundreds of occupations, from baker to pilot to IT specialist, and many of them are learned through an apprenticeship.
wichtigste: An occupation is an activity that you have learned and that you earn money with.
The baker bakes bread and croissants.
The vet helps sick animals.
The postman delivers letters and parcels.
The fire brigade puts out fires, the carpenter builds furniture out of wood.
The hairdresser cuts hair and the pilot flies aeroplanes.
Many young people in Switzerland do an apprenticeship after school.

abschnitte.text: An **occupation** is work for which you have learned special knowledge and skills. The baker knows how to knead dough and bake bread and croissants. The vet studied for a long time to treat sick animals. With their occupation, people earn money and do something for society.

There are **trades** such as carpenter, bricklayer or electrician. In healthcare, nurses, doctors and physiotherapists work. In the service sector there are, for example, the hairdresser, the postman or the office clerk. The pilot flies aeroplanes, and in the **fire brigade** professionals and volunteers put out fires.

In Switzerland, about two thirds of young people do an **apprenticeship**, also called vocational training, after compulsory school. They work three or four days a week at a company and attend vocational school for one or two days. This system is called **dual vocational education**. At the end there is a Federal Certificate of Proficiency, EFZ for short, or for two-year apprenticeships a Federal Vocational Certificate, EBA for short.

From year 7 or 8 onwards, pupils start thinking about **choosing a career**. During a **taster apprenticeship** you can work at a company for a few days and get to know the job. Careers advice services in every canton help with tests and interviews. The website berufsberatung.ch presents all the occupations in Switzerland.

Education does not end after the apprenticeship. With the **vocational baccalaureate** you can study at a university of applied sciences. You can also attend a college of higher education or take a master craftsman’s exam. Other young people go to grammar school (Gymnasium) and then study at a university, for example medicine, to become a vet or a doctor.

In the past there were occupations such as charcoal burner, rope maker or telephone operator, which have almost disappeared today. Instead, new occupations appear, such as IT specialist, mediamatician or experts in renewable energy. Today many people also change their occupation at some point in their lives. Almost all occupations are now open equally to women and men.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vocational training at a company and at a vocational school.
Young people doing an apprenticeship; in German they used to be called “Lehrlinge”.
A few days at a company to try out an occupation.
The Federal Certificate of Proficiency that you receive after an apprenticeship.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can learn around 250 different occupations through an apprenticeship.
Commercial employee has been the most popular apprenticeship in Switzerland for many years.
Swiss apprentices regularly win many medals at the world skills championships, the WorldSkills.

teile.einleitung: Countries trade with each other. Often they charge customs duties on imported goods. With a free trade agreement, countries agree to reduce these duties and other barriers.
wichtigste: A free trade agreement is a treaty between countries.
It reduces customs duties and other trade barriers.
This makes exports and imports easier.
Switzerland has a free trade agreement with the EU from 1972.
Together with EFTA, Switzerland has many other agreements.
Free trade agreements are sometimes politically controversial.

abschnitte.text: A **customs duty** is a charge paid when goods are imported across the border. Customs duties make foreign products more expensive. Besides customs duties there are other **trade barriers**, for example different regulations or limits on quantities. They make trade between countries harder. In a **free trade agreement**, countries agree to lower or remove such barriers.

Without customs duties, companies can sell their goods abroad more easily. This helps the **export industry**. For consumers, imported goods can become cheaper. Switzerland is a small country and earns a lot of money abroad. That is why such agreements are especially important for it.

In 1960 Switzerland was one of the founding members of **EFTA**, the European Free Trade Association. In 1972 it concluded a **free trade agreement** for industrial goods with what is now the EU. Today Switzerland has a large network of agreements, many of them together with the other EFTA states. It has a well-known agreement of its own with **China**, which has been in force since 2014.

Not everyone judges free trade agreements in the same way. Supporters stress that they protect jobs in export companies and make goods cheaper. Critics fear that local farmers or businesses will come under pressure. Some also call for stricter rules on the environment and working conditions. In Switzerland, such agreements can sometimes even be put to a popular vote.

gewusst: Agricultural products are only partly included in many of Switzerland’s free trade agreements, in order to protect local farmers.
In 2021 the Swiss people voted on a free trade agreement with Indonesia and accepted it.

teile.einleitung: The insurance card is a plastic card the size of a credit card that you receive from your health insurer. You show it at the doctor’s, in hospital or at the pharmacy so that the costs can be billed to the health insurer. Since 2010, every person with basic insurance in Switzerland has had one.
wichtigste: Every person with basic insurance receives an insurance card from their health insurer.
The card shows, among other things, your name, date of birth, AVS number and health insurer.
You show it at the doctor’s, in hospital and at the pharmacy.
With the card, the pharmacy can bill the health insurer directly.
On the back is the European Health Insurance Card.
When you change health insurer, you get a new card.
You should always carry the card in your purse or wallet.

abschnitte.text: The front shows your name and date of birth. Added to this are the **AVS number**, which begins with 756, and the name of the health insurer. Each card also has its own card number and an expiry date. There is no photo on the Swiss insurance card. The card is only valid for the person whose name is on it.

At the doctor’s or the pharmacy you show your **insurance card** so that it is clear which health insurer you are insured with. The pharmacy can then bill medicines directly to the health insurer. This procedure is called **tiers payant**, which means “the third party pays”. With doctors’ bills, the tiers garant system is often used, in which you receive the bill and submit it to the health insurer. Without the card, you may have to pay for a medicine yourself first.

On the back of the Swiss insurance card, the **European Health Insurance Card** is printed. It is valid in the countries of the EU as well as in Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway. Anyone who falls ill there on holiday is treated like a local person with it. Even so, there can be costs that basic insurance does not cover, such as transport back to Switzerland. That is why many people also have travel insurance.

The insurance card belongs only to you and must not be passed on to others. If you lose it, you report this to the health insurer and get a new one. When you **change health insurer**, the new insurer sends you a new card. You should then cut up the old card and throw it away. Children also have their own card, which is usually kept by their parents.

In the past, every health insurer had its own ID cards. In 2010, the uniform **insurance card** was introduced for all insured people in Switzerland. It is the same size as a bank card. Since then, doctors’ surgeries, hospitals and pharmacies have been able to read the information in the same way. This is meant to avoid billing errors and save work.

begriffe.erklaerung: Health insurer’s card that shows where you are insured.
Personal social insurance number, which in Switzerland begins with 756.
Billing in which the pharmacy or hospital bills the health insurer directly.
Card with which you are treated in Europe if you fall ill.

gewusst: The number 756 at the start of the AVS number is Switzerland’s international numeric code.
The card is about 8.6 by 5.4 centimetres, exactly like a bank card.

teile.einleitung: Swiss Post delivers letters and parcels to everyone in Switzerland. The yellow PostBuses and the bank PostFinance also belong to it. Swiss Post is wholly owned by the Confederation and is one of the largest employers in the country.
wichtigste: Swiss Post delivers letters and parcels all over Switzerland.
Swiss Post belongs to the Confederation.
The PostBuses are yellow and also travel to remote mountain villages.
Swiss Post was founded in 1849 as the federal post.
PostBus, PostFinance and PostLogistics also belong to Swiss Post.
Swiss Post’s headquarters is in Bern.

abschnitte.text: Every day **Swiss Post** delivers millions of letters and hundreds of thousands of parcels to people. It must make sure that everyone in Switzerland can receive letters and parcels, even in remote mountain valleys. This is called the **universal service**. Swiss Post employs around 45,000 people (as of 2024) and has its headquarters in Bern.

In the past, many cantons had their own postal service. With the new federal state, the Confederation took over the post for the whole of Switzerland in 1849. For a long time, post, telephone and telegraph together formed the **PTT**. In 1998 they were separated, and Swiss Post and the telephone company Swisscom were created.

**PostBus** is part of Swiss Post and the largest bus company in Switzerland. The yellow buses run on over a thousand routes, often over passes and to mountain villages. Their typical three-tone horn plays a tune from the overture to the opera “William Tell” by Gioachino Rossini. In the past, the PostBuses brought the post to the villages as well as passengers.

**PostFinance**, where many people have an account, also belongs to Swiss Post. With it you can pay bills, save money and use cards. This service used to be called Postcheck. PostFinance is one of the most important financial institutions for payments in Switzerland.

Because people write more emails and messages, Swiss Post sends fewer and fewer letters. But because of online shopping, more and more parcels are sent. In large **parcel centres** such as Härkingen in the canton of Solothurn, they are sorted by machines. Since 1991 Switzerland has had faster A-Post and cheaper B-Post.

Swiss Post is a public limited company wholly owned by the **Confederation**. The Federal Council sets the goals it must reach. In the Postal Act, Parliament decides which services Swiss Post must offer everywhere. Because many post offices are hardly used any more, some are replaced by branches in village shops.

begriffe.erklaerung: Services that must be offered to everyone everywhere in the country at fair prices.
The former organisation for post, telephone and telegraph.
A small picture to stick on, with which you pay the postage for a letter.
A large hall where parcels are sorted automatically.

gewusst: In 1843 the canton of Zurich was the second place in the world, after Great Britain, to issue postage stamps.
On narrow mountain roads, the PostBuses’ three-tone horn warns oncoming traffic before the next bend.
Swiss Post uses many electric scooters to deliver letters especially quietly and in a climate-friendly way.

teile.einleitung: Tox Info Suisse is the Swiss advice centre for poisoning. On the number 145, experts help around the clock. They tell you what to do if someone has swallowed or touched something poisonous.
wichtigste: You can reach Tox Info Suisse on the number 145.
Advice is available day and night.
Experts tell you whether you need to do anything and what.
If someone is having trouble breathing or is unconscious, call 144 straight away.
You should not make a child vomit unless the experts say so.
Cleaning products and medicines belong out of children’s reach.

abschnitte.text: If a child has swallowed something poisonous, first call **145**. **Tox Info Suisse** answers. Doctors and experts ask what has happened. They want to know exactly what was swallowed, how much and when. Then they say whether you can stay at home or need to go to the doctor.

Sometimes poisoning is very dangerous. If the child is having trouble **breathing**, no longer responds or is **unconscious**, call **144** straight away. That is the number for the ambulance service. The same applies in case of fits. The rescue service will then come as quickly as possible.

Many enquiries concern small children. They like putting things in their mouths. Often it is about **medicines**, **cleaning products**, plants or cosmetics. You can also call Tox Info about **mushrooms** and animal bites. Fortunately, in most cases things turn out well.

It is important to stay calm. You should **not make a child vomit** unless the experts say so. Some substances cause even more damage when vomited up. Keep the **packaging** of the product so that you can say exactly what it is on the phone. You can carefully rinse out the mouth.

It is best if poisoning never happens in the first place. Medicines and cleaning products belong **high up** or in a locked cupboard. Never pour cleaning products into drinks bottles. Warning symbols on the packaging show which products are dangerous.

gewusst: Tox Info Suisse is based in Zurich and has been giving advice since the 1960s.
Advice on the number 145 is free, you only pay the cost of the call.

teile.einleitung: Digitec Galaxus is the largest online retailer in Switzerland. On the internet the company sells millions of different products, from computers and mobile phones to toys, clothes and food. The majority of the company belongs to Migros.
wichtigste: Digitec Galaxus sells products over the internet.
The company is the largest online retailer in Switzerland.
Digitec was founded in Zurich in 2001.
Galaxus was added in 2012 as an online department store for almost all products.
Migros owns the majority of Digitec Galaxus.
Digitec Galaxus is also active in Germany and other European countries.

abschnitte.text: **Digitec Galaxus** is an online shop with two parts. **Digitec** mainly sells electronics such as computers, mobile phones, televisions and games consoles. **Galaxus** is a department store on the internet that sells almost everything, from household appliances and toys to sports equipment. Customers order online and receive the goods at home in a parcel or collect them from a branch.

In 2001 three young men founded the company Digitec in Zurich, at first to sell computer parts. One of the founders was Marcel Dobler, who later became a member of the National Council. The business grew quickly, and in 2012 the Galaxus shop was added. In the same year **Migros** came in as the majority shareholder.

So that parcels arrive quickly, Digitec Galaxus has a large **logistics centre** in Wohlen in the canton of Aargau. Hundreds of thousands of products are stored there on shelves. Staff and machines collect the items ordered and pack them. Many orders placed by the evening are delivered the very next day.

On the Digitec Galaxus pages, customers can **review** products and ask questions. Other buyers and experts answer them. The company also writes its own test reports and guides. In addition, for many products it shows how often they had to be sent back or repaired.

More and more people shop on the internet, especially since the coronavirus crisis of 2020. Digitec Galaxus competes with large foreign sellers such as Amazon, Zalando or Temu. For some years Galaxus has also been active in Germany, Austria and other countries. But **online shopping** also has disadvantages, such as a lot of packaging and many delivery journeys.

begriffe.erklaerung: Goods are ordered over the internet and delivered to your home.
Everything needed so that goods arrive in the right place: storing, packing, transporting.
Someone who owns more than half of a company and can therefore have a say.
A shop that sells very many different kinds of products.

gewusst: The name Galaxus is reminiscent of the word galaxy and is meant to show how huge the range is.
At Digitec Galaxus you can choose from several million products.
The company is known for its funny and often cheeky product descriptions.

teile.einleitung: Interest is the price of borrowed money. If you lend money, you receive interest for it, and if you borrow money, you have to pay interest. Interest plays an important role in saving, in buying a house and for the whole economy.
wichtigste: Interest is the price you pay for borrowed money.
If you put money into a savings account, the bank pays you interest.
500 francs at 2 per cent interest earn 10 francs in interest after one year.
With compound interest, earlier interest also earns interest.
At 5 per cent interest, 1000 francs grow to 1102.50 francs in 2 years.
In Switzerland, the Swiss National Bank sets the policy interest rate.

abschnitte.text: If you lend a friend 10 francs, you cannot use it yourself for a week. **Interest** is a reward for doing without your money. At the same time it makes up for the risk that you might not get the money back. Interest is usually given as a **percentage** per year.

If Jan invests 500 francs at 2 per cent interest, you calculate 500 times 2 divided by 100. So after one year he receives 10 francs in interest. If the interest stays in the account, it earns interest too the following year; this is **compound interest**. In this way, 1000 francs at 5 per cent become 1102.50 francs after two years.

If you pay money into a **savings account**, you are really lending it to the bank. The bank pays the account holder interest for this. The bank lends the money on, for example as a **loan** to a company or as a mortgage for a house. For these loans it charges higher interest, and the bank lives on the difference.

The **Swiss National Bank** (SNB) sets the policy interest rate. It influences how much interest banks charge for loans and pay on savings accounts. If the SNB lowers the policy rate, loans become cheaper and the economy gets a boost. If it raises it, it slows down rising prices, so-called inflation.

From 2015 to 2022 the policy rate in Switzerland was negative, namely minus 0.75 per cent. This meant that banks had to pay something for money held at the National Bank. The SNB wanted to prevent the franc from becoming too strong. During this time there was almost no interest at all for savers.

Interest already existed over 4000 years ago in Mesopotamia, where grain was lent in return for interest. In the Middle Ages the Church long forbade Christians to charge interest. In Islam too, charging interest is forbidden according to tradition, which is why there are special banking models there. Today interest is a completely normal part of the economy in most countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much interest you receive or pay as a percentage per year.
Money that you borrow and must pay back later with interest.
The most important interest rate of a country, set by the national bank.
An unfairly high interest rate, which is forbidden in Switzerland.

gewusst: In Switzerland, small consumer loans have a maximum interest rate of 10 per cent, and credit cards 12 per cent a year.
The German word Zins comes from the Latin “census”, which means a charge or an assessment.
During the period of negative interest rates, some companies kept large amounts of cash in safes instead of taking it to the bank.

teile.einleitung: Holcim is a Swiss company and one of the largest makers of building materials in the world. Its most important product is cement, without which you could not make concrete for houses, bridges and tunnels. The company began over a hundred years ago in a small village in Aargau.
wichtigste: Holcim mainly produces cement, concrete and gravel.
The company was founded in 1912 in Holderbank in the canton of Aargau.
The name Holcim is made up of Holderbank and Ciment.
In 2015 Holcim merged with the French company Lafarge.
In 2025 Holcim split off its North American business; the new company is called Amrize.
Its headquarters is in Zug.
Making cement produces a lot of CO2, so Holcim is looking for more environmentally friendly methods.

abschnitte.text: **Cement** is a grey powder that serves as a binding agent. If you mix it with water, sand and gravel, you get **concrete**, which becomes rock hard after a while. To make cement, limestone and marl or clay are ground and burned in a huge rotary kiln at about 1450 degrees. This produces lumps called **clinker**, which are then finely ground.

In 1912 a cement factory was founded in the village of Holderbank in Aargau. Over many decades, the **Schmidheiny** business family built the company up into a worldwide group. For a long time the company was simply called Holderbank; it only got the name Holcim in 2001. Today its headquarters is in Zug.

In 2015 Holcim merged with the French company **Lafarge** to form LafargeHolcim. In 2021 the name was shortened back to Holcim. In 2025 Holcim separated off its large business in the USA and Canada. This became the independent company **Amrize**, which is also listed on the stock exchange.

Holcim runs several cement works in Switzerland, for example in Eclépens in the canton of Vaud and in Untervaz in the Grisons. There are also many gravel pits and concrete plants. Swiss cement is in dams, motorway bridges and tunnels. Huge amounts of concrete are also needed for large structures such as railway tunnels.

Making cement produces a great deal of **carbon dioxide**, that is, CO2. Worldwide, the cement industry causes a large share of greenhouse gases, according to estimates about seven to eight per cent. Holcim is trying to emit less CO2 by recycling old concrete and using new types of cement. In this way, rubble from demolished houses becomes new building material again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A grey powder that hardens with water and holds sand and gravel together.
A mixture of cement, water, sand and gravel that becomes rock hard.
Burned lumps of lime and clay from which cement is ground.
When two companies join together to form a single one.

gewusst: After water, concrete is the most used material in the world.
The name Holcim contains the village of Holderbank and the French word “ciment” for cement.

teile.einleitung: The financial market is the general term for all markets where money, securities and financial products are traded. This is where people who want to invest money meet those who need money, for example companies and states.
wichtigste: Money, shares, bonds, foreign currencies and derivatives are traded on the financial market.
Short-term capital up to about one year is traded on the money market, long-term capital on the capital market.
New securities are issued for the first time on the primary market.
In Switzerland, FINMA supervises banks, insurance companies and stock exchanges.
A call option gives the right to buy an underlying asset at a fixed price.
Diversification lowers risk by spreading money across many investments.
Return, security and liquidity form the magic triangle of investing.

abschnitte.text: The **financial market** connects people who have money to spare with those who need money. Savers, pension funds and insurance companies invest their money there.
