Companies and states raise money, for example through shares or bonds. Trading takes place on stock exchanges, but also directly between banks.

A distinction is made by length of time. On the **money market**, money is lent for a short time up to about one year, for example between banks overnight. The **capital market** is about long-term money, for example shares and bonds that run for many years. There is also the **foreign exchange market**, where currencies such as francs, euros and dollars are exchanged.

On the **primary market**, new securities are issued for the first time, for example when a company goes public. The money flows directly to the company or the state. After that, the securities are sold on between investors on the **secondary market**, usually on the stock exchange. This way an investor can sell their shares again at any time.

**Derivatives** are financial products whose value depends on another value, the underlying asset. A call option gives its buyer the right to buy an underlying asset at a fixed price. In **short selling**, you sell borrowed shares and buy them back more cheaply later, so you earn money from falling prices. Such deals are risky and more something for experts.

Since 2009 the **Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority FINMA** in Bern has supervised banks, insurance companies, stock exchanges and funds. It is meant to protect investors and make sure the financial centre stays stable. The Swiss National Bank also controls interest rates and the money supply. The financial crisis of 2008 showed how important good supervision is, because many banks around the world got into difficulty at the time.

Anyone who invests money has three goals that get in each other’s way: **return**, security and **liquidity**, meaning how quickly the money is available. That is why people speak of the magic triangle, because all three goals cannot be reached at once. A savings account is safe and liquid but brings little return; shares bring more in the long term but go up and down a lot. With **diversification**, spreading money across many different investments, risk can be reduced.

begriffe.erklaerung: A market for long-term investments such as shares and bonds.
The authority that supervises banks, insurance companies and stock exchanges in Switzerland.
A financial product whose value depends on another value.
How quickly you can turn an investment into cash.
Spreading money across many different investments.

gewusst: Currencies worth several trillion dollars are traded every day on the worldwide foreign exchange market.
The saying “Don’t put all your eggs in one basket” describes exactly the idea of diversification.
Switzerland is one of the largest centres in the world for managing wealth from abroad.

teile.einleitung: Omega is a famous Swiss watch brand from Biel. An Omega watch was there at the first Moon landing in 1969, and Omega keeps time at the Olympic Games. Today the company belongs to the Swatch Group.
wichtigste: Omega is a Swiss watch brand based in Biel in the canton of Bern.
The company goes back to a workshop that Louis Brandt founded in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1848.
The name Omega comes from the last letter of the Greek alphabet.
In 1969 the Omega Speedmaster travelled to the Moon with the astronauts of Apollo 11.
Since 1932 Omega has repeatedly timed events at the Olympic Games.
Omega belongs to the Swatch Group, the largest watch group in Switzerland.
The film agent James Bond also wears an Omega in many films.

abschnitte.text: In 1848 **Louis Brandt** began assembling pocket watches in La Chaux-de-Fonds in the Neuchâtel Jura. In 1880 his sons moved the company to **Biel**, where they made watches in a factory. In 1894 they developed a particularly good movement, which they called Omega. Because it was so successful, Omega later became the name of the whole company.

Omega is the last letter of the **Greek alphabet** and is written like this: Ω. The letter stands for completion, that is, something that is entirely finished and perfect. It can still be seen on every Omega watch today. In physics, the sign Ω is also used for the unit ohm.

In the 1960s the American space agency **NASA** tested various watches under extreme conditions. The Omega **Speedmaster** passed all the tests and was chosen for the astronauts. In 1969 Buzz Aldrin wore his Speedmaster during the first Moon landing with Apollo 11. Since then it has often been called the “Moonwatch”.

In 1932 Omega took over the **timekeeping** at the Olympic Games in Los Angeles for the first time. Since then Omega has been the official timekeeper at a great many Olympic Games. Today Omega measures to a thousandth of a second with light barriers, electronic starting pistols and cameras. This makes it possible to decide the winner even in very close races.

Since the founding of the **Swatch Group** in the 1980s, Omega has belonged to this large watch group. The watches are made in Biel and are considered luxury watches. Besides the Speedmaster, well-known models are the Seamaster and the Constellation. In the James Bond films, the secret agent has mostly worn a Seamaster since 1995.

begriffe.erklaerung: The inner workings of a watch, which move the hands.
A watch with a built-in stopwatch.
Measuring exactly how long something takes, for example a race.
The sequence of all the letters of a writing system.

gewusst: The Speedmaster is a mechanical watch that is wound by hand, and yet it worked on the Moon.
On Apollo 13 a Speedmaster helped the astronauts to time an important engine burn exactly.

teile.einleitung: On is a young Swiss company from Zurich that makes running shoes and sportswear. Its shoes can be recognised by the small hollow pods in the sole, called CloudTec. The tennis star Roger Federer also has a stake in the company.
wichtigste: On makes running shoes, sports shoes and sportswear.
The company was founded in Zurich in 2010.
Its founders are Olivier Bernhard, David Allemann and Caspar Coppetti.
The special sole technology is called CloudTec.
Roger Federer has had a stake in On since 2019 and has helped develop shoes.
Since 2021 On shares have been traded on the stock exchange in New York.

abschnitte.text: On develops **running shoes**, hiking boots, tennis shoes and sportswear. The shoes are popular in many countries, not only for sport but also in everyday life. They are mainly made in Asia, but designed in Zurich. Within a few years On has become a brand known all over the world.

On’s sole is made of many small **hollow pods** that look like little tubes. When your foot lands, they squash together and cushion the step. When you push off, they become firm again so that you can build up momentum. This technology is called **CloudTec**, because running is meant to feel like running on clouds.

The former professional triathlete **Olivier Bernhard** worked on a new running shoe together with an engineer. He made his first experiments with pieces of garden hose that he glued under shoes. In 2010 he founded the company On in Zurich with his friends David Allemann and Caspar Coppetti. Their shoes soon won prizes.

In 2019 the tennis star **Roger Federer** became a partner in On. He helped to develop his own tennis shoes and leisure shoes. Through him the brand became even better known all over the world. Many runners at the Olympic Games also wear shoes from On.

On is researching shoes that you give back after use so that they can be recycled. For this there is a **subscription** model called Cyclon. The company is also testing materials made from exhaust gases or plants. In 2021 On went public on the **stock exchange** in New York and today it is worth several billion francs.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that absorbs an impact so that it is less hard.
The underside of a shoe that touches the ground.
Someone who owns part of a company.
A marketplace where shares in companies are bought and sold.

gewusst: The first prototype of an On shoe had pieces of garden hose on the sole.
Roger Federer is not just an advertising face but a co-owner of On.

teile.einleitung: Banknotes are a country’s paper money; in Switzerland they come in values from 10 to 1000 francs. They are issued by the Swiss National Bank and protected against forgery by many clever security features.
wichtigste: Banknotes are made of special paper.
In Switzerland, the National Bank issues the banknotes.
The smallest Swiss banknote is the 10-franc note, the largest is the 1000-franc note.
The 10 note is yellow, the 20 red, the 50 green and the 100 blue.
There are also the brown 200 note and the purple 1000 note.
The current series was introduced between 2016 and 2019.
Many security features protect the notes against forgery.

abschnitte.text: A **banknote** is a note of money that you use to pay. Together with coins it makes up **cash**. A banknote is really just printed paper, but it has a value because everyone trusts it. In Switzerland only the Swiss **National Bank** may issue banknotes, while coins are minted by the Federal Mint Swissmint in Bern.

Switzerland has six banknotes: 10 francs in yellow, 20 francs in red, 50 francs in green, 100 francs in blue, 200 francs in brown and 1000 francs in purple. Each note is a different size: the higher the value, the longer the note. This means that people with a visual impairment can also tell the notes apart. The **1000-franc note** is one of the most valuable banknotes in the world.

The ninth banknote series was introduced from 2016 to 2019, starting with the 50 note. Its theme is “The many facets of Switzerland”. Each note shows one characteristic of the country, for example the 10 note its organisational side, the 50 note its experiential side and the 100 note its humanitarian side. On all the notes you can see a **hand** and a globe, which moves from note to note.

So that nobody can forge the notes, they have many **security features**. When you move a note, pictures and colours change their appearance, and a globe moves across the note. Held up to the light, a Swiss cross shines through the paper. Under UV light hidden patterns glow, and some areas can be felt with your fingers.

Banknotes are made of **special paper**, not ordinary paper. The new Swiss notes consist of several layers: cotton paper on the outside and a plastic layer in the middle. This makes them tougher and they last longer. The Swiss notes are printed by the company Orell Füssli in Zurich.

The first paper money appeared around 1000 years ago in **China**. In Europe, banknotes came into use in the 17th century, for example in Sweden. In Switzerland, various banks used to issue their own notes until the National Bank started its work in 1907. Since 2021 none of the old notes of the eighth series are valid any more, but you can exchange them at the National Bank with no time limit.

begriffe.erklaerung: A note of money made of special paper.
The state’s bank, which issues the money and keeps the franc stable.
Coins and banknotes that you hold in your hand.
A picture in the paper that you can only see when you hold it up to the light.

gewusst: In 2016 the new 50-franc note was voted the most beautiful banknote of the year by collectors.
Switzerland is one of the few countries with a 1000 note, which is worth much more than the largest euro note of 200 euros.
Swiss banknotes no longer show portraits of famous people, but hands and images from Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Mammut is a Swiss company that makes equipment for mountaineering, climbing and hiking. It all began in 1862 with ropes. Its logo shows a mammoth, the Ice Age animal with long tusks.
wichtigste: Mammut makes equipment for mountain sports and outdoor activities.
The company was founded in the canton of Aargau in 1862.
At the beginning Mammut made ropes.
A mammoth can be seen in the logo.
It is based in Seon in the canton of Aargau.
Today Mammut sells climbing ropes, jackets, rucksacks and avalanche transceivers.

abschnitte.text: Mammut makes **climbing ropes**, climbing harnesses, helmets, rucksacks, jackets and shoes. The products are meant for people who hike, climb or go ski touring in the mountains. They also include equipment for safety in avalanches. Mammut products are sold in many countries.

In 1862 Kaspar Tanner founded a **rope works** in Dintikon in Aargau. At that time he made ropes for farmers and craftsmen. Later the ropes were also used by mountaineers. Over time Mammut became one of the best-known brands of climbing ropes in the world.

The name and the logo are a reminder of the **mammoth**, an extinct animal from the Ice Age. The woolly mammoth was related to elephants and had thick fur and long, curved tusks. The animal stands for strength and endurance in cold and snow. Mammut’s products are meant to have exactly these qualities too.

Mammut also makes devices for emergencies, for example an **avalanche transceiver** called Barryvox. With it, people buried under an avalanche can be found more quickly. There are also avalanche rucksacks with an airbag. Such devices save lives in the Alps every year.

Mammut’s headquarters is in **Seon** in the canton of Aargau. For a long time Mammut belonged to the Swiss group of companies Conzzeta. In 2021 Mammut was sold to an investment company. The company supports professional mountaineers and expeditions all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A business where ropes are made.
A stretchy rope that catches climbers if they fall.
A radio device used to find people buried under snow.
Meaning outside; it refers to activities in nature.

gewusst: A climbing rope is stretchy so that it slows a fall gently.
The woolly mammoth shown in the logo died out several thousand years ago, whereas the company has existed for over 160 years.

teile.einleitung: A currency is the money used to pay in a country. In Switzerland it is the Swiss franc, in many European countries the euro. Each currency has its own name, its own coins and banknotes and a three-letter code.
wichtigste: A currency is the official means of payment of a country or a group of countries.
Switzerland’s currency is the Swiss franc, with the code CHF.
The “CH” in CHF stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name of Switzerland.
One franc has 100 centimes.
The Principality of Liechtenstein also pays with the Swiss franc.
The euro has been in circulation as cash since 2002.
The USA uses the US dollar, Japan the yen.

abschnitte.text: In 1850 the franc became the common currency of the whole of Switzerland. Before that, many cantons had their own money, which made shopping complicated. Today the **Swiss National Bank** (SNB) issues the banknotes. The coins are minted by the federal mint **Swissmint** in Bern.

In Switzerland there are coins of 5, 10 and 20 centimes and of half a franc, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The banknotes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. The current **banknote series** was introduced between 2016 and 2019 and shows themes such as time, light or language. Banknotes have many security features so that they are very hard to forge.

There are about 180 different currencies in the world. Well-known examples are the **US dollar** in the USA, the yen in Japan, the pound sterling in Great Britain and the yuan in China. The US dollar is the most important currency in world trade, for example for oil. Each currency has an international three-letter code, such as USD, JPY or EUR.

The **euro** was introduced in 1999, at first only for transfers and bookkeeping. Since 1 January 2002 there have been euro coins and euro banknotes. Today people pay with the euro in around 20 countries of the European Union, for example in Germany, France, Italy and Austria. Switzerland does not belong to the EU and has therefore kept its own currency.

Money has three important jobs. It is a **medium of exchange**, so that you do not have to swap potatoes for shoes. It is a measure of value that lets you compare prices. And you can save it in order to buy something later. For this to work, everyone must trust the currency.

Liechtenstein has used the Swiss franc since 1924 and has a treaty with Switzerland about it. So Liechtenstein does not print its own banknotes. Because many tourists come to Switzerland, you can also pay with euros in some shops. But you usually get your change in francs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A three-letter abbreviation for each currency, for example CHF for the franc.
A country’s bank that issues the money and makes sure its value stays stable.
Money you can touch, that is, coins and banknotes.
The smaller part of the franc; 100 centimes make one franc.

gewusst: The name franc comes from France, where there were already coins called “franc” in the Middle Ages.
The 1000-franc note is one of the banknotes with the highest value in the world.
The smallest Swiss coin, the 5-centime piece, is yellow because it is made of a mixture of copper, zinc and nickel.

teile.einleitung: You need a tissue when your nose is running or you have to sneeze. It helps to stop germs being passed on to other people so easily. What matters is what you do with it afterwards.
wichtigste: Used tissues contain germs.
A paper tissue is only used once.
Afterwards you throw it in the bin.
After blowing your nose, you wash your hands.
If you do not have a tissue, sneeze into the crook of your arm.

abschnitte.text: When you have a **cold**, there are many **viruses** in the mucus in your nose. When you sneeze and cough, tiny droplets fly through the air. Other people can be infected by them. A **tissue** catches these droplets. This way you protect your family and your class.

You do not put a used **paper tissue** back in your trouser pocket. Otherwise the germs in it can get onto your hands. It is best to throw it straight into a **bin** with a lid. Then wash your **hands** with water and soap. Washing thoroughly takes about 20 to 30 seconds.

abschnitte.titel: Sneezing into the crook of your arm
abschnitte.text: Sometimes you do not have a tissue with you. Then you sneeze or cough into the **crook of your arm**. That is the inside of your elbow. This way the germs do not land on your hands. After all, we touch door handles, toys and other things with our hands.

In the past, almost everyone used **cloth handkerchiefs**. You can wash them and use them again. To get rid of the germs, they are washed at a high temperature. Today **paper tissues** are widespread, because you can throw them away after using them once. Both help if you use them properly.

gewusst: A powerful sneeze can fling droplets several metres.
Many colds are passed on through the hands, which is why handwashing is so effective.

teile.einleitung: A loss happens when you spend more money than you take in, or when something loses value. Companies make a loss when their costs are higher than their revenue. Private individuals can also suffer losses, for example through theft, storms or falling share prices.
wichtigste: A company makes a loss when its costs are higher than its revenue.
Loss is the opposite of profit.
If you buy materials for 80 francs and take in 65 francs, you make a loss of 15 francs.
If a share falls from 50 to 40 francs, the loss is 20 per cent.
A hailstorm can cause a loss for a farm.
After a burglary, household contents insurance can replace what was lost.
If a company goes bankrupt, it can no longer pay its debts and is wound up.

abschnitte.text: A **loss** is the opposite of profit. It happens when the **costs** are greater than the **revenue**. If a class buys materials for a flea market for 80 francs and takes in only 65 francs, it makes a loss of 15 francs. In accounting, a loss is often shown with a minus sign.

Losses are often worked out as a percentage. Nora buys a share for 50 francs and later sells it for 40 francs. She loses 10 francs, which is 20 per cent of the purchase price. Anyone who buys **shares** must expect that their value can also fall; this is why people speak of **risk**.

Losses can have many causes. On a farm, a **hailstorm** can destroy the harvest. A shop loses money if too few customers come or if the prices of raw materials rise sharply. Crises such as the coronavirus pandemic in 2020 also led to big losses for many restaurants and travel agencies.

You can **insure** yourself against some losses. **Household contents insurance**, for example, replaces stolen things after a burglary or damage caused by fire and water. Farmers can insure themselves against hail, in Switzerland for example with Swiss Hail. With insurance, many people pay a premium, and anyone who suffers damage gets money.

If a company makes losses over a long period, it uses up its **equity capital**. If it can no longer pay its debts, it goes **bankrupt** and is wound up. Creditors who do not get their money receive a certificate of unpaid debt. A well-known example from Switzerland is the grounding of the airline Swissair in October 2001.

A loss is not always the end. Many companies make losses in their first years until they have enough customers. What matters is understanding the causes and changing something, for example cutting costs or adjusting prices. In private life, too, a **budget** helps you not to spend more than you have.

begriffe.erklaerung: When costs are greater than income.
When a company can no longer pay its debts and is wound up.
A community that pays for its members’ damage in return for a premium.
A document confirming that a creditor has not received their money.
The possibility of losing money or something else.

gewusst: On 2 October 2001 all Swissair aircraft stayed on the ground because there was no more money for fuel.
Some well-known companies made losses for years before they made a profit for the first time.
In Switzerland, a certificate of unpaid debt only expires after 20 years.

teile.einleitung: Läderach is a Swiss chocolate maker from the canton of Glarus. The company is famous for its FrischSchoggi (fresh chocolate), large slabs of chocolate from which pieces are broken off in the shop. There are Läderach shops in many Swiss cities and abroad too.
wichtigste: Läderach is a chocolate maker from the canton of Glarus.
The company was founded in 1962 by the confectioner Rudolf Läderach.
It is based in Ennenda near Glarus.
Läderach is known for its FrischSchoggi, thick slabs with nuts, fruit and other ingredients.
The company makes its own chocolate from cocoa beans.
Läderach is a family business and has its own shops in many countries.

abschnitte.text: Läderach makes **pralines**, truffles and chocolate bars. The products are mainly sold in its own shops. There, large slabs of chocolate lie in the counter, and the staff break pieces off them. You pay by weight, just as with cheese.

In 1962 the confectioner **Rudolf Läderach** founded his own company in Glarus. He invented a method for making thin, hollow chocolate balls for truffles more easily. He sold these hollow shells to confectioners all over Switzerland. Later his son Jürg took over the company and made Läderach famous with its own shops.

**FrischSchoggi** is Läderach’s best-known product. These are thick slabs of chocolate containing whole nuts, almonds, fruit or pieces of biscuit. Because it is freshly made, you should eat it soon. There are dozens of kinds, for example with hazelnuts, raspberries or caramel.

Läderach makes its chocolate itself from **cocoa beans**; this is called “bean to bar”. For this the company runs its own chocolate factory in the canton of Glarus. The beans come from warm countries in Africa and Latin America. In the factory they are roasted, ground and turned into chocolate with sugar and milk.

The headquarters in **Ennenda** is in the Glarnerland, a mountain valley in eastern Switzerland. From there Läderach has spread a great deal. Today there are Läderach shops in many Swiss railway stations and cities. The company also runs shops in Germany, the USA and Asia.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small piece of chocolate with a filling.
A round praline with a soft, creamy filling.
The seed of the cocoa tree, from which chocolate is made.
A job in which you make gateaux, pralines and fine pastries.

gewusst: At Läderach you often buy chocolate by weight, as at a cheese shop.
The invention that made Läderach big was hollow chocolate shells for truffles.

teile.einleitung: Gross domestic product, GDP for short, is the most important figure for measuring the economic output of a country. It shows how much all the goods and services produced within the country in a year are worth.
wichtigste: GDP measures the value of the final goods and services produced within the country.
Unlike nominal GDP, real GDP is adjusted for price changes.
If nominal GDP grows by 5 per cent and prices rise by 2 per cent, real GDP grows by about 3 per cent.
Gross national income counts the income of a country’s residents, including income from abroad.
GDP does not generally include unpaid housework and care work.
In Switzerland, SECO publishes the quarterly estimates of GDP.
In terms of GDP per head, Switzerland is one of the richest countries in the world.

abschnitte.text: **Gross domestic product** adds up the value of all **final goods** and services produced in a country in a year. Final goods are things that reach the end customer, for example a bike or a haircut. Intermediate inputs such as the steel for the bike are not counted separately, otherwise they would be counted twice. When GDP rises, people say the economy is growing.

One method is the **expenditure approach**. You add up consumption, investment, government spending and exports and subtract imports. With consumption of 400, investment of 100, government 150, exports 300 and imports 250 billion francs, this gives a GDP of 700 billion francs. Imports are subtracted because these goods were produced abroad.

**Nominal GDP** is calculated using current prices. If only prices rise, it grows even though nothing more is being produced. That is why experts take inflation out and obtain **real GDP**. If nominal GDP grows by 5 per cent and prices by 2 per cent, real growth is about 3 per cent.

GDP counts everything produced within the country’s borders, no matter who produces it. **Gross national income** (GNI), on the other hand, counts the income of all residents, even if it was earned abroad. For Switzerland the difference is interesting, because many cross-border commuters work here and Swiss companies earn a lot of money abroad. To compare countries, GDP is often divided by the number of inhabitants, giving **GDP per head**.

Switzerland’s GDP in 2023 was around 800 billion francs. Per head, this makes Switzerland one of the richest countries in the world. The **State Secretariat for Economic Affairs** (SECO) estimates GDP every quarter, and the Federal Statistical Office calculates the exact annual figures. If GDP shrinks for two quarters in a row, this is called a **recession**.

GDP does not measure everything that is important for a good life. Unpaid work such as cooking, looking after children or volunteering is not included. GDP also does not show environmental damage, health or how satisfied people are. A road accident can even increase GDP, because repairs and hospital costs are counted too. That is why there are additional measures of prosperity and quality of life.

begriffe.erklaerung: A finished product that reaches the end consumer.
GDP with price increases taken out.
A period in which the economy shrinks.
The federal State Secretariat for Economic Affairs.

gewusst: Modern GDP was developed in the 1930s by the economist Simon Kuznets in the USA.
Besides GDP, the Kingdom of Bhutan also measures the “Gross National Happiness” of its people.
If unpaid housework in Switzerland were paid, it would be worth several hundred billion francs a year.

teile.einleitung: Freitag is a company from Zurich that makes bags out of old lorry tarpaulins. Every bag is unique, because every piece of tarpaulin has a different colour and a different pattern. Freitag is a well-known example of upcycling.
wichtigste: Freitag makes bags out of old lorry tarpaulins.
The company was founded in Zurich in 1993 by the brothers Markus and Daniel Freitag.
Upcycling means that a new, valuable product is made out of waste.
Every Freitag bag is one of a kind.
Besides tarpaulins, bicycle inner tubes and car seat belts are also used.
The Freitag shop in Zurich West is made of stacked shipping containers.

abschnitte.text: **Freitag** is a Swiss brand of bags, rucksacks and accessories. The bags are made from used **lorry tarpaulins**, which once protected loads on lorries from the rain. They are waterproof, tough and all look different. The name comes from the surname of the two founders.

In 1993 the graphic designers **Markus and Daniel Freitag** were looking for a waterproof bag for their bike rides through Zurich. From the window of their flat they saw lorries with colourful tarpaulins driving past. From these they sewed a courier bag, with bicycle inner tubes as edges and a car seat belt as the shoulder strap. So many people liked the bag that it became a company.

Freitag is a well-known example of **upcycling**. This means making a new product out of waste or used material that is worth more than the original material. In recycling, on the other hand, material is usually melted down or shredded. Every year Freitag collects hundreds of tonnes of old tarpaulins all over Europe.

First the old tarpaulins are cut up and washed in large machines, often with collected rainwater. Then staff cut out the pieces by hand, choosing which part of the pattern will be visible. That is why every bag is **one of a kind**. Finally the pieces are sewn together.

In 2006 Freitag opened a shop in Zurich West in a tower made of 17 old **shipping containers**. The Freitag Tower is over 25 metres high and became a landmark of the neighbourhood. From the top there is a good view of the railway tracks and the city. Today Freitag has shops in many cities around the world, for example in Tokyo and Berlin.

begriffe.erklaerung: A new, valuable product is made out of waste.
A large, waterproof plastic cover, for example for lorries.
An object that exists only once.
Old material is collected and processed into new raw material.

gewusst: The first Freitag bag was sewn in the brothers’ flat.
A Freitag bag is in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
Freitag has a swapping platform where you can exchange your bag for another one.

teile.einleitung: An accident can lead to expensive treatment. That is why everyone in Switzerland is insured against accidents, but not everyone in the same way. Anyone who is employed is insured through their employer. Children and many others are insured through their health insurer.
wichtigste: Employees are insured under the Accident Insurance Act, UVG for short.
From 8 hours a week with the same employer, the protection also applies in your free time.
Children are insured through their health insurer with accident cover.
For accidents under the UVG there is no deductible and no excess.
Apprentices are employees and are therefore insured through their training company.
Self-employed people have to arrange their own accident cover.

abschnitte.text: The **Accident Insurance Act**, **UVG** for short, governs compulsory accident insurance. Under it, all **employees** in Switzerland are insured against **occupational accidents** and **occupational diseases**. The employer must register them with an accident insurer. Many companies are insured with **Suva**, others with private insurers. The employer pays the premium for occupational accidents.

Anyone who works at least **8 hours a week** for the same employer is also insured against **accidents in their free time**. This applies, for example, to a skiing accident on holiday. Anyone who works less is only insured through their employer for occupational accidents. Accidents in their free time are then paid for by the **health insurer**. That is why someone who works 4 hours a week may need their health insurer after a football accident.

**Children** have no employer. That is why, for them, the health insurer with **accident cover** also pays for accidents. So if a child breaks their arm while cycling, the health insurer pays. **Apprentices**, on the other hand, are employees of their training company. If they work at least 8 hours a week, they are also insured in their free time through the company.

Accident insurance under the UVG pays the **treatment costs** with no **deductible** and no **excess**. If you cannot work, there is a **daily allowance** of 80 per cent of the insured wage. If there is lasting damage, there may be a pension. If the accident is only covered by the health insurer, the normal cost sharing applies instead.

Compulsory UVG insurance applies to employees. **Self-employed people** are not automatically insured under the UVG. They have accidents included with their health insurer or can take out UVG insurance **voluntarily**. This is important, because otherwise no daily allowance is paid, for example.

gewusst: Suva is the largest accident insurer in Switzerland and has its headquarters in Lucerne.
Anyone who is insured against all accidents through their employer can exclude accident cover from their health insurance and so save on the premium.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who goes on holiday can fall ill or have an accident. In some countries, treatment in hospital is very expensive. That is why it is worth checking your insurance cover before a trip.
wichtigste: Abroad, basic insurance only pays for emergencies.
It pays at most twice what the treatment would cost in Switzerland.
In countries such as the USA or Canada, this is often not enough.
Travel insurance or supplementary insurance for abroad covers higher costs.
Transport back to Switzerland is often insured too.
In the EU, the European Health Insurance Card on the back of the insurance card helps.

abschnitte.text: Compulsory **basic insurance** also applies abroad, but only for **emergencies**. An emergency is treatment that cannot be postponed until you return. The insurer pays at most **twice** the amount that the same treatment would cost in Switzerland. If the bill is higher, you have to pay the rest yourself.

In some countries, hospital costs are much higher than in Switzerland. Well-known examples are the **USA**, **Canada** or **Australia**. Just a few days in hospital there can cost a great deal of money. That is why experts recommend additional insurance, especially for **long-distance travel**.

**Travel insurance** or **supplementary insurance for abroad** pays treatment costs that go beyond basic insurance. It often includes **transport back** to Switzerland. Some insurance also pays if you have to cancel the trip because of illness. This is called **cancellation insurance**. Exactly what is insured is set out in the contract.

On the back of the Swiss insurance card is the **European Health Insurance Card**. It is valid in the countries of the EU and EFTA. With it, in an emergency you are treated like a local insured person. Even so, there can still be costs, for example for transport back home.

It is best to ask your own health insurer what is covered in the country you are visiting. Many people already have suitable **supplementary insurance** without knowing it. Credit cards or associations sometimes also offer travel cover. It is important to take the insurer’s emergency number with you.

gewusst: The European Health Insurance Card is also valid in Iceland, Norway and Liechtenstein.
Transport back by air ambulance can be very expensive, which is why it is included in many travel insurance policies.

teile.einleitung: The current account shows a country’s economic relations with other countries. It includes not only goods but also services, income and transfers. It is an important part of the balance of payments.
wichtigste: The current account records a country’s exchange with other countries.
It contains trade in goods, that is, the balance of trade.
On top of that come services, income and current transfers.
Income includes, for example, wages and interest from abroad.
Switzerland usually has a surplus on its current account.
In Switzerland, the National Bank compiles these statistics.

abschnitte.text: The first part of the **current account** is **trade in goods**, that is, exports and imports of goods. This is the balance of trade. On top of that come **services**. When tourists from abroad spend their holidays in Switzerland, that is an export of services. Services from banks, insurance companies or transport firms for foreign customers count too.

Another part is **income**. This includes **employment income**, that is, wages that flow across the border. If, for example, cross-border commuters work in Switzerland and live abroad, their wages flow abroad. Then there is **investment income** such as interest and dividends. Swiss companies and investors own a lot abroad and receive earnings from it.

**Current transfers** are payments for which nothing is received directly in return. They include, for example, money that people send to their families abroad, or contributions to international organisations. **Development aid** is part of this too. These amounts are smaller than trade, but still important.

If you add all the parts together, you get the **current account balance**. For many years Switzerland has usually had a **surplus**. This means that it takes in more from abroad than it pays out to other countries. In Switzerland, the **Swiss National Bank** compiles the balance of payments. It publishes the figures regularly.

gewusst: A current account surplus means that a country is building up more wealth abroad.
Together with the financial account, the current account is part of a country’s balance of payments.

teile.einleitung: Basic insurance premiums differ greatly from one health insurer to another. Anyone who compares can save a lot of money. A neutral tool for this is Priminfo, the Confederation’s premium calculator.
wichtigste: The same services cost different premiums at different insurers.
In basic insurance, all insurers pay for the same services.
Priminfo is the official premium calculator of the Federal Office of Public Health.
There you can see all the approved premiums for where you live.
It is worth comparing every autumn, when the new premiums are announced.
You can change your basic insurance until 30 November.

abschnitte.text: In **basic insurance**, all insurers pay for the **same services**. That is set out in the law. But the premiums differ greatly from one insurer to another. So anyone who chooses a cheaper insurer gets the same protection for less money. That is why **comparing premiums** is worth it.

With **Priminfo**, the **Federal Office of Public Health**, FOPH for short, runs an official premium calculator. It is neutral and free. You enter where you live, your age, deductible and insurance model. Then the calculator shows all the approved premiums for your region. This lets you see quickly which insurer is cheap.

When comparing, you do not only look at the price. It is also important whether the **insurance model** suits you, for example the family doctor or Telmed model. The insurer’s **service** can also differ. As well as Priminfo, there are **private comparison services**. These often receive money from insurers when someone changes through them.

The new premiums are announced each **autumn**. That is the best moment for a comparison. Anyone who wants to change cancels their basic insurance by **30 November**. You can also keep your **supplementary insurance** with the old insurer. It has its own rules and notice periods.

gewusst: For exactly the same services, the premium in the same place can differ by several hundred francs a year depending on the insurer.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who cannot work after an accident or because of illness still gets money to live on. This is what the daily allowance is for. It replaces part of the wages for each day on which you are unable to work.
wichtigste: The daily allowance replaces part of the wages when you are unable to work.
After an accident, accident insurance under the UVG pays a daily allowance.
If you are completely unable to work, it is 80 per cent of the insured wage.
It is paid from the third day after the accident.
If you are partly unable to work, the daily allowance is lower.
For illness, a separate daily allowance insurance is needed.

abschnitte.text: Employees in Switzerland are insured against accidents under the **UVG**. If someone cannot work after an accident, accident insurance pays a **daily allowance**. If they are completely unable to work, it is **80 per cent** of the insured earnings. The daily allowance is paid from the **third day** after the accident. The employer covers the first days.

Sometimes you can already work a little again after an accident. Then you are only **partly unable to work**. The doctor decides what percentage you can work. The daily allowance is reduced accordingly. Anyone who can work half the time, for example, gets half the daily allowance.

With **illness**, things are regulated differently. The employer must continue paying wages for a certain time. Many companies have taken out **sickness benefit insurance** for this. In Switzerland it is not compulsory for everyone. Self-employed people have to take care of it themselves.

The daily allowance is calculated from the **insured earnings**. These are the wages someone received before the accident. However, the insured wage has an upper limit. That is why people who earn a very large amount get less than 80 per cent of their whole wage. The daily allowance is paid until you can work again or receive a pension.

gewusst: The German word “Taggeld” shows the idea: for every day on which you cannot work, there is an amount of money.
The daily allowance from accident insurance is also paid for weekends and public holidays.

teile.einleitung: Climeworks is a young company from Zurich that filters CO2 directly out of the air. The greenhouse gas is then, for example, turned into rock deep underground. The company’s best-known plants are called Orca and Mammoth and are in Iceland.
wichtigste: Climeworks filters the greenhouse gas CO2 directly out of the air.
The company was founded in 2009 by Christoph Gebald and Jan Wurzbacher.
Climeworks is a spin-off of ETH Zurich.
The large plants Orca and Mammoth are in Iceland.
In Iceland the CO2 is turned into stone in basalt rock.
The process is called Direct Air Capture.

abschnitte.text: **Climeworks** builds machines that suck in air and remove the carbon dioxide from it. CO2 is a **greenhouse gas** that contributes to global warming. If it is removed from the air permanently, a small part of global warming can be offset. Customers such as companies or private individuals pay for a certain amount of CO2 to be removed.

Large fans suck air into so-called collectors. Inside them is a filter material that the CO2 sticks to. When the filter is full, it is heated to about 100 degrees, and the CO2 is released again. This process is called **Direct Air Capture**, meaning capturing directly from the air.

Christoph Gebald and Jan Wurzbacher met while studying at **ETH Zurich**. In 2009 they founded Climeworks as a spin-off of the university. In 2017 they opened their first plant in Hinwil in the canton of Zurich, which supplied CO2 to a greenhouse. There the extra CO2 helped the plants grow better.

In 2021 Climeworks put the **Orca** plant into operation in Iceland, which can filter up to 4000 tonnes of CO2 a year. In 2024 came the much larger **Mammoth** plant, which is eventually meant to manage up to 36,000 tonnes a year. Iceland is well suited because it has a lot of energy from geothermal heat. The partner company Carbfix pumps the CO2 with water underground, where it turns to stone in the basalt within about two years.

Many experts think that in future CO2 will have to be removed from the air in order to reach the climate targets. But the technology is still very expensive and needs a lot of energy. So far the plants filter only a tiny part of what humanity emits every year. That is why the most important thing is still not to produce so much CO2 in the first place.

begriffe.erklaerung: Carbon dioxide, a gas produced when petrol, oil or coal is burned.
A gas in the air that holds in heat and warms the Earth.
A new company that comes out of a university or another company.
A dark rock formed from cooled lava.

gewusst: The Orca plant is named after the Icelandic word “orka”, which means energy.
Humanity emits almost 40 billion tonnes of CO2 every year, millions of times more than Orca can filter.
Climeworks’ collectors are stacked like containers and can be extended as much as needed.

teile.einleitung: Taxes are sums of money that people and companies have to pay to the state. With them the state pays for things that benefit everyone, for example schools, roads and the police. In Switzerland, the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities collect taxes.
wichtigste: Taxes are charges you have to pay to the state without getting anything directly in return.
The state uses taxes, for example, for schools, roads and the police.
In Switzerland, the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities collect taxes.
Every year adults fill in a tax return to declare their income and wealth.
Income tax increases as income rises; this is called progression.
You pay value added tax at the same time as you shop.
The amount of tax differs from canton to canton and from municipality to municipality.

abschnitte.text: **Taxes** are sums of money that every person and every company must pay to the state according to fixed rules. Unlike when shopping, you do not get a particular product back in return. Instead, the state uses the money to pay for tasks for everyone, for example **schools**, roads, the police, hospitals and the army. In Switzerland, voters often help decide how high taxes are.

In Switzerland, the **Confederation**, the **cantons** and the **municipalities** collect taxes. The Confederation collects, for example, direct federal tax and value added tax. Cantons and municipalities mainly collect income and wealth taxes. Each municipality uses its **tax multiplier** to decide how much its residents pay, so there are big differences, for example between Zug and Geneva.

Every year adults fill in a **tax return**. In it they state how much they have earned and how much wealth they own. Certain costs, for example for travel to work or for children, may be deducted. The tax office then calculates how much you have to pay. You usually become liable for tax yourself from the year in which you turn 18.

Income tax is **progressive**. This means that people with a high income pay not only more francs but also a larger share of their income. In this way, those who are better off contribute more to shared tasks. Very small incomes often have to pay no tax or almost none.

Children pay taxes too without noticing, namely **value added tax** (VAT). It is included in the price of almost every purchase and has mostly been 8.1 per cent since 2024; a lower rate applies to food and books. There are also, for example, the mineral oil tax on petrol and the tobacco tax. A withholding tax of 35 per cent is deducted from interest on bank savings, and you get it back through your tax return.

Taxes have existed for thousands of years; even the ancient Egyptians and Romans collected charges. In the past people often paid with grain or cattle, for example with the **tithe**, a tenth of the harvest. Today paying taxes is a legal duty. Anyone who deliberately hides income commits **tax evasion** and can expect penalties.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form in which you declare your income and wealth every year.
A tax that is included in the price of almost all goods.
A number that a municipality or canton uses to set the level of taxes.
The more you earn, the larger the share you pay in tax.

gewusst: Value added tax was only introduced in Switzerland in 1995; before that there was a turnover tax on goods.
Because taxes differ so much depending on where you live, some people and companies move to cantons with low taxes.
In many municipalities, the municipal assembly votes on the tax multiplier every year.

teile.einleitung: Trade means that goods or services are exchanged for money or other goods. Even in the Stone Age, people swapped flints, salt or shells. Today goods travel all over the world on ships, trains and lorries, and Switzerland is a very important trading country.
wichtigste: In trade, goods or services are exchanged for money or other goods.
In barter, goods are swapped directly for other goods.
Export is the sale of goods abroad, import is bringing goods in from abroad.
By value, Switzerland exports mostly chemical and pharmaceutical products.
Taken as a whole, the European Union is Switzerland’s most important trading partner.
A customs duty is a charge on goods that are brought across the national border.
Retail trade sells goods directly to end customers.

abschnitte.text: In the beginning there was **barter**: people swapped grain for tools, for example. This was awkward, because both sides had to need exactly what the other was offering. That is why means of payment caught on, first shells or pieces of metal, later coins and banknotes. With **money**, trade became much easier and faster.

Famous trade routes were the **Silk Road** from China to Europe and the Amber Road from the Baltic Sea to the Mediterranean. Goods have also been transported over Alpine passes such as the Gotthard since the Middle Ages. Mule drivers led mules carrying goods over the passes. Cities on trade routes, such as Basel on the Rhine, became rich as a result.

**Wholesale trade** buys large quantities from manufacturers and sells them on to shops. **Retail trade** sells to end customers, that is, to us. The largest retailers in Switzerland are Migros and Coop. Online shopping is also becoming more and more important.

In **exports**, Switzerland sells goods abroad; in **imports**, it brings goods into the country. Switzerland mainly exports medicines and chemicals, as well as machines, watches and precision instruments. Imports include, for example, cars, clothes, energy and many foods. Goods reach Switzerland by ship via the Rhine ports in Basel.

A **customs duty** is a charge on goods brought across the border. On 1 January 2024 Switzerland abolished customs duties on industrial products, but there are still duties on many agricultural products. Switzerland has a free trade agreement from 1972 and several bilateral treaties with the European Union. The World Trade Organization WTO has its headquarters in Geneva.

Taken as a whole, the **European Union** is the most important trading partner, especially Germany, Italy and France. As a single country, the USA is very important for Swiss exports. China is also one of the big trading partners. Because Switzerland is small and has hardly any raw materials, it depends heavily on trade with other countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: Selling goods abroad.
Bringing goods in from abroad.
A charge on goods that cross a national border.
Shops that sell goods directly to customers.
Trade between countries with no or few customs duties.

gewusst: Salt used to be so valuable that it was called white gold.
Switzerland sells a very large share of its products abroad, and for medicines by far the largest share.
The World Trade Organization WTO has its headquarters in Geneva on Lake Geneva.

teile.einleitung: The balance of trade shows how many goods a country sells abroad and how many it buys from abroad. If exports are greater, this is called a surplus. Switzerland usually has a surplus in its trade in goods.
wichtigste: The balance of trade compares exports and imports of goods.
Export means sending goods out, import means bringing goods in.
If exports are greater, there is an export surplus.
If imports are greater, there is a deficit.
Switzerland usually has a surplus in its trade in goods.
Pharmaceutical products are among the most important Swiss exports.

abschnitte.text: If a Swiss company sells watches to Japan, that is an **export**. If a Swiss shop buys bananas from Ecuador, that is an **import**. The **balance of trade** adds up the value of all the goods a country sends out and brings in. It is usually calculated for a whole year. Then the two totals are compared.

If the value of exports is greater than the value of imports, this is called an **export surplus**. The balance of trade is then positive. If it is the other way round, there is a **deficit** and the balance is negative. A deficit is not automatically bad. It can also mean that a country gets many goods cheaply from abroad.

Switzerland has few raw materials and has to import a lot, for example energy, cars and food. At the same time it sells many high-quality goods abroad. Among the most important exports are **pharmaceutical products** and chemicals, **machines** and **watches**. That is why Switzerland usually has a surplus in its trade in goods. Important trading partners are the EU countries and the USA.

In Switzerland, the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** records all goods that cross the border. This produces the foreign trade statistics. **Gold** is a special case: Switzerland processes a great deal of gold that only passes through the country. That is why the figures are often given both with and without gold.

gewusst: The balance of trade is part of the larger current account, which also includes services and income.
A large share of the world’s gold is processed in Swiss refineries.

teile.einleitung: The stethoscope is one of the best-known tools of doctors. With it they listen to how the heart and lungs are working. Listening in this way is called auscultation.
wichtigste: With the stethoscope you listen to the heart and lungs.
It has two earpieces, a tube and a round chest piece.
The chest piece is placed on the chest or the back.
The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by the French doctor René Laennec.
It is also used to measure blood pressure.

abschnitte.text: A **stethoscope** has two **earpieces**, which go into the doctor’s ears. They are connected by a tube. At the end is the round **chest piece**. It often has a thin **diaphragm** that picks up sounds. The sounds travel through the tube to the ear.

With every beat, the heart makes two sounds that sound like “boom boom”. These sounds are made when the **heart valves** close. The doctor listens to whether the heart is beating regularly. For the **lungs**, she listens to the sound of breathing. Whistling or rattling can show that the lungs are ill, for example with bronchitis.

In the past, doctors put their ear directly on the chest. In **1816**, the French doctor **René Laennec** rolled a sheet of paper into a tube. With it he could hear the heart much better. After that he built a tube made of wood. He made up the name stethoscope from Greek words for “chest” and “to look at”.

The stethoscope also helps with measuring **blood pressure**. For this, a cuff is put around the upper arm and pumped up. As it is slowly let down, you hear sounds in the crook of the elbow. From these you read off the upper and lower values. Today there are also electronic devices for this.

gewusst: There are electronic stethoscopes that can amplify and record sounds.
Vets also use stethoscopes to listen to the heart and lungs of animals.

teile.einleitung: A company is an organisation that produces goods or offers services, usually in order to earn money. It can be a small village bakery or a global corporation such as Nestlé. In Switzerland there are hundreds of thousands of companies, most of them small.
wichtigste: A company produces goods or offers services.
A sole proprietorship belongs to one single person.
In a public limited company, the capital is divided into shares.
A start-up is a young company with a new business idea.
In Switzerland, companies are entered in the commercial register.
Equity capital is the money that the owners put into their company themselves.
Around 99.7 per cent of companies in Switzerland have fewer than 250 employees.

abschnitte.text: A **company** produces goods or offers services and sells them to customers. To do this it needs staff, premises, machines and money. The aim is usually a **profit**, so that the company can survive and grow. Examples are a hairdresser, a farm, a joinery or a large bank.

The simplest form is the **sole proprietorship**, which belongs to one single person, who is also liable with their private wealth. With the limited liability company, GmbH for short, and the **public limited company** (AG), only the company’s assets are liable. In Switzerland an AG needs at least 100,000 francs of share capital, a GmbH 20,000 francs. Migros and Coop, on the other hand, are **cooperatives** that belong to their members.

In an AG the capital is divided into many parts, the **shares**. Whoever owns a share is a co-owner and often receives a share of the profit, the dividend. The money that the owners put in themselves is called **equity capital**. If a company borrows money, for example from a bank, this is called borrowed capital.

Anyone who founds a company needs a business idea, a plan and start-up capital. A **start-up** is a young company with a new, often technical idea that wants to grow quickly. Many Swiss start-ups come about around the universities ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne. Companies are entered in the public **commercial register**, where anyone can look up who is behind them.

In Switzerland around 99.7 per cent of all companies have fewer than 250 employees; they are called **SMEs**, small and medium-sized enterprises. They employ around two thirds of all employees. There are also world-famous large corporations such as Nestlé in Vevey, Roche and Novartis in Basel or ABB. Many family businesses have existed for generations.

A company has different departments such as purchasing, production, sales, marketing and accounting. The **executive management** makes the important decisions; in an AG it is supervised by the board of directors. Many companies train apprentices, which has a long tradition in Switzerland with the **apprenticeship** system. Companies pay wages, taxes and social contributions and are therefore very important for a country.

begriffe.erklaerung: A company whose capital is divided into shares.
A public list of all registered companies.
Money that the owners put into the company themselves.
Small and medium-sized enterprises with fewer than 250 employees.
A young company with a new business idea.

gewusst: Many companies in Switzerland have fewer than 10 employees; they are called micro-enterprises.
Nestlé was founded in Vevey in the 19th century by Henri Nestlé and is today one of the largest food companies in the world.
In the commercial register you can check online free of charge who runs a company.

teile.einleitung: A wound is an injury to the skin, for example a graze after a fall. You can treat small wounds well yourself if you know how.
wichtigste: A small, dirty wound is first rinsed out with clean water.
Then you can disinfect it and stick a plaster on it.
Before treating it, you wash your hands.
Heavily bleeding or deep wounds need to be seen by a doctor.
A vaccination protects against tetanus.
As it heals, the body forms a crust called a scab.

abschnitte.text: When you fall over, you often graze your knee. This is a **graze**, where only the top layer of skin is injured. If you cut yourself with a knife, you get a **cut**. There are also puncture wounds, bite wounds and gashes. The deeper a wound is, the more careful you have to be.

First you wash your own hands. Then you rinse a dirty wound with **clean water** so that sand and dirt are removed. After that you can treat it with a **disinfectant**. Then a **plaster** or a dressing goes on. The plaster protects the wound from new dirt.

abschnitte.titel: When to go to the doctor?
abschnitte.text: If a wound is bleeding heavily, press a clean cloth on it and get help. Deep or gaping wounds must be looked at by a doctor, and sometimes they are stitched. You should also show bite wounds from animals. With dirty wounds, you check whether the **vaccination** against **tetanus** is still valid. This dangerous disease can get into a wound through soil.

After a short time, a small wound stops bleeding because the blood **clots**. Then a crust forms, called a **scab**. New skin grows underneath. You do not pick off the scab, otherwise the wound heals more slowly. If a wound becomes red and hot and hurts more and more, it may be infected, and then you go to the doctor.

gewusst: The skin is constantly renewing itself: dead flakes of skin fall off unnoticed every day.
Small scratches often heal within a few days without leaving a scar.

teile.einleitung: The dentist checks whether your teeth are healthy and treats holes. In Switzerland you usually pay for dental treatment yourself, so good dental care is also good for your wallet.
wichtigste: The dentist checks your teeth and looks for holes.
You go for regular check-ups.
Basic insurance usually does not pay for normal dental treatment.
Basic insurance only pays for certain serious illnesses that could not be avoided.
Damage to teeth from an accident is paid for by accident insurance.
For children, this is the health insurer’s accident cover.

abschnitte.text: The **dentist** looks into your mouth with a small mirror. She checks whether there is a **hole**, which is called **tooth decay**. A hole is cleaned and closed with a **filling**. Often a **dental hygienist** helps by removing plaque and tartar. Anyone who goes for regular check-ups spots problems early.

In many cantons and municipalities in Switzerland there is **school dental care**. Schoolchildren are checked regularly by a dentist. Often an expert also visits the class and shows how to brush properly. The rules and costs differ depending on the canton. This is meant to help all children have healthy teeth.

The health insurer’s **basic insurance** usually does not pay for normal dental treatment. You pay for fillings and check-ups yourself or through **supplementary dental insurance**. Basic insurance only pays for certain serious illnesses that could not be avoided. Because holes usually come from a lack of care, the rule is: good **toothbrushing** saves money. Anyone who looks after their teeth needs fewer expensive treatments.

Ali falls off his scooter and breaks a tooth. That is an **accident**, so **accident insurance** pays. Employees are insured under the Accident Insurance Act, **UVG**. Children and other people without a job are protected by the health insurer’s **accident cover**. A tooth that has been knocked out should be kept moist, and you go to the dentist straight away.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
Children have 20 milk teeth, and adults usually have 32 permanent teeth including the wisdom teeth.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland there are two ways in which doctors’ bills are paid. With the tiers garant system, the patient receives the bill and first pays it herself. Afterwards she claims her share back from the health insurer.
wichtigste: With tiers garant, the surgery sends the bill to the patient.
The patient pays the bill herself.
Then she submits the bill to the health insurer.
The insurer reimburses its share.
The deductible and excess are deducted.
Tiers garant is the counterpart to tiers payant.

abschnitte.text: **Tiers garant** is French and roughly means “the third party guarantees”. The “third party” is the **health insurer**. It does not pay the surgery directly, but guarantees repayment to the insured person. This person is the **debtor** of the bill towards the surgery. The law makes tiers garant the basic rule if nothing else has been agreed.

First the doctor treats the patient. Then the surgery sends the **bill** to her home. The patient pays it within the payment deadline. Then she submits the bill or the **reimbursement form** to the insurer. The insurer transfers to her the share that goes beyond the **deductible** and **excess**.

One advantage is that you see every bill yourself. That way you know exactly what a treatment costs and can spot mistakes. One disadvantage is that you have to pay the money up front. With high bills, this can be difficult for a family. That is why it is worth submitting bills quickly.

Many **doctors’ surgeries** bill under tiers garant, depending on their contract with the insurers. Therapies such as physiotherapy are also often billed this way. In **hospitals** and **pharmacies**, on the other hand, **tiers payant** usually applies. The bill says which system applies.

gewusst: The French word “tiers” means “third”, because as well as the patient and the doctor, the insurer is involved as a third party.
Anyone who cannot pay a high bill up front can ask the insurer whether it will pay directly.

teile.einleitung: For insurance, it is important whether an injury is caused by an accident or by an illness. This determines which insurance pays. An accident is a sudden, unintended event from outside.
wichtigste: An accident is sudden, unintended damage caused by something from outside.
One example is falling off a bike.
An illness, on the other hand, develops inside the body.
A distinction is made between occupational and non-occupational accidents.
Some injuries are treated like accidents, even if there is no clear outside cause.
In Switzerland, the BFU works to prevent accidents.

abschnitte.text: Swiss law describes an **accident** precisely. It is **sudden** and **unintended** damage to the body. It is caused by an **unusual external factor**. One example is a fall on the ice or a collision while playing football. Anyone who injures themselves on purpose has not had an accident.

An **illness** usually develops inside the body itself, for example flu or appendicitis. An accident, on the other hand, comes suddenly from outside. This distinction is important for **insurance**. In accidents, the employer’s **accident insurance** often pays. In illnesses, the **health insurer** pays.

If an accident happens at work or on the way to work, it is called an **occupational accident**. Accidents in your free time are called **non-occupational accidents**. These include accidents during sport, in the home or on holiday. In Switzerland, most accidents happen in people’s free time. For children, the health insurer pays through its accident cover.

Some injuries happen without a clear external cause, for example a **torn ligament** when twisting. The law lists such injuries. In many cases, accident insurance still pays for them. They are called **accident-like injuries**.

Many accidents can be avoided. In Switzerland, the **BFU**, the Swiss Council for Accident Prevention, deals with this. It gives tips for road traffic, sport and the home. A **cycle helmet**, good shoes and paying attention help a lot.

gewusst: An accident on the direct way to work usually counts as an occupational accident.
Falls are one of the most common causes of accidents in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Pilatus Aircraft is a Swiss aircraft manufacturer from Stans in the canton of Nidwalden. The company is named after Mount Pilatus near Lucerne. Its aircraft fly all over the world, for example as rescue aircraft, training aircraft or business aircraft.
wichtigste: Pilatus Aircraft builds aircraft in Stans in the canton of Nidwalden.
The company was founded in 1939 and is named after Mount Pilatus.
The PC-6 Porter can take off and land on very short runways.
The PC-12 is a single-engine propeller aircraft used, for example, by flying doctors in Australia.
With the PC-24, Pilatus also builds a business jet.
Many air forces, including the Swiss Air Force, train their pilots with Pilatus aircraft.

abschnitte.text: Pilatus Aircraft is the only large **aircraft manufacturer** in Switzerland. The company builds its aircraft in Stans, right next to Buochs airfield. It is named after **Pilatus**, a mountain near Lucerne that is over 2100 metres high. Pilatus employs several thousand people and is an important employer in central Switzerland.

Pilatus was founded in 1939, shortly before the Second World War. At first the company mainly repaired aircraft of the Swiss Army. Soon it was building its own aircraft, for example simple training aircraft. With the **PC-6 Porter**, which first flew in 1959, Pilatus became known all over the world.

The PC-6 Porter is a so-called **STOL aircraft**. This means that it can take off and land on very short runways of only about 200 metres. That is why it is used in the mountains, in the jungle and on glaciers. Parachutists also often jump out of a Porter.

The training aircraft **PC-7**, PC-9 and PC-21 are used by many air forces to train military pilots. The PC-12 is a versatile propeller aircraft used, for example, by the flying doctors in Australia. The PC-24 is a small jet that can even land on grass runways. It first flew in 2015.

Pilatus aircraft are considered very robust and reliable. The Swiss **Air Force** uses the PC-7 and the PC-21 to train pilots, and the aerobatic team PC-7 Team puts on displays with them. But most of the aircraft are sold abroad. Because military aircraft are among them, some exports are the subject of political debate.

begriffe.erklaerung: An abbreviation for aircraft that can take off and land on very short runways.
A rotating blade at the front of the aircraft that pulls it forwards.
The part of the armed forces responsible for defence in the air.
The strip on which an aircraft takes off and lands.

gewusst: In 1960 a PC-6 Porter landed on the Dhaulagiri Glacier in the Himalayas at a height of over 5700 metres.
With the PC-7 Team, the Swiss Air Force has its own aerobatic team flying Pilatus aircraft.

teile.einleitung: Lonza is a Swiss company that makes active ingredients and medicines for other pharmaceutical companies. Its largest plant is in Visp in the canton of Valais. Lonza takes its name from a small river in Valais.
wichtigste: Lonza makes active ingredients for medicines on behalf of other companies.
The company was founded in Valais in 1897 and named after the River Lonza.
Its largest plant is in Visp in the canton of Valais.
Its headquarters is in Basel.
Originally Lonza produced electricity and chemicals.
During the coronavirus pandemic Lonza produced the active ingredient for a vaccine in Visp.

abschnitte.text: Lonza works in **contract manufacturing**. This means that other companies invent a medicine, and Lonza makes the active ingredient for them. Many modern medicines are made with the help of living cells in huge tanks called **bioreactors**. Lonza builds large and very clean factories for this.

Lonza was founded in Valais in 1897 and named after the River **Lonza** in the Lötschental. At first the company used hydropower to generate electricity. With this electricity it made chemicals such as calcium carbide and later fertiliser. Over time Lonza specialised more and more in manufacturing for the **pharmaceutical industry**.

Lonza’s largest plant is in **Visp** in Upper Valais. It is one of the most important employers in the whole canton of Valais. In recent years Lonza has invested billions of francs in new facilities there. That is why the company is very important for Visp and the surrounding area.

During the coronavirus pandemic Lonza produced the active ingredient for the **mRNA vaccine** of the American company Moderna in Visp. New production lines were built for this in a very short time. The vaccines then went to many countries. As a result Lonza also became known to many people who had known nothing about the company before.

Today Lonza has sites in Europe, North America and Asia. The company employs many thousands of specialists, for example biologists, chemists and engineers. Lonza shares are traded on the Swiss stock exchange. Lonza is one of the largest contract manufacturers of medicines in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The substance in a medicine that works in the body.
A company makes a product that another company invented and sells.
A large tank in which living cells produce a substance.
All the companies that research and make medicines.

gewusst: Lonza started out as a company that generated electricity with hydropower from the mountains of Valais.
Most people take medicines without knowing that the active ingredient may come from Visp.

teile.einleitung: Income is all the money someone receives, for example pocket money, wages or presents. It is the basis of every budget, because you can only spend what you have received first.
wichtigste: Income means sums of money that you receive.
For young people, income is mainly pocket money.
A wage is money you receive for your work.
The wage before deductions is called gross wage, after deductions net wage.
Many employees in Switzerland receive a 13th monthly salary.
In Switzerland, parents receive a child allowance for each child.
If you work 6 hours at 12 francs, you earn 72 francs.

abschnitte.text: **Income** is all the money that flows into your purse or your account. For children and young people this is mainly **pocket money**, money given as birthday presents or small earnings. Adults usually have a wage as their most important income. The opposite of income is spending.

Many children get regular pocket money from their parents so that they learn how to handle money. Budget Advice Switzerland publishes guideline amounts by age for this. Young people can also earn a little extra, for example by babysitting, mowing lawns or delivering newspapers. If Mia helps in her neighbour’s garden for 6 hours at 12 francs an hour, she earns **72 francs**.

Anyone who works gets a **wage** for it. The agreed wage is called the **gross wage**. Contributions for the AVS, unemployment insurance and the pension fund are deducted from it. What then arrives in the account is the **net wage**. Apprentices also receive an apprentice’s wage, which rises with each year of the apprenticeship.

In Switzerland, many employees receive a **13th monthly salary**. This means that each year they get not twelve but thirteen monthly salaries. The extra salary is often paid out in December. Whether you get it is written in the employment contract or in the collective labour agreement.

In Switzerland, parents receive a **child allowance** for each child, and from the age of 16 an education allowance, as long as the child is in education. The amount is set by each canton, but there is a minimum amount for the whole of Switzerland. Other income can be interest on a savings account, rent or pensions. Retired people, for example, receive an AVS pension.

If you know your income, you can make a **budget** and plan how much you can spend and save. Regular income such as wages or pocket money is easy to plan. It is best to put part of irregular income, such as money given as presents, aside. A good rule is never to spend more than you earn.

begriffe.erklaerung: The wage before any deductions.
The wage that is actually paid out after deductions.
Money that parents receive on top of their wage for each child.
The Old-Age and Survivors’ Insurance, which pays pensions in old age.

gewusst: In Switzerland, usually about 10 to 15 per cent of the gross wage is deducted for social insurance.
The AVS was introduced in 1948 and is one of Switzerland’s most important social security schemes.
Some cantons pay much higher child allowances than the legal minimum.

teile.einleitung: Pocket money is a small amount of money that children get regularly from their parents and are allowed to manage themselves. In Switzerland it is usually called Sackgeld. With pocket money, children learn how to handle money.
wichtigste: In Switzerland pocket money is often called Sackgeld.
Usually parents give their children pocket money.
Many children get their pocket money every week.
The child may decide for themselves what to spend their pocket money on.
With pocket money you learn how to handle money.
If you get 3 francs a week, you have 6 francs after 2 weeks.
Once the pocket money is spent, you have to wait until next time.

abschnitte.text: **Sackgeld** is money that children get regularly and manage themselves. In Germany it is called **Taschengeld**, and in English pocket money. It is usually given by parents, sometimes also by grandparents or godparents. It is not a wage for housework, but is meant to help with learning.

Younger children often get their pocket money **every week**, because a week is easy for them to keep track of. Older children and young people often get it once a month. How much they get is decided by the parents, depending on age and family. Budget Advice Switzerland publishes recommendations that many families use as a guide.

With pocket money you learn to **handle money**. You notice that money is limited and that you cannot buy everything at once. If you get 3 francs a week, you have 6 francs after 2 weeks and can afford something bigger if you wait. If the money is already spent, you have to wait until the next **payday**.

The pocket money belongs to the child, so in principle the child may **decide for themselves** what to spend it on. Parents can set rules, for example no unhealthy things or no games meant for older children. Bad buys are part of learning too. If you have once bought something useless, you think harder next time.

Part of the pocket money can go into the **piggy bank** or the youth savings account. This way you can save up for a bigger wish, such as a bike or a game. A small notebook in which you write down income and spending is helpful. This way you keep track, just as with a real **budget**.

In Switzerland there is the **youth wage** (Jugendlohn) model for older children and young people. They get a larger amount and use it to pay for things such as clothes, their mobile phone or leisure themselves. This lets them practise dividing money up over a whole month. From about the age of 13, young people can also earn a bit extra with small jobs such as babysitting or delivering newspapers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss word for pocket money.
A plan of how much money you have and what you spend it on.
A larger amount with which young people pay for clothes and leisure themselves.
A wish for which you put money aside.

gewusst: The word Sackgeld comes from Hosensack, the Swiss word for a trouser pocket.
Many experts advise against cancelling pocket money as a punishment, because it is about learning to handle money.
Some children keep a little pocket money book in which they write down every purchase.

teile.einleitung: With tiers payant, the health insurer pays the bill directly to the hospital, pharmacy or surgery. The insured person then only receives a bill for their share of the costs. So they do not have to pay any money up front.
wichtigste: With tiers payant, the healthcare provider bills the insurer directly.
The insurer first pays the whole bill.
Afterwards it asks the insured person for the deductible and excess.
Hospitals and pharmacies usually bill this way.
The insured person receives a copy of the bill.
Doctors’ surgeries often use tiers garant, depending on their contract.

abschnitte.text: **Tiers payant** is French and means “the third party pays”. The third party is the **health insurer**. It pays the bill directly to the **healthcare provider**.
