Healthcare providers are, for example, hospitals, pharmacies or laboratories. The patient does not have to pay anything up front.

After the treatment, the hospital or pharmacy sends the bill to the insurer. The insurer checks it and pays it. Then it sends the insured person a statement of their **cost sharing**. This shows the **deductible** and **excess**. You then pay this amount to the insurer.

At the **pharmacy** you show your **insurance card**. The pharmacy then bills the medicines directly to the insurer. **Hospitals** also bill inpatient treatment directly to the insurer. This makes sense, because such bills are often very high. Doctors’ surgeries, on the other hand, often use **tiers garant**, depending on their contract.

Even with tiers payant, you should know what a treatment cost. That is why the insured person receives a **copy of the bill**. This lets them check whether everything is correct. If you discover a mistake, report it to the insurer or the healthcare provider. This helps to avoid unnecessary costs.

gewusst: Without tiers payant, you would often have to pay thousands of francs up front for a hospital stay.
The insurance card contains the information a pharmacy needs to bill directly.

teile.einleitung: The market economy is an economic system in which supply and demand decide what is produced and what it costs. It is not the state that plans production; instead many companies and customers decide for themselves. Like most countries in Europe, Switzerland has a market economy with social rules.
wichtigste: In a market economy, supply and demand determine prices.
The equilibrium price is where the quantity supplied and the quantity demanded are the same.
A maximum price set by the state below the equilibrium price leads to excess demand.
A monopoly is a market form with only one seller and many buyers.
External effects are effects on people not involved that are not included in the price.
The term social market economy was coined by Alfred Müller-Armack.
In Switzerland, the Competition Commission COMCO watches over competition.

abschnitte.text: In a **market economy**, companies decide for themselves what they produce, and consumers decide what they buy. Where supply and demand meet, a **market** comes into being. The opposite is the **planned economy**, in which the state decides what is produced, as in the former Soviet Union. As early as 1776, the Scottish economist Adam Smith described how markets are steered as if by an invisible hand.

If a product is wanted but scarce, its price rises. If there is a lot of it and few people want it, the price falls. The **equilibrium price** is where the quantity supplied and the quantity demanded are exactly the same. If the state sets a maximum price below this, more people want to buy than there are goods, and **excess demand** arises.

**Price elasticity** shows how strongly demand reacts to changes in price. If the price rises by 10 per cent and the quantity bought falls by 20 per cent, the elasticity is minus 2. With basic foods such as bread, people react little; with luxury goods they often react strongly. Companies use this knowledge to set their prices.

If there are many sellers, there is strong **competition**, and prices tend to stay low. In a **monopoly** there is only one seller, who can set prices almost alone. If a few large companies share a market, this is called an oligopoly. If companies secretly agree on prices, they form a forbidden cartel.

After the Second World War, the German economist **Alfred Müller-Armack** coined the term social market economy. It means that the market is free, but the state ensures social balance, for example with social insurance. The state also steps in with **external effects**, for example when a factory pollutes the environment and other people bear the costs. Ludwig Erhard put the model into practice in West Germany.

In Switzerland, the Federal Constitution guarantees **economic freedom**. The **Competition Commission**, COMCO for short (WEKO in German), fights illegal cartels and can impose large fines. The Price Supervisor makes sure that companies with great market power do not charge excessive prices. With the AVS and unemployment insurance there is also social balance.

begriffe.erklaerung: The quantity of a product that sellers offer.
The quantity of a product that buyers want to have.
A market with only one single seller.
A forbidden agreement between companies about prices or markets.
When several sellers compete for the same customers.

gewusst: At a weekly market you can watch the market economy live: in the evening, leftover fruit is often sold more cheaply.
In his book, Adam Smith explained the division of labour using the example of a pin factory.
Economic freedom is expressly laid down as a fundamental right in the Swiss Federal Constitution.

teile.einleitung: Die Mobiliar is the oldest private insurance company in Switzerland. It was founded in 1826 and is based in Bern. Anyone insured with it gets help if, for example, something is damaged or lost through fire, water or theft.
wichtigste: Die Mobiliar is the oldest private insurance company in Switzerland.
It was founded in 1826 and is based in Bern.
The word Mobiliar means the movable things in a flat, for example furniture.
Die Mobiliar is organised as a cooperative.
It has general agencies all over Switzerland.
Many Swiss households have household contents insurance with Die Mobiliar.

abschnitte.text: The word **Mobiliar** comes from the Latin “mobilis”, which means movable. It means all the movable things in a flat, such as furniture, clothes, crockery and books. The company was founded in 1826 to insure exactly these things against fire. That is why it used to be called the Swiss Furniture Insurance Company (Schweizerische Mobiliar-Versicherungsgesellschaft).

With **insurance**, many people pay a contribution every year, the **premium**. If one of them suffers damage, the insurance company uses this money to pay for the damage. This way nobody has to bear a large loss alone. Die Mobiliar insures, for example, household contents, cars, buildings and companies.

Die Mobiliar has its headquarters in **Bern**. It does not belong to shareholders on the stock exchange, but is organised as a cooperative. When business is going well, it gives part of the profit back to the insured. Die Mobiliar employs several thousand people in Switzerland.

Die Mobiliar has around 80 **general agencies** in all regions of Switzerland. There, experts advise customers and deal with claims. If a hailstorm damages cars, for example, they quickly organise help. This way the staff know the conditions in their region well.

Storms, floods and hail cause great damage in Switzerland every year. Die Mobiliar therefore supports municipalities with projects to protect against **natural hazards**. Together with the University of Bern it runs a research lab on natural risks. There, for example, scientists study where floods are likely.

begriffe.erklaerung: Many people pay in together so that help can be given when damage happens.
The amount you pay regularly for insurance.
All the movable things in a flat, such as furniture, clothes and electronics.
A regional office of an insurance company.

gewusst: Die Mobiliar is almost 200 years old and therefore older than the Swiss federal state of 1848.
Die Mobiliar gives part of its profit back to its customers as a share of the surplus.
A single violent hailstorm in Switzerland can cause damage worth hundreds of millions of francs.

teile.einleitung: Schindler is a Swiss company that makes, installs and maintains lifts and escalators. It was founded in Lucerne in 1874 and today operates all over the world. If you take a lift in a tower block, a railway station or a shopping centre, there is a good chance you are standing in a Schindler lift.
wichtigste: Schindler makes lifts and escalators.
The company was founded in Lucerne in 1874.
Today its headquarters is in Ebikon in the canton of Lucerne.
Schindler is one of the largest lift companies in the world.
A large part of the business is maintaining existing installations.
The Schindler and Bonnard families own the majority of the company.

abschnitte.text: In 1874 **Robert Schindler** and Eduard Villiger founded a small workshop in **Lucerne**. At first they built various machines. The company soon specialised in **lifts**. Towards the end of the 19th century Schindler supplied its first electric lifts.

A lift consists of a **car** that travels up and down in a shaft. The car hangs on strong steel cables or belts. On the other side hangs a **counterweight**, so that the motor needs less power. Several brakes make sure that the car can never simply fall down.

Today Schindler operates in over a hundred countries. About 70,000 people work for the company worldwide (as of 2024). Schindler has installed lifts in famous tower blocks all over the world. Its biggest competitors are companies such as **Otis** from the USA and Kone from Finland.

Lifts and escalators must be checked regularly. For this Schindler has thousands of **service technicians** at work. Many installations are now connected to the internet and report faults automatically. This means experts can often make repairs before a lift gets stuck.

Without lifts there would be no **tower blocks**, because nobody would walk up 50 floors every day. Lifts are also very important for people in wheelchairs, with prams or with heavy luggage. In stations and airports, escalators carry many people quickly from floor to floor. Schindler installations can also be found in Zurich main station and in many Swiss hospitals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A car that carries people or goods between floors, also called an elevator.
A staircase whose steps move by themselves, also called a moving staircase.
A heavy weight that balances the car and saves the motor work.
Regular checking and care so that a machine stays safe.

gewusst: According to the company, Schindler installations carry well over a billion people every day.
Schindler has developed a lift where you choose your floor on a screen before you get in.
The counterweight is usually about as heavy as the car when it is half full.

teile.einleitung: Bühler is a Swiss engineering company from Uzwil in the canton of St Gallen. Its machines grind grain into flour and produce chocolate, pasta and animal feed. Although hardly anyone knows the company, almost every person in the world probably eats something every day that was made with a Bühler machine.
wichtigste: Bühler is an engineering company based in Uzwil SG.
The company was founded in 1860 by Adolf Bühler and still belongs to the Bühler family today.
A Bühler mill grinds grain into flour.
Bühler is considered the world market leader for grain mills.
A “hidden champion” is a world market leader that hardly anyone knows.
Bühler employs over 12,000 people worldwide.

abschnitte.text: **Bühler** is a family business from Uzwil in eastern Switzerland. Adolf Bühler founded it in 1860 as a small foundry. Today Bühler is active in over 140 countries and has many factories and service centres all over the world. The company still belongs to the founding family.

Bühler is famous for its **grain mills**. In them, wheat, maize or rice is cleaned, husked and ground into flour. According to the company, a large share of the grain processed worldwide is processed on Bühler machines. This makes Bühler important for feeding billions of people.

Bühler also builds plants for chocolate, pasta, breakfast cereals and animal feed. Bühler machines roast coffee beans and sort rice. The company also makes **die-casting machines**, which are used to cast car parts out of aluminium. Its range even includes coatings for glass and spectacle lenses.

Bühler is a typical **hidden champion**, a hidden world leader. Such companies lead the world in their field, but are hardly known to the public. This is because they do not sell products to end customers in shops, but machines to other companies. Switzerland has a particularly large number of such hidden world market leaders.

Bühler trains many apprentices in Uzwil, for example polymechanics and design engineers. The company does research on new foods, for example on proteins from peas or insects. It also wants to make its machines more economical so that they use less energy and water. In this way, feeding the growing world population is meant to become more sustainable.

begriffe.erklaerung: A branch of industry that develops and builds machines.
A company that is world market leader but hardly known.
The company that sells the most in a field all over the world.
Liquid metal is pressed into a mould at high pressure.

gewusst: Bühler has its own training centre in Uzwil, where many apprentices start their apprenticeship every year.
A large share of the world’s chocolate is processed on Bühler plants.
Uzwil, a village with only around 13,000 inhabitants, is the headquarters of a group that operates worldwide.

teile.einleitung: The hospital contribution is a small amount that adults pay themselves for each day in hospital. It is 15 francs a day. The idea behind it: anyone who is in hospital saves money at home, for example on food.
wichtigste: The hospital contribution is 15 francs per day in hospital.
It applies to an inpatient stay, in other words when you stay in hospital at least overnight.
Children do not have to pay a hospital contribution.
Young adults up to 25 in education or training are also exempt.
The contribution does not apply with maternity either.
The contribution comes on top of the deductible and excess.
There is no yearly upper limit for the hospital contribution.

abschnitte.text: The **hospital contribution** is set out in the Health Insurance Act. It has to be paid when you are in hospital as an **inpatient**. It is 15 francs a day. For a week in hospital, this adds up to around 100 francs. The health insurer charges it together with the deductible and excess.

The contribution is meant to take into account that during a hospital stay you save on **living costs** at home. Anyone in hospital does not have to shop and cook for themselves, for example. That is why you pay a small part of the accommodation and meals yourself. The contribution is deliberately kept small. It is not meant to cover the high costs of treatment.

Children up to 18 pay no contribution. Young adults up to 25 who are still in **education or training** are also exempt. Women do not pay it for hospital stays due to **maternity**, for example for a birth. Young adults should send the health insurer confirmation that they are in education. Otherwise the contribution may be charged anyway.

The difference between outpatient and inpatient is important. **Outpatient** means that you go home on the same day after the treatment. Then there is no hospital contribution. **Inpatient** means that you stay in hospital at least one night. More and more procedures are now done as outpatient treatment, because this is often cheaper and more pleasant for many people.

The hospital contribution is a fixed amount and does not depend on the size of the hospital bill. The actual treatment costs are shared between the health insurer and the **canton of residence**. For inpatient treatment, the canton now pays at least 55 per cent. The health insurer covers the rest, minus the insured person’s cost sharing. Altogether a day in hospital often costs well over 1000 francs.

begriffe.erklaerung: 15 francs a day that adults pay themselves during a hospital stay.
Treatment where you stay in hospital at least one night.
Treatment after which you go home on the same day.
Document from the school or training company showing that you are in education or training.

gewusst: For 30 days in hospital, the hospital contribution adds up to 450 francs.
The hospital contribution does not count towards the maximum excess of 700 francs.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Bank, SNB for short, is the central bank of Switzerland. It issues the banknotes and makes sure that the franc keeps its value. It has its head offices in Bern and Zurich and started its work in 1907.
wichtigste: The Swiss National Bank is the central bank of Switzerland.
It began its business activities in 1907.
Its two head offices are in Bern and Zurich.
For the SNB, price stability means consumer prices rising by less than 2 per cent a year.
From 2011 to 15 January 2015 there was a minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs to the euro.
One third of its profit distribution goes to the Confederation and two thirds to the cantons.
The SNB is a public limited company governed by special law.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank** is the central bank of Switzerland and so the “bank of the banks”. It began its business activities on 20 June 1907. Its two head offices are in **Bern**, on the Bundesplatz opposite the Federal Palace, and in **Zurich**. It is independent, which means that the government may not give it orders.

The SNB’s most important task is **price stability**. By this it means consumer prices rising by less than 2 per cent a year. It also issues the **banknotes**, manages the currency reserves and makes sure that payments between banks work. The coins, on the other hand, are made by Swissmint on behalf of the Confederation.

Since June 2019 the SNB has steered monetary policy with the **SNB policy rate**. Before that it used a target range for the three-month Libor. From January 2015 to June 2022 there was a **negative interest rate** of minus 0.75 per cent. It also buys or sells foreign currencies such as euros and dollars to influence the franc.

In September 2011 the franc was very strong, which harmed the export industry. The SNB therefore introduced a **minimum exchange rate** of 1.20 francs to the euro and bought huge amounts of euros to keep it. On 15 January 2015 it surprisingly removed the minimum rate. The franc then rose sharply in value within minutes, which made headlines around the world.

The SNB is a **public limited company governed by special law**; its tasks are laid down in the National Bank Act. Its shares are traded on the stock exchange, but most of them belong to cantons and cantonal banks. The shareholders receive only a small, limited dividend. The bank is run by the three-member **Governing Board**, which is led by a chairman or chairwoman.

The SNB owns large **foreign currency reserves** and around 1040 tonnes of gold. Depending on how the markets develop, it makes large profits or large losses in a year. If the profit is high enough, it pays out money: one third goes to the Confederation and two thirds to the cantons. For many cantons this distribution is an important part of their income.

begriffe.erklaerung: The highest bank of a country, which issues the money.
The most important interest rate, which the central bank uses to steer the economy.
Money in other currencies, for example euros or dollars.
An exchange rate below which a currency is not supposed to fall.
The three-member management of the National Bank.

gewusst: Part of the SNB’s gold reserves is stored abroad, for example in Great Britain and Canada.
The SNB is one of the few central banks in the world whose shares can be bought on the stock exchange.
The removal of the minimum exchange rate on 15 January 2015 is often called the “franc shock”.

teile.einleitung: Cailler is the oldest Swiss chocolate brand that still exists. François-Louis Cailler founded it in 1819 on Lake Geneva. Today Cailler chocolate is made in Broc in the canton of Fribourg, where you can also visit the factory.
wichtigste: Cailler is the oldest Swiss chocolate brand that still exists.
François-Louis Cailler founded the company in 1819 in Corsier near Vevey.
The Cailler factory is in Broc in the canton of Fribourg.
Since 1929 Cailler has belonged to the food group Nestlé.
Milk from the Gruyère region is used for the milk chocolate.
The visitor attraction Maison Cailler draws many visitors every year.

abschnitte.text: In 1819 **François-Louis Cailler** opened one of the first mechanical chocolate factories in Switzerland in Corsier near Vevey. At that time chocolate was still an expensive luxury product. Cailler had learned in Italy how to process cocoa. His brand still exists today, over 200 years later.

Daniel Peter was François-Louis Cailler’s son-in-law. In 1875 in Vevey he succeeded in mixing chocolate with milk, and so **milk chocolate** was created. This was difficult, because the water in milk and the fat in cocoa do not combine well. This invention made Swiss chocolate world famous.

In 1898 Alexandre Cailler, a grandson of the founder, built a new factory in **Broc** in the canton of Fribourg. The village lies in the Gruyère region, where there are many farms with cows. So the factory always had fresh milk nearby. To this day, the milk for Cailler chocolate is supplied by farmers from the surrounding area.

In 1911 Cailler joined together with the companies Peter and Kohler. In 1929 the company became part of **Nestlé**, the large food group from Vevey. Nestlé has kept the Cailler brand and sells it mainly in Switzerland. Well-known products are the chocolates Frigor, Ambassador and Femina.

Since 2010 there has been the visitor attraction **Maison Cailler** in Broc. There you learn how cocoa grows, how chocolate is made and how it used to be sold. At the end you may taste different kinds. Maison Cailler is one of the most visited destinations in the canton of Fribourg.

begriffe.erklaerung: The beans of the cocoa tree, from which chocolate is made.
A small piece of chocolate with a filling.
A region in the canton of Fribourg, known for cheese and milk.
A name by which you recognise a company’s products.

gewusst: It took Daniel Peter several years before his milk chocolate really worked.
Broc has its own railway station called Broc-Fabrique right next to the chocolate factory.
Swiss people eat about 10 kilograms of chocolate per head each year, which puts them among the world leaders.

teile.einleitung: In basic health insurance you can choose between different insurance models. They differ in how you get treatment and how high the premium is. But the services paid for are the same in all of them.
wichtigste: All models of basic insurance pay for the same services.
Only the route to treatment and the amount of the premium change.
In the standard model you have a free choice of doctor.
The standard model usually has the highest premium.
In the family doctor model you first go to your own family doctor.
Anyone who does not keep to the rules of a model risks the insurer not paying.

abschnitte.text: An **insurance model** sets out which route you have to take when you are ill. Basic insurance always pays for the same **services**, no matter which model you choose. This is required by the health insurance law. What differs is whether you may choose freely or have to ask a particular contact point first. In return, the **premium** is different.

In the **standard model** you have a **free choice of doctor**. So you may go directly to any doctor or specialist without asking anyone first. This is convenient, because you do not have to follow any rules. In return, the premium is usually higher than with the other models. Anyone who does not choose anything else is automatically insured in the standard model.

In the **family doctor model** you always go to your own family doctor first. In the **HMO model**, the first point of contact is a group practice, known as a health centre. In the **Telmed model** you first call a medical advice line. This contact point decides whether you need to see a specialist. Because unnecessary treatments are avoided this way, the premium is lower.

Anyone who has chosen a cheaper model must keep to its rules. If you go straight to a specialist in the family doctor model without good reason, the insurer may not pay for the treatment. Anyone who repeatedly ignores the rules can be moved back into the **standard model**. In a real **emergency**, however, you may always get help straight away. The exact rules are set out in the health insurer’s conditions.

gewusst: Many adults in Switzerland today have chosen an alternative model instead of the standard model.
The term HMO comes from English and stands for “Health Maintenance Organization”.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss franc is the money of Switzerland. One franc has 100 centimes (Rappen), and internationally it is abbreviated to CHF. It is considered one of the most stable currencies in the world and is also used in Liechtenstein.
wichtigste: Switzerland’s money is called the franc.
1 franc is 100 centimes, half a franc is 50 centimes.
The international abbreviation is CHF.
The Swiss franc has existed since 1850.
In Liechtenstein people also pay with the Swiss franc.
The banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
To make 1 franc you need 10 coins of 10 centimes.

abschnitte.text: The **franc** is the official currency of Switzerland. One franc is divided into 100 **centimes** (Rappen), so 2 francs are 200 centimes. The abbreviation **CHF** stands for “Confoederatio Helvetica franc”, Confoederatio Helvetica being the Latin name for Switzerland. In everyday life people often also write “Fr.”.

Before 1850 many cantons had their own money, and altogether there were hundreds of different coins. With the Coinage Act of 1850, the young federal state introduced the **Swiss franc** for the whole country. At that time it was based on the French franc. Since 1907 the Swiss National Bank has issued the banknotes.

There are seven coins: 5, 10 and 20 centimes and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. To make 1 franc, for example, you need 10 coins of 10 centimes. The **banknotes** come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. The current series of notes was introduced from 2016 and shows themes such as time, light, wind, water and language, which shape Switzerland.

Besides Switzerland, **Liechtenstein** also uses the Swiss franc as its official money. This has been the case since 1924 and was later set out in a currency treaty. In the German exclave of Büsingen on the Upper Rhine, too, people often pay with francs in everyday life. In many border towns, shops accept both francs and euros.

The franc is considered a **safe currency**, because Switzerland is politically stable and has an independent National Bank. In crises, people from all over the world buy francs, and then it becomes more expensive. A strong franc makes holidays abroad cheaper, but makes Swiss export goods more expensive for other countries. That is why the National Bank watches the **exchange rate** closely.

Today many people pay by card or with the payment app **TWINT**. Even so, cash is still very popular in Switzerland. The 1000-franc note is one of the most valuable banknotes in the world. Because there are no longer any 1-centime coins, cash payments at the till are rounded to 5 centimes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The official money of a country.
The hundredth part of a franc.
The international abbreviation for the Swiss franc.
How much one currency is worth in another currency.
A note of money made of paper or plastic.

gewusst: Swiss banknotes have a portrait-format design and can also be looked at upright.
The 1000-franc note is one of the most valuable banknotes in circulation worldwide.
The name Rappen comes from a bird picture on old coins, which people mockingly took to be a raven (Rabe).

teile.einleitung: Ricola is a Swiss company known all over the world for its herb sweets. The sweets are made in Laufen in the canton of Basel-Landschaft. The classic mixture contains 13 different herbs.
wichtigste: Ricola mainly makes herb sweets and herbal tea.
The company is based in Laufen BL.
The classic herb mixture is made up of 13 herbs.
The company was founded in 1930 by Emil Richterich.
The name Ricola stands for Richterich and Compagnie Laufen.
Ricola still belongs to the founding family today.
The herbs are grown by farmers in Swiss mountain areas.

abschnitte.text: In 1930 the baker and confectioner **Emil Richterich** bought a small bakery in **Laufen**. There he made various sweets. In 1940 he invented the **herb sugar** (Kräuterzucker), a sweet with 13 herbs. This sweet became a great success and is still the company’s best-known product today.

The classic mixture includes **thyme**, sage, peppermint, elder, ribwort plantain and lady’s mantle, among others. The herbs are meant to soothe the throat and taste fresh. They are not bought abroad, but grown by around a hundred farming families in Switzerland. Many fields are in **mountain areas** such as Valais, the Emmental or the Val Poschiavo.

The sweets are made in Laufen and sold to many countries around the world. They are especially popular in Europe, the USA and Asia. In 1967 the company was given the name **Ricola**, an abbreviation of Richterich and Compagnie Laufen. Besides sweets, Ricola also sells herbal teas and sugar-free kinds.

Ricola also became famous through funny television adverts. In them, people from other countries argue about who invented the sweets, until a Swiss person asks: “Who invented it?” The adverts often show **Alpine landscapes** and meadows of herbs. In this way Ricola links its sweets with the image of clean Swiss nature.

Several Ricola buildings were designed by the Basel architects **Herzog & de Meuron**. The herb centre in Laufen from 2014 has walls made of rammed earth. Inside, the dried herbs are cleaned and mixed. Architecture fans from all over the world travel to Laufen especially to look at the buildings.

begriffe.erklaerung: Plants whose leaves or flowers are used for their scent, taste or effect.
A company that belongs to a family and is often run by it.
Selling goods abroad.
A job in which you make sweets, gateaux and pastries.

gewusst: Ricola sells most of its sweets abroad rather than in Switzerland.
The herbs are grown without chemical sprays.
A Ricola building in Laufen has clay walls that look like layers of rock.

teile.einleitung: Sugar is found in many foods and tastes sweet. But too much sugar is harmful to the teeth, because it can cause holes.
wichtigste: A lot of sugar harms your teeth.
Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid.
The acid attacks the tooth enamel, and this is how tooth decay develops.
A good mid-morning snack is, for example, an apple and water.
Sugary drinks also contain a lot of sugar.
Brushing your teeth and eating fewer sweet things protect your teeth.

abschnitte.text: **Sugar** is a substance that tastes sweet and gives the body energy. In Switzerland, sugar is mainly made from **sugar beet**, and in other countries also from sugar cane. Sugar is not only found in sweets. Syrup, lemonade, yoghurt or ketchup often contain a lot of sugar too. Fruit naturally contains fruit sugar.

Tiny **bacteria** live in the mouth. They feed on sugar and produce **acid** as they do so. This acid attacks the hard **tooth enamel**. Over time a hole can form like this, which is called **tooth decay**. It is especially harmful if you keep eating or drinking something sweet all day long.

For the break at school, **fruit**, vegetables, bread or nuts are suitable. **Water** is the best drink. That is why an apple and water make a good mid-morning snack for your teeth. It is better to eat sweet things rarely and after a meal rather than in between. Afterwards it helps to rinse your mouth with water.

As well as less sugar, good **toothbrushing** in the morning and evening helps most of all. A toothpaste with **fluoride** makes tooth enamel more resistant. There are also sweets with **sugar substitutes**, which do less harm to the teeth. In Switzerland you can recognise such products by the symbol with the smiling tooth man and the umbrella. Sugar-free chewing gum after eating can also help.

gewusst: The tooth man with the umbrella is a protective symbol for tooth-friendly sweets and comes from Switzerland.
A can of lemonade can contain several sugar cubes’ worth of dissolved sugar.

teile.einleitung: Givaudan is a Swiss company that makes flavours and fragrances. Whether a yoghurt tastes of strawberry or a shampoo smells of apple, there is often a Givaudan mixture behind it. Even so, only a few people know the name.
wichtigste: Givaudan is the largest maker of flavours and fragrances in the world.
Its headquarters is in Vernier near Geneva.
The company was founded in 1895 by the brothers Léon and Xavier Givaudan.
Givaudan sells its mixtures to other companies, which use them to make food, perfumes and cleaning products.
That is why the name Givaudan hardly ever appears on packaging.
Many thousands of people work for the company worldwide.

abschnitte.text: Givaudan makes **flavours** for food and drinks and **fragrances** for perfumes, soaps and washing powders. The company works in two large divisions, one for taste and one for scent. Its customers are other companies, for example makers of sweets, soft drinks or cosmetics. They buy ready-made mixtures and put them into their own products.

The brothers Léon and Xavier Givaudan founded the company in Zurich in 1895. Just a few years later it moved to **Vernier** in the canton of Geneva, where it is still based today. From 1963 Givaudan belonged to the Basel pharmaceutical group **Roche**. In 2000 Givaudan became an independent company again and was listed on the Swiss stock exchange. Later it bought several other flavour companies, for example Quest International in 2007.

A **perfumer** mixes a new fragrance from hundreds of raw materials. Some substances come from nature, for example from flowers, woods or fruits; others are made in the laboratory. A well-trained perfumer can tell more than a thousand scents apart. The training takes many years, and Givaudan runs its own school for it. A well-known perfume can consist of over a hundred individual ingredients.

A **flavour** gives a food its typical taste and smell. Strawberry yoghurt, paprika crisps or lemonade often contain flavourings. The experts are called **flavourists**; they are constantly tasting and smelling new mixtures. Today Givaudan is also researching how meat substitutes made from plants can taste like real meat. The company is also looking for ways to make food with less sugar and salt still taste good.

Givaudan has sites and factories in a great many countries on all continents. The company buys raw materials such as **vanilla** from Madagascar or flowers from various parts of the world. In Switzerland, many employees work at the headquarters in Vernier. Givaudan shares are among the most valuable on the Swiss stock exchange.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that gives a food a particular taste and smell.
A substance that smells good and is used, for example, in perfume or soap.
An expert who invents and mixes new fragrances.
An expert who develops new flavours for food and drinks.

gewusst: You have probably already eaten or smelled something today that contains substances from Givaudan.
A perfumer trains their nose every day, just as an athlete trains their muscles.

teile.einleitung: A bank account is like an invisible purse at the bank, where your money is kept safe and recorded. With an account you can receive money, save, pay by card and settle bills.
wichtigste: A bank account is an account at a bank where money paid in and paid out is recorded.
The IBAN is an international account number.
A Swiss IBAN begins with the letters CH.
A savings account is used to put money away for the longer term.
With the PIN code you confirm payments and cash withdrawals.
An account is overdrawn when more money has been taken out than was in it.
On the bank statement you can see all deposits and withdrawals.

abschnitte.text: A **bank account** is a list at the bank that shows how much money belongs to you. Every deposit and every withdrawal is written down there; this is called **recording** or booking. The current amount is called the **balance**. If Sina has 250 francs, pays in 80 francs and withdraws 120 francs, her balance afterwards is 210 francs.

Every account has its own number, the **IBAN**, which stands for International Bank Account Number. A Swiss IBAN begins with **CH** and has 21 characters in total. Anyone who wants to transfer money to you needs your IBAN and your name. You may give out your IBAN, but never the password for your online banking.

You need a **current account** or salary account for everyday life, for example to receive your wages and pay bills. A **savings account** is for putting money aside for the longer term, and you often get a little more interest there. Many banks offer special youth accounts with no fees. For small children, parents or grandparents usually open an account.

An account often comes with a **debit card**, which you can use to pay in shops or to withdraw cash from the Bancomat. For this you need the **PIN code**, a secret number usually with four to six digits. You must learn your PIN by heart and must never tell it to anyone or write it on the card. Many young people also pay with TWINT, a Swiss payment app that is linked to the account.

An account is **overdrawn** when more money has been spent than was in it. The balance is then negative, that is, in the minus. The bank usually charges high interest on this amount. That is why banks usually prevent youth accounts from being overdrawn.

The **bank statement** lists all deposits and withdrawals with the date and amount. It is worth checking it regularly, so that you notice unknown payments straight away. Banks never ask for passwords by email or text message; such messages are attempts at fraud, and this is called **phishing**. In Switzerland, savings of up to 100,000 francs per person and bank are protected by deposit protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: The international number of a bank account, beginning with CH in Switzerland.
A secret number used to confirm card payments.
How much money is in the account at the moment.
Fraudulent messages that criminals use to try to get passwords.

gewusst: The two digits after CH in the IBAN are check digits that let a computer spot typing mistakes.
Many banks open an account even for newborn babies.
The IBAN was introduced so that transfers between countries work more easily and without mistakes.

teile.einleitung: A need is the feeling that something is missing and the wish to put this right. Some needs, such as food, drink and sleep, are things every person requires to survive; others are wishes that you can also do without.
wichtigste: Every person needs food and drink to live.
Basic needs are things you cannot live well without, such as food, a home, clothing and sleep.
A flat or a house offers protection from cold, rain and danger.
A new toy or a new bike is a wish and not a basic need.
When money is tight, you should buy food first.
Money cannot fulfil every wish.
The body needs sleep every night to recover.

abschnitte.text: If you are hungry, you want to eat something; if you are thirsty, you want to drink. This feeling that something is missing is called a **need**. In economics, needs are the reason why people buy and make things. The things that satisfy our needs are called **goods**, for example bread, shoes or a bike.

Some needs are vital; they are called **basic needs**. They include food, drink, sleep, clothing and a home for shelter. In winter you need warm clothes so that you do not freeze. Health, safety and people who love you are also very important for a good life. When money is tight, these basic needs are covered first.

Besides the basic needs there are many **wishes**. A new bike, a toy, a mobile phone or a holiday by the sea are nice, but not essential for life. A sentence such as “I would like a new bike” describes a wish. Many wishes also come from advertising or because friends have something new. It is worth thinking about what you really need.

In the 1940s the American psychologist **Abraham Maslow** arranged needs into levels. This later became the well-known **pyramid of needs**. At the very bottom are physical needs such as food and sleep, above that safety, then friendship and belonging. Higher up come recognition and, at the very top, the wish to develop your abilities.

Most people have more wishes than they can fulfil with their money. This **scarcity** forces us to make decisions. If you buy something, you cannot spend the same money again on something else. That is why it helps to sort wishes by importance and to save up for big wishes.

Money cannot fulfil every wish. Friendship, love, time with your family or a beautiful sunset cannot be bought. These **non-material** needs are often even more important for happiness than things. The United Nations **Convention on the Rights of the Child** of 1989 states that every child has a right to food, education, health and play.

begriffe.erklaerung: The feeling that something is missing and the wish to get it.
A need that you absolutely require to live, such as food or sleep.
Something you would like to have but do not really need.
Things people use to satisfy their needs.

gewusst: A person can survive only a few days without water, but several weeks without food.
School-age children need about 9 to 11 hours of sleep a night.
Maslow himself never drew a pyramid; this picture was invented later by other people.

teile.einleitung: Inflation means that the prices of goods and services rise in general over a longer period. Then you can buy less with the same money. The opposite, when prices fall in general, is called deflation.
wichtigste: Inflation means that prices rise in general over a longer period.
With inflation, the purchasing power of money falls.
If prices fall in general, this is called deflation.
The Swiss National Bank speaks of price stability when inflation is below 2 per cent a year.
The Federal Statistical Office calculates the Swiss Consumer Price Index.
With 3 per cent inflation, a basket of goods costing 100 francs costs 103 francs after a year.
In Switzerland, inflation is often also called Teuerung, meaning things getting dearer.

abschnitte.text: With **inflation**, not just individual prices rise, but many prices at the same time. In Switzerland people often speak of **Teuerung** (rising prices). If prices rise by 3 per cent, shopping that cost 100 francs costs 103 francs a year later. The word comes from the Latin “inflare”, which means to blow up or puff up.

**Purchasing power** tells you how much you can buy with a certain amount of money. If prices rise but wages do not, you can afford less. Savings also lose value if the interest on the savings account is lower than inflation. That is why wages and pensions are often adjusted for inflation.

Every month the **Federal Statistical Office** calculates the **Swiss Consumer Price Index**, CPI for short. To do this, it watches the prices of a basket of goods with a household’s typical spending. It includes, for example, food, rents, clothes, electricity, transport and leisure. If you compare the price of the basket with the previous year, you get the inflation rate.

Inflation can arise when more money is in circulation than goods are on offer. When energy or raw materials become more expensive, many other prices rise too. In 2022, for example, high energy prices after the start of the war in Ukraine pushed inflation up sharply in many countries. In Switzerland it stayed much lower, at just under 3 per cent on average for the year, than in Germany, for example.

When prices rise extremely fast, this is called **hyperinflation**. In Germany in 1923, a loaf of bread at times cost billions of marks, and money was practically worthless. **Deflation** is also dangerous, because people then put off purchases and the economy can shrink. That is why the aim is low, stable inflation.

In Switzerland, the **Swiss National Bank** ensures price stability. If inflation rises, it raises the policy interest rate so that less money is spent. If inflation is very low, it can lower the rate. The strong franc also helps Switzerland, because it makes goods from abroad cheaper.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss word for inflation, that is, rising prices.
How much you can buy with your money.
When prices fall in general over a longer period.
A selection of typical goods whose prices are compared regularly.
Prices rising extremely fast, so that money becomes almost worthless.

gewusst: During the hyperinflation of 1923 in Germany, children played with bundles of worthless banknotes.
With inflation of 2 per cent, prices roughly double every 35 years.
In the Swiss basket of goods, housing makes up a particularly large share.

teile.einleitung: If you receive a doctor’s bill under the tiers garant system, a reimbursement form is often enclosed. With this form you claim the money back from the health insurer. You pay the bill and send the form to the insurer.
wichtigste: The reimbursement form comes with the bill under tiers garant.
It lists the treatments in detail.
You pay the bill and submit the form to the insurer.
The insurer pays back its share.
You should also submit forms for amounts below the deductible.

abschnitte.text: With **tiers garant**, the patient pays the bill herself. For her to get her money back, the insurer needs precise details. These are on the **reimbursement form**. It lists which services were provided and what they cost. The bill for paying and the form for the insurer belong together.

First you pay the bill, for example with the **QR payment slip**. Then you send the reimbursement form to the **health insurer**. You can do this by post or through the insurer’s app. The insurer checks the form and pays back its share. The deductible and excess are deducted.

Many people think a small bill below the **deductible** is not worth submitting. In this case the insurer does not pay anything back. But it counts the amount towards the deductible. Only in this way does it know when the deductible has been used up. After that it helps to pay further bills.

gewusst: You should not simply throw the reimbursement form away, otherwise the insurer has nothing to base the repayment on.

teile.einleitung: The share price is the price at which a share is traded on the stock exchange. It changes all the time, sometimes even every second. Behind it lies a simple principle: supply and demand.
wichtigste: A share is a small part of a company.
The share price is the current price of a share on the stock exchange.
It depends on supply and demand.
If many people want to buy, the price rises, and if many want to sell, it falls.
News about the company or the economy can move the price a lot.
The most important stock exchange in Switzerland is the SIX Swiss Exchange in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: A **share** is a part of a company, a **public limited company**. Anyone who owns a share is a **shareholder** and therefore owns a small piece of the company. Many large companies have millions of shares. They are traded on the **stock exchange**. There buyers and sellers meet, today almost only electronically.

The price comes about when buyers and sellers agree on a price. If many people want to buy a share but only a few want to sell, the price rises. If many want to sell but only a few want to buy, it falls. This is the principle of **supply and demand**. It works in exactly the same way at a flea market or with trading cards.

Whether someone wants to buy depends on what they expect from the company. If a company makes good **profits** or brings out a successful product, demand often rises. Bad news often makes the price fall. The general **economic situation**, interest rates and events around the world also play a part. Nobody can predict for sure where a price will go.

Swiss shares are mainly traded on the **SIX Swiss Exchange** in Zurich. Prices are given in **francs**. If you multiply the price by the number of all the shares, you get the stock market value of a company, its **market capitalisation**. Among the most valuable companies on the Swiss stock exchange are large pharmaceutical and food groups.

gewusst: In the past, traders shouted prices to each other in the trading hall. Today trading takes place almost entirely by computer.
If prices rise for a long time, people speak of a “bull market”, and if they fall for a long time, of a “bear market”.

teile.einleitung: Some medicines are only available at the pharmacy with a prescription. The prescription is written by a doctor. It tells the pharmacy which medicine someone needs and how much of it.
wichtigste: A prescription is a written instruction for a medicine.
Doctors write prescriptions.
The prescription shows the medicine, the amount and how to take it.
Some medicines are available without a prescription, others only with one.
Basic insurance pays for many medicines if they are prescribed by a doctor.
Today there are also electronic prescriptions.

abschnitte.text: A **prescription** shows the name of the patient. Added to this are the name of the medicine, the **dosage** and the amount. The dosage says how much to take and when. The prescription has the date and the doctor’s signature. That way the pharmacy knows that everything is correct.

In Switzerland, the authority **Swissmedic** divides medicines into groups. Some can be bought freely, for example some remedies for a sore throat. Others are only available after advice at the pharmacy. Strong medicines, such as many **antibiotics**, are only available with a prescription. This prevents people from taking wrong or dangerous remedies.

The pharmacist checks the prescription carefully. She explains how to take the medicine correctly. She also checks whether it goes well with other medicines. For medicines that you need for a long time, there is a **repeat prescription**. With it you can collect the remedy several times.

**Basic insurance** pays for medicines that are prescribed by a doctor and are on an official list. This list is called the **list of specialities**. The **deductible** and **excess** apply: you pay part yourself. You usually pay for medicines without a prescription entirely yourself.

gewusst: The symbol Rx on prescriptions comes from the Latin word “recipe”, which means “take”.
In German, the word “Rezept” is also used for cooking recipes, because both say exactly what you should take.

teile.einleitung: Monetary policy means all the measures a central bank uses to control how much money is in circulation in an economy and how expensive it is to borrow money. Its most important aim is usually price stability, meaning that prices neither rise nor fall too much. In Switzerland, monetary policy is made by the Swiss National Bank.
wichtigste: Monetary policy is made by a country’s central bank, in Switzerland by the SNB.
The most important aim of most central banks is price stability.
The most important tool is the policy interest rate.
In an expansionary monetary policy, the central bank lowers its policy rates.
In open market operations, the central bank buys or sells securities on the market.
Quantitative easing means that the central bank buys bonds on a large scale.
A negative policy rate means that banks have to pay interest on certain deposits at the central bank.

abschnitte.text: Monetary policy is the job of the **central bank**, the bank of the banks. It decides how much money there is and at what interest rate banks can obtain money. In Switzerland this is the Swiss National Bank, in the euro area the European Central Bank in Frankfurt, and in the USA the Federal Reserve. Central banks are usually **independent**, so that politicians cannot simply have money printed.

The most important aim is **price stability**. Prices should rise only slowly over the years, so that money keeps its value. The SNB speaks of price stability when consumer prices rise by less than 2 per cent a year. At the same time, central banks also keep an eye on the **economic cycle**, that is, on whether the economy is doing well.

abschnitte.titel: The policy rate as a tool
abschnitte.text: The **policy interest rate** is the most important lever. If the central bank lowers it, borrowing money becomes cheaper, companies invest more and the economy gets a boost; this is called **expansionary monetary policy**. If it raises the policy rate, money becomes more expensive and inflation is slowed; this is a restrictive monetary policy. The effect on prices usually only shows after months.

In **open market operations**, the central bank buys or sells securities on the market and in this way changes the money supply. After the financial crisis of 2008, many central banks bought huge amounts of bonds; this is called **quantitative easing**. For years the SNB also bought foreign currencies such as euros and dollars to prevent the franc from becoming too strong. Some central banks even introduced **negative interest rates**, the SNB from 2015 to 2022.

Economists describe money with the quantity equation M · V = P · Y. Here M is the money supply, V the **velocity of circulation** of money, P the price level and Y the quantity of goods produced. The difference between the nominal interest rate and the **real interest rate** is also important. With 3 per cent interest and 1 per cent inflation, the real interest rate is about 2 per cent, because that is how much more you can actually afford.

Monetary policy affects everyone, even if you do not see it directly. If interest rates rise, for example, **mortgages** for houses become more expensive, but there is more interest on savings accounts. If they fall, it is the other way round. The SNB usually announces its decisions four times a year, and the media report on them in detail.

begriffe.erklaerung: The state’s bank, which issues money and sets the policy interest rate.
The interest rate the central bank uses to control how expensive borrowing is.
When prices rise in general and money loses value.
A security that states or companies use to borrow money.
The interest rate after inflation has been taken off.

gewusst: With negative interest rates, banks in Switzerland at times had to pay to park money at the National Bank.
Because of its foreign currency purchases, the SNB’s balance sheet grew to several hundred billion francs.
Many central banks aim for inflation of around 2 per cent, because slightly rising prices are considered healthier than falling ones.

teile.einleitung: Spending is all the money someone pays for things or services. If you know and plan your spending, you keep track of your money and manage it better.
wichtigste: Spending means sums of money you pay for goods or services.
Fixed costs are the same every month, for example the rent.
Variable costs change from month to month.
In Switzerland, a health insurance premium must be paid for every person.
Food covers a basic need and is therefore especially important.
Small regular costs such as subscriptions add up to large amounts over a year.
If you spend less than you earn, you can save.

abschnitte.text: Every time you buy something, you have an **expense**. It might be an ice cream at the kiosk, a bus ticket or a new mobile phone. The opposite of spending is **income**, the money you receive. So that you do not spend more than you have, it is worth writing your spending down.

**Fixed costs** come regularly and are always the same amount, for example rent, a mobile phone contract or insurance. **Variable costs** change from month to month, such as food, clothes, going out or presents. You can save little on fixed costs in the short term. With variable costs, on the other hand, you can decide for yourself how much you spend.

Some costs are compulsory in Switzerland. Every person, even every baby, must have **health insurance** and pay a monthly **premium** for it. For children, the parents pay. Adults also pay taxes, and anyone who works pays contributions to the AVS. You should always plan for these costs first.

Some spending is important and some is less important. Food, housing and clothes cover **basic needs** and come first. A new game or trendy shoes are wishes that can wait. When money is tight, it helps to pay for the basic needs first and then see what is left over.

A music subscription for 15 francs a month costs 12 times 15 a year, that is **180 francs**. A jumper for 60 francs with a 20 per cent **discount** costs only 48 francs. If you do sums like these, you quickly notice which purchases are worth it. Comparing prices between different shops or different pack sizes can also save a lot of money.

A lot of spending happens on the spur of the moment, because something looks good or is on special offer. People sometimes regret such **impulse buys** later. A good trick is to sleep on it for a night before a bigger purchase. Paying without cash by card or mobile phone also tempts you to spend more, because you do not see the money in your hand.

begriffe.erklaerung: Costs that are the same amount every month, such as the rent.
Costs that change from month to month.
The amount you pay regularly for an insurance policy.
A price reduction, so that something is sold more cheaply.

gewusst: A daily coffee for 5 francs costs over 1800 francs over a year.
In Switzerland, the rent for a flat is the biggest single expense for many households.
Health insurance has been compulsory for everyone in Switzerland since 1996.

teile.einleitung: The deductible is the amount you pay yourself in a year before the health insurer covers costs. Adults can choose a higher deductible, the optional deductible. In return, the premium becomes cheaper.
wichtigste: The lowest deductible for adults is 300 francs, the highest 2500 francs.
The higher the deductible, the lower the premium.
A high deductible is worth it for people who rarely need treatment.
A low deductible is worth it if you regularly have high costs.
The deductible applies to a whole calendar year.
You cannot change it in the middle of the year because of an illness.

abschnitte.text: In basic insurance you first pay doctor’s and medicine costs yourself until a certain amount is reached. This amount is called the **deductible**. Only after that does the health insurer pay. In addition, you usually also pay an **excess** of 10 per cent of the further costs, up to a fixed upper limit. Lower amounts apply to children, and their deductible is often even zero.

For adults, the standard deductible is **300 francs**. But you can choose a higher **optional deductible**: 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 or 2500 francs. For the higher deductible, the insurer gives a discount on the premium. So anyone who chooses 2500 francs pays a much lower premium. In return, you bear more of the costs yourself if you fall ill.

With a deductible of 2500, Tim saves 1400 francs a year in premiums compared with a deductible of 300. He has hardly any doctor’s costs. So he saves money as long as he needs little treatment. But if he falls ill, he pays up to **2200 francs** more deductible himself. That is why a low deductible is often better for people with a **chronic illness** or high costs every year.

The deductible always applies to the whole **calendar year**. A change is only possible at the start of a new year. Anyone who wants a lower deductible must tell the insurer in good time, before the end of November. You cannot change in the middle of the year just because you suddenly fall ill. Otherwise everyone would only choose the low deductible when they need it.

gewusst: The word “franchise”, used in German and French for the deductible, comes from French and originally meant exemption.
For children there are separate deductible levels from 0 to 600 francs.

teile.einleitung: PostFinance is the financial institution of Swiss Post. Many people in Switzerland have an account there and use it to pay their bills. Almost every bill in Switzerland today is a QR-bill that you can scan with your mobile phone.
wichtigste: PostFinance belongs to Swiss Post.
Its roots go back to 1906, when the Post introduced the postal cheque service.
Since 2013 PostFinance has been a public limited company with a banking licence.
It is one of the largest financial institutions in Switzerland for payments.
In 2022 the QR-bill replaced the old red and orange payment slips.
By law, PostFinance may not give its own loans and mortgages.

abschnitte.text: PostFinance is a **financial institution** where you can open an account, save money and pay bills. It belongs entirely to **Swiss Post**, which in turn belongs to the Confederation. Millions of people and many companies in Switzerland have an account with PostFinance. Its yellow cards and cash machines are well known.

In 1906 the Post introduced the **postal cheque service** (Postcheckdienst). With it, people could transfer money without sending cash in a letter. PostFinance grew out of this bit by bit. Since 2013 PostFinance has been a separate public limited company and has a licence as a bank.

In the past, bills in Switzerland were paid with red and orange **payment slips**. In 2020 the **QR-bill** was introduced, and since October 2022 the old slips have no longer been valid. On the QR-bill there is a square code with a Swiss cross in the middle. If you scan it with a banking app, all the details are taken over automatically.

abschnitte.titel: What PostFinance may and may not do
abschnitte.text: PostFinance has a **universal service mandate**, which means that everyone in Switzerland should be able to make payments. In return, under the Postal Act, PostFinance may not give loans or mortgages for houses itself. That is why it earns its money mainly from fees and investments. Whether this should change is discussed again and again in politics.

Many young people open their first **account** at a bank or at PostFinance. For children and young people there are often special youth accounts with low fees or none at all. With a card and an app, you keep track of your money. It is important never to tell anyone your PIN codes and passwords.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place at a bank where your money is stored and managed.
A square pattern of dots that you can scan with your mobile phone.
A large loan used to buy a house or a flat.
Services that must be available to everyone in the country.

gewusst: Before the postal cheque service, many people simply sent banknotes in letters.
The Swiss QR code on bills has a small Swiss cross in the middle.

teile.einleitung: Novartis is one of the largest pharmaceutical groups in the world and has its headquarters in Basel. The company researches and makes medicines against many diseases, for example cancer, heart disease and eye conditions. Novartis was formed in 1996 from two old Basel companies.
wichtigste: Novartis is a pharmaceutical group with its headquarters in Basel.
The company was formed in 1996 from the merger of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz.
The name Novartis comes from Latin and means something like “new art” or “new skill”.
Novartis researches and sells new medicines, for example against cancer and heart failure.
In Basel there is the Novartis Campus with buildings by famous architects.
The pharmaceutical group Roche is also based in Basel.

abschnitte.text: Novartis develops new **medicines** and makes them. These include drugs against cancer, heart disease, eye diseases and diseases of the immune system. A well-known example is Glivec, a medicine against a certain form of blood cancer. It often takes more than ten years before a new medicine comes onto the market.

Since the 19th century Basel has been a city of **chemistry**. Companies such as Ciba, Geigy and Sandoz were founded there, which at first made dyes. Ciba and Geigy merged in 1970 to form Ciba-Geigy. In 1996 Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz merged to form **Novartis**, which at the time was one of the largest company mergers in the world.

The **Novartis Campus** is in the St. Johann district of Basel. Thousands of researchers and employees work there. Many buildings were designed by well-known architects from all over the world. The campus is like a small town with laboratories, offices, restaurants and parks.

Every year Novartis spends many billions of francs on **research**. Experts search for new active ingredients and test them in studies. New approaches include cell and gene therapies, in which the body’s own cells are changed. A medicine may only be sold once an authority such as Swissmedic has checked and approved it.

In recent years Novartis has concentrated strongly on new, innovative medicines. In 2019 the eye care company Alcon was split off. In 2023 came the split-off of **Sandoz**, which makes cheap copies of medicines. Today tens of thousands of people work for Novartis worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large company that researches and makes medicines.
Two companies joining together to form a single one.
A cheap copy of a medicine with the same active ingredient as the original.
The Swiss authority that checks and approves medicines.

gewusst: The companies that came before Novartis originally made dyes for fabrics and clothes.
Basel is home to two of the largest pharmaceutical groups in the world, Novartis and Roche.

teile.einleitung: Counterfeit money means copied banknotes or coins. So that it is easy to spot, real notes have many security features. If you know what to look out for, you will not be fooled so easily.
wichtigste: Counterfeit money means forged notes or coins.
Real Swiss banknotes have many security features.
You check them by feeling, tilting and looking through them.
Making counterfeit money or knowingly passing it on is a criminal offence.
Suspicious notes are handed to the police.

abschnitte.text: You check real banknotes with three simple steps. **Feel**: the paper feels special, and some areas are slightly raised so that you can feel them. **Tilt**: when you move the note, certain pictures and colours change. **Look through**: when you hold the note up to the light, features become visible that you cannot otherwise see. It is best to compare it with a note that you know is real.

Swiss banknotes are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**. The current series, the ninth, came into circulation between 2016 and 2019. It is considered one of the most secure in the world. The notes are made of a combination of paper and plastic. That is why they are tough and hard to copy.

abschnitte.titel: What to do if you are suspicious
abschnitte.text: If you receive a suspicious note, you should not pass it on. Take it to the **police** or to a bank. Counterfeit money is not replaced, even if you received it without meaning to. Making counterfeit money or knowingly spending it is a **criminal offence** in Switzerland. That is why shops often take a close look at large notes.

gewusst: Swiss notes have different lengths depending on their value. This also helps people with a visual impairment to tell them apart.
Coins are forged too, but much less often than banknotes.

teile.einleitung: Kühne + Nagel is one of the largest logistics companies in the world. The company organises how goods get from one place to another by ship, aeroplane, lorry and rail. It was founded in Germany and today is based in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Kühne + Nagel organises the transport of goods all over the world.
The company was founded in Bremen in 1890 by August Kühne and Friedrich Nagel.
Its headquarters is in Schindellegi in the canton of Schwyz.
Kühne + Nagel is one of the largest organisers of sea freight and air freight worldwide.
The largest shareholder is the entrepreneur Klaus-Michael Kühne.
The company has tens of thousands of employees in a great many countries.

abschnitte.text: **Logistics** means that goods arrive in the right place at the right time. A logistics company such as Kühne + Nagel plans the route, books space on ships and aeroplanes and deals with the papers at customs. Often the company does not own the ships itself, but rents space on them. Such companies are also called **freight forwarders**.

In 1890 August Kühne and Friedrich Nagel founded a forwarding company in the port city of **Bremen** in northern Germany. Later the Kühne family took over the company on its own. In the 1970s the company moved its headquarters to Switzerland. Today the head office is in **Schindellegi** on Lake Zurich, in the municipality of Feusisberg.

A large share of goods travels across the oceans in **containers** on ships. Urgent or valuable goods such as medicines or electronics go by aeroplane. On land, they continue by lorry and train. Kühne + Nagel also runs large warehouses where goods are stored, packed and sent off.

The company has offices and warehouses in around a hundred countries. It works for customers from many industries, for example car makers, fashion companies and pharmaceutical groups. During the coronavirus pandemic, logistics helped to bring vaccines, kept cold, to many countries. Without such companies, the shelves in the shops would often be empty.

Kühne + Nagel shares are traded on the **Swiss stock exchange**. But most of them belong to Klaus-Michael Kühne, a grandson of the founder. He is one of the richest people in Switzerland. Through a foundation he supports research and education in logistics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Planning how goods are stored and transported.
A company that organises transport for others.
A large metal box of standard size for transporting goods.
The checks and charges when goods are brought across a national border.

gewusst: Switzerland has no sea, but it is home to some of the most important transport companies in the world.
Many clothes, mobile phones and toys in Swiss shops have made a long journey in a container.

teile.einleitung: When cycling, you can fall off, even if you are careful. A cycle helmet then protects your head. It can prevent or reduce serious injuries.
wichtigste: A cycle helmet protects your head in a fall.
It reduces the risk of serious head injuries.
The helmet must fit well and be adjusted correctly.
After a hard fall, you need a new helmet.
In Switzerland, a helmet is compulsory for fast e-bikes.

abschnitte.text: Inside, a **cycle helmet** has a layer of firm foam. In a fall, this foam is squashed. In this way it absorbs part of the force before it reaches the **head**. On the outside, the helmet has a smooth, hard shell. It helps the head slide over the ground instead of catching on it.

A helmet only protects you if it fits well. It sits level on your head and covers your **forehead**. About two fingers fit between your eyebrows and the helmet. The **straps** form a V under your ears. The chin strap is tight enough that just one finger fits under it.

abschnitte.titel: When you need a new one
abschnitte.text: After a hard **fall**, the foam inside is often damaged. You cannot always see this from the outside. That is why you replace the helmet after an accident. Sunlight and age also weaken the material over the years. Children also grow, and the helmet still has to fit.

In Switzerland there is **no helmet requirement** for ordinary bikes. But experts such as the **BFU** recommend a helmet for everyone. For fast **e-bikes**, which provide assistance up to 45 kilometres per hour, a helmet is compulsory. Good brakes, lights and clearly visible clothing are also part of safety.

gewusst: Many helmets have a test mark that shows they meet a safety standard.
A helmet with a light or bright colours makes cyclists easier to see in traffic.

teile.einleitung: Nestlé is the largest food company in the world and has its headquarters in Vevey on Lake Geneva. Nestlé owns many well-known brands such as Nescafé, Nespresso, KitKat and Maggi. It all began in the 19th century with an infant cereal for babies.
wichtigste: Nestlé is the largest food company in the world.
Its headquarters is in Vevey in the canton of Vaud.
Its success began with an infant cereal for babies, developed by Henri Nestlé in 1867.
Henri Nestlé was a pharmacist from Frankfurt am Main who lived in Vevey.
In 1905 Nestlé merged with a condensed milk company from Cham.
Nestlé owns brands such as Nescafé, Nespresso, Maggi, Thomy, KitKat and Cailler.
Nestlé sells its products in almost every country in the world.

abschnitte.titel: Henri Nestlé and the infant cereal
abschnitte.text: **Henri Nestlé** came from Germany and worked as a pharmacist in Vevey. At that time many babies died because their mothers could not breastfeed them and there was no good substitute food. Around 1867 Nestlé developed an **infant cereal** made of milk, wheat flour and sugar. The product soon sold in many countries, and the bird’s nest in the logo is a reminder of the name Nestlé.

In 1866 the American Page brothers founded a factory for **condensed milk** in Cham in the canton of Zug. In 1905 it merged with Henri Nestlé’s company. The chocolate maker **Daniel Peter** from Vevey used condensed milk and in 1875 brought out a milk chocolate that became world famous. His company later also became part of Nestlé.

In 1938 Nestlé brought the instant coffee **Nescafé** onto the market. Later many other brands were added, for example Nespresso, Maggi, KitKat, Cailler and pet food from Purina. Mineral water and ice creams were also part of the range for a long time. Many people eat something from Nestlé every day without knowing it.

Nestlé’s headquarters is in **Vevey** on the shore of Lake Geneva. There is also the Alimentarium there, a museum about food. In front of the museum, a giant fork sticks out of the lake and has become a landmark of the town. Nestlé also runs large research centres in the Lausanne area.

Nestlé employs several hundred thousand people worldwide in many factories. Its share is one of the most important on the Swiss stock exchange. As a large group, Nestlé also faces **criticism**, for example over advertising baby food in poor countries or on the subject of water. The company says it wants to make healthier products and become more environmentally friendly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very large company to which many other companies belong.
Milk from which part of the water has been removed so that it keeps for a long time.
A powder that is mixed with water or milk to make a porridge for babies.
An expert who makes and sells medicines.

gewusst: Nestlé’s logo shows a bird’s nest, because “Nestle” means “little nest” in the Swabian dialect of German.
The big fork in front of the Alimentarium in Vevey is eight metres high and stands in Lake Geneva.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Bank can influence the exchange rate of the franc by buying or selling foreign currencies. This is called foreign exchange intervention. It is an important tool of Swiss monetary policy.
wichtigste: Foreign exchange means foreign currencies, such as euros or dollars.
In an intervention, the SNB buys or sells foreign currency.
If it buys foreign currency with francs, it weakens the franc.
If it sells foreign currency, it strengthens the franc.
A franc that is too strong harms the export industry.
Because of interventions, the SNB has very large foreign currency reserves.

abschnitte.text: **Foreign exchange** means money held in foreign currencies, for example in euros, dollars or yen. It is traded on the **foreign exchange market**. That is where the **exchange rate** comes about, that is, the price of one currency in another. As with shares, it depends on supply and demand. If many people want to buy francs, its value rises.

The **Swiss National Bank**, SNB for short, can create francs itself. If it uses them to buy euros or dollars, more francs come onto the market. The supply of francs rises, and the franc becomes **weaker**. If, on the other hand, the SNB sells foreign currency and buys francs back, the franc becomes **stronger**. Stepping in like this is called an **intervention**.

If the franc is very strong, Swiss products become expensive abroad. Watches, machines or holidays in Switzerland then sell less well. In addition, imports become cheaper, and prices at home can fall. The SNB’s task is to ensure **stable prices**. Interventions are one of its tools, alongside the **policy interest rate**.

A well-known example is the **minimum exchange rate** against the euro. From 2011 to January 2015, the SNB made sure that one euro cost at least 1.20 francs. To do this, it bought large amounts of euros. When it removed the minimum rate, the franc rose very sharply in a single day. Because of all these purchases, the SNB today has very large **foreign currency reserves**.

gewusst: Measured against the size of the country, the SNB’s foreign currency reserves are among the largest in the world.
The SNB publishes how much foreign currency it has bought or sold, but only after a certain delay.

teile.einleitung: Rolex is one of the most famous watch brands in the world and is based in Geneva. The brand’s logo is a golden crown. With the Rolex Oyster, the company brought the first waterproof wristwatch onto the market in 1926.
wichtigste: Rolex makes expensive wristwatches.
The Rolex logo shows a crown.
The Rolex Oyster of 1926 was the first waterproof wristwatch.
The company was founded in London in 1905 by Hans Wilsdorf.
Since 1919 Geneva has been the home of Rolex.
Rolex belongs to a foundation and is not listed on the stock exchange.

abschnitte.text: In 1905 the German **Hans Wilsdorf**, together with his brother-in-law Alfred Davis, founded a watch company in London. In 1908 he registered the name **Rolex**, which is short and easy to pronounce in all languages. After the First World War the company moved to **Geneva**. Rolex still has its headquarters there today.

In 1926 Rolex presented the **Oyster**. The case was sealed as tightly as an oyster, hence the name. It was the first waterproof wristwatch. In 1927 the Englishwoman **Mercedes Gleitze** swam across the English Channel wearing an Oyster, and afterwards the watch was still running.

In 1931 Rolex brought out a watch with a **rotor**, which winds the watch through the movement of the arm. In 1945 came the Datejust, which shows the date in a small window. Other well-known models are the Submariner diving watch and the Explorer. Many Rolex watches are assembled by hand and checked very carefully.

The logo with the **crown** is meant to show that Rolex wants to be the queen among watches. Rolex watches usually cost from several thousand to tens of thousands of francs. Some old models sell for millions at auctions. Rolex also sponsors big sporting events, for example in **tennis**, golf and sailing.

Hans Wilsdorf had no children. He transferred the company to the **Hans Wilsdorf Foundation**, which still owns Rolex today. The foundation uses its money to support charitable causes, especially in Geneva. Because Rolex is not on the stock exchange, the company publishes hardly any figures on turnover and profit.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sealed so tightly that no water can get in.
A weight in the watch that turns and winds the spring as it does so.
An organisation whose wealth is used for a particular purpose.
An especially expensive product that you do not need in order to live.

gewusst: In 2012 a Rolex test watch on the outside of a submarine belonging to James Cameron dived down into the Mariana Trench, almost 11 kilometres deep.
The name Rolex has no secret meaning; Wilsdorf simply wanted a short word that would fit well on a dial.
Rolex makes almost all the parts of its watches itself and even casts the gold in its own foundry.

teile.einleitung: The toothbrush is the most important tool for keeping your teeth healthy. For it to clean well, you have to look after it properly and replace it regularly.
