wichtigste: You need a new toothbrush when the bristles are worn and bent.
This is usually the case every few months.
There are small brushes with soft bristles for children.
After brushing, you rinse the brush and let it dry.
Every person has their own toothbrush.

abschnitte.text: A **toothbrush** consists of a handle and a head with lots of **bristles**. Today the bristles are usually made of plastic. For children there are small heads with soft bristles that are gentle on the gums. As well as the manual toothbrush there are also **electric toothbrushes**. Both clean well if you use them properly.

abschnitte.titel: When do you need a new one?
abschnitte.text: Over time the bristles wear out. They then splay apart and become bent. A brush like this no longer cleans your teeth properly. That is why you replace it as soon as the bristles are worn, roughly **every few months**. A new brush can also make sense after a bad cold.

After brushing, you rinse the toothbrush well with water. Then you stand it head up in a cup so that it can **dry**. In a damp, closed container, germs can multiply more easily. Every person needs their **own** toothbrush, and you do not share it. A toothbrush goes together with a toothpaste containing **fluoride**, which strengthens the teeth.

gewusst: A long time ago, people cleaned their teeth with chewing sticks, whose ends they chewed into fibres.
Toothbrushes with plastic bristles have only existed since the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: Money is not only created at the printing works. Most money exists only as a number in accounts. This deposit money is created mainly when banks give out loans.
wichtigste: Money creation means that new money is created.
In Switzerland, cash is issued by the National Bank.
Deposit money is money in accounts, not in your hand.
Most deposit money is created through loans from commercial banks.
There is much more deposit money than cash.
The National Bank influences money creation through interest rates.

abschnitte.text: **Cash** means notes and coins that you can hold in your hand. In Switzerland the **Swiss National Bank** issues the banknotes, and Swissmint mints the coins on behalf of the Confederation. **Deposit money**, on the other hand, is money in an account. It exists only as an entry at a bank. When you pay by card or online banking, you move deposit money.

When someone gets a loan from a **commercial bank**, the bank writes the amount into their account. It does not simply take money away from other customers to do this. New **deposit money** is created. This process is called **money creation**. When the customer pays back the loan, this money disappears again. This is how most of the money in a modern economy comes about.

Banks cannot create as much money as they like. They have to follow legal rules and have enough **equity capital**. They also need customers who want a loan and can pay it back. The National Bank controls money creation through the **policy interest rate**. When interest rates are low, more loans are taken out and more money is created.

How money is created was also a political topic in Switzerland. The **Sovereign Money Initiative** (Vollgeld-Initiative) wanted only the National Bank to be allowed to create money. Supporters thought this was safer. Opponents feared disadvantages for banks and the economy. In 2018 the people and the cantons clearly rejected the initiative.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the amount of deposit money is many times greater than the amount of cash.
When the National Bank buys foreign currency, new money in francs is created too.

teile.einleitung: A bond is a security with which states or companies borrow money from many investors. Anyone who buys a bond becomes a creditor, receives interest regularly and gets their money back at the end of the term.
wichtigste: Anyone who buys a bond becomes a creditor of the issuer.
In Switzerland, bonds are often also called “Obligationen”.
The fixed yearly interest on a bond is called the coupon.
At the end of the term, the nominal value is paid back.
If the general level of interest rates rises, the price of existing bonds falls.
Rating agencies assess how safe a debtor is, and AAA is the best grade.
A zero-coupon bond pays no regular interest and is issued below its nominal value.

abschnitte.text: If a state or a large company needs a lot of money, for example for a tunnel or a new factory, it can issue a **bond**. A large loan is divided into many small pieces that investors can buy. So the buyer lends money and becomes a **creditor**. Unlike with a share, they do not become a part-owner, but receive fixed interest.

Every bond has a **nominal value**, for example 100 or 5000 francs. Fixed interest called the **coupon** is paid on it every year. In the past, people actually cut a small piece of paper off the certificate and exchanged it for money at the bank. So a bond with a nominal value of 5000 francs and a 2 per cent coupon brings 100 francs of interest every year. At the end of the **term**, you get the nominal value back.

Bonds are traded on the stock exchange, and their price is called the **price**. If interest rates rise generally, new bonds are more attractive, so the price of old ones falls. If interest rates fall, the price of old bonds rises. The **current yield** is calculated by dividing the coupon by the price: a 4-franc coupon at a price of 80 francs gives 5 per cent.

Not every debtor is sure to pay back. That is why **rating agencies** such as Standard & Poor’s, Moody’s or Fitch assess the ability to pay, which is called **creditworthiness**. The best grade is AAA, and grades in the C range mean a high risk. The less safe the debtor, the higher the interest they usually have to pay. The Swiss Confederation has the top grade AAA.

A **zero-coupon bond** pays no yearly interest. Instead, it is sold for less than the nominal value and paid back at the full nominal value at the end, and the difference is the return. There are also government bonds, corporate bonds and bonds from cantons and cities. Swiss federal bonds are called **“Eidgenossen”** and are regarded as very safe.

Many pension funds and insurers invest a large part of their money in bonds, because they bring predictable returns. Private individuals can also buy bonds through their bank. In Switzerland, interest rates on safe bonds were very low for many years and at times even below zero. Bonds are regarded as safer than shares, but usually bring less return.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who has lent money and is due to get it back.
The fixed interest that a bond pays every year.
The amount paid back at the end of the term.
How reliably a debtor can pay back their money.

gewusst: Great Britain only paid back in 2015 the last debts from bonds, some of which dated from the 18th century.
The term coupon comes from detachable interest slips on paper certificates, which were cut off with scissors.
Some countries have issued bonds with a term of 100 years.

teile.einleitung: Profit is the money a company has left when all its costs are subtracted from all its income. It shows whether a business is worthwhile. Whether a kiosk, a farm or a global corporation, they all calculate on the same principle.
wichtigste: Profit is calculated as revenue minus costs.
Turnover is all the money from all sales.
Turnover and profit are not the same, because the costs still have to be paid out of the turnover.
If costs are higher than revenue, there is a loss.
Shareholders often receive part of the profit as a dividend.
Non-profit organisations do not want to make a profit, but to serve a good cause.
In Switzerland, taxes are also charged on company profits.

abschnitte.text: A company takes in money when it sells goods or services. But it has to pay for a lot out of this, for example purchasing, wages, rent and electricity. What is left over afterwards is the **profit**. If the **costs** are greater than the income, the company makes a loss.

abschnitte.titel: Doing the sums at the kiosk
abschnitte.text: A kiosk sells 50 ice creams at 3 francs each and so takes in 150 francs; this is the **turnover**. Each ice cream cost 1.80 francs to buy in, so 90 francs altogether. The profit is therefore 150 minus 90, that is 60 francs. In reality there are also costs such as rent and electricity, which must be subtracted too.

Profit is often worked out as a percentage. A bike dealer buys a bike for 400 francs and sells it for 500 francs. He earns 100 francs, which is 25 per cent of the purchase price. The **profit margin** shows how much of the selling price remains as profit, and it varies greatly from industry to industry.

Part of the profit goes to the Confederation and the canton as **profit tax**. A company can use another part to invest, for example in new machines or more staff. In a public limited company, the shareholders often receive a **dividend**, which is their share of the profit. Profit can also be saved as a reserve for harder times.

Not all organisations want to make a profit. **Non-profit organisations** such as the Swiss Red Cross or Pro Juventute work for a good cause. They too must manage their money well so that their income covers their costs. They put any surplus back into their work instead of paying it out to owners.

Profit shows that a company offers something that people want to buy. Only profitable companies can pay wages and secure jobs in the long run. At the same time, people discuss how much profit is fair and how it should be shared. Large Swiss companies such as **Nestlé** or Roche make profits in the billions every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the money a company takes in through sales.
Spending that is necessary for a business, for example wages and rent.
A share of the profit that shareholders receive.
The part of the selling price that remains as profit.

gewusst: A company can have a huge turnover and still make a loss if its costs are even greater.
Supermarkets often earn only a few centimes per product sold, but still make a profit because of the large quantities.
In accounting, a year’s profit is also called annual profit or net profit.

teile.einleitung: A bank is a company that looks after customers’ money, lends money and helps with payments. Almost every family in Switzerland has an account at a bank.
wichtigste: At a bank you can open an account where your own money is recorded.
Putting money into the account is called paying in, taking money out of the account is called withdrawing.
The bank statement shows what has happened in the account.
Money that you borrow from the bank is called a loan.
Before the holidays you can, for example, change francs into euros at the bank.
In Switzerland, the cantonal banks belong to a canton.
Banks earn money by charging more interest on loans than they pay on savings.

abschnitte.text: A bank has three important jobs. It keeps its customers’ money in an **account**. It lends money, for example for a house or a company, and this is called a **loan**. And it carries out payments, so that you can pay bills or transfer money. Bank staff work at the bank and give customers advice.

If you put money into your account, you make a **deposit**. If you take money out of the account, you make a withdrawal. You get cash at the counter or from the **Bancomat**, the cash machine. Today many people do their banking with online banking on the computer or with an app on their mobile phone. On the **bank statement** you can see all the money paid in and paid out.

If you save money at the bank, you sometimes get a small extra amount for it, the **interest**. If you borrow money, you have to pay interest. The interest on loans is higher than the interest on savings, and the bank lives on the difference. So with the money saved by many customers, the bank can give loans to other people.

Switzerland is world famous for its banks, and the **financial centre** is an important part of the economy. The biggest bank is UBS, which took over Credit Suisse in 2023. Almost every canton has its own **cantonal bank**, for example the Zurich or the Bern Cantonal Bank. There are also Raiffeisen banks, PostFinance, regional banks and private banks.

The banks in Switzerland are supervised by the Financial Market Supervisory Authority FINMA. If a bank goes bust, savings of up to 100,000 francs per customer are protected by **deposit protection**. The Swiss **National Bank** is a special bank: it issues the banknotes and makes sure the franc stays stable. However, it does not keep accounts for private individuals.

Before the holidays you can change francs into **euros** or another currency at the bank. The word bank comes from the Italian “banco”, which means table. In the Middle Ages, money changers sat at such tables at the market in Italian cities. Later the first big banks appeared in cities such as Florence and Genoa.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of record at the bank where your money is entered.
Money that you borrow from the bank and pay back with interest.
An amount that you pay for borrowing or receive for saving.
A bank that belongs to a canton.

gewusst: The word bankrupt comes from the Italian “banca rotta”, the broken table of a money changer who could no longer pay.
The oldest bank in the world that still exists is the Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, founded in 1472.
There are 24 cantonal banks in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A budget is a plan in which you write down how much money you receive and what you want to spend it on. If you make a budget, you keep track, can save in a targeted way and avoid debt.
wichtigste: A budget sets planned income against planned spending.
In a balanced budget, income and spending are the same.
If spending is higher than income, there is a deficit.
The rent for a flat is one of the fixed costs in a household budget.
A reserve in the budget is there for unexpected costs.
If you save 25 per cent of 40 francs of pocket money, you still have 30 francs to spend.
States, cantons and companies also draw up a budget every year.

abschnitte.text: A **budget** is a money plan for a certain period, usually a month or a year. On one side is the **income**, for example pocket money or wages. On the other side is the **spending**, for example on your mobile phone, going out or clothes. The difference shows whether money is left over or missing.

Tim has a monthly budget of 120 francs. He spends 45 francs on his mobile phone, 30 francs on going out and 20 francs on clothes. Together that is 95 francs, so he has 25 francs left over. He can **save** this or use it for something special.

If income and spending are the same, the budget is **balanced**. If money is left over, this is called a **surplus**. If you spend more than you earn, there is a **deficit**. You can only cover a deficit with savings or with debt, so you should avoid it.

A household budget has **fixed costs** that are the same every month, such as rent, health insurance and subscriptions. On top of that come variable costs for food, clothes and leisure. Sensible planning also includes a **reserve** for the unexpected, for example a dentist’s bill or a broken bike. Experts recommend also planning provisions for annual bills such as taxes.

It is best to write down all your spending for a month, in a notebook or an app. Then you see where the money really goes. A popular trick is to save a fixed amount first and only then spend the rest. The organisation **Budget Advice Switzerland** (Budgetberatung Schweiz) offers free templates and guideline figures for pocket money and household budgets.

abschnitte.titel: Budgets of the state and companies
abschnitte.text: It is not only families who make a budget. The Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities also plan their income and spending every year. The federal budget is debated and approved by Parliament. Companies use a budget to plan how much they want to sell and invest.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plan for income and spending.
When spending is higher than income.
Money you put aside for unexpected costs.
Costs that come up regularly at the same amount.

gewusst: The word budget comes from the Old French “bougette”, a small leather pouch for money.
Every year the federal budget includes spending of over 80 billion francs.
Many Swiss young people who get into debt have never made a budget before.

teile.einleitung: A coin is a round piece of money made of metal. Coins have existed for over 2500 years, and they are still part of our cash today. In Switzerland there are seven different coins, from the small 5-centime piece to the large Fünfliber.
wichtigste: Coins are pieces of money made of metal.
Swiss coins are round.
The smallest coin you can pay with in Switzerland today is the 5-centime piece.
The largest Swiss coin is the 5-franc piece, the Fünfliber.
Today there are 7 different coins in Switzerland.
Swiss coins are made in Bern.
Helvetia can be seen on the 1-franc piece.

abschnitte.text: A **coin** is a piece of money made of metal, with a value stamped on it. The front and back show pictures, numbers and the year it was made. In the past, a coin was worth as much as the gold or silver in it. Today the stamped value, the **face value**, is usually higher than the value of the metal.

The first coins appeared about 2600 years ago in the Kingdom of **Lydia** in what is now Turkey. Later the Greeks and Romans minted coins with the heads of gods and emperors. In Switzerland, before 1850, many cantons and cities had their own coins. With the Swiss franc in 1850 came the same coins for the whole country.

Today there are seven coins in Switzerland: 5, 10 and 20 **centimes** (Rappen) and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The 5-franc piece is the largest and is popularly called the **Fünfliber**. The ½-, 1- and 2-franc pieces show **Helvetia**, the female figure who represents Switzerland. The Fünfliber shows an Alpine herdsman, and the centime coins show a woman’s head representing freedom.

Swiss coins are made by **Swissmint** in Bern, the federal mint. Round discs, the blanks, are punched out of strips of metal. These are stamped with great pressure between two dies. Most Swiss coins are made of copper and nickel, the 5-centime piece of gold-coloured aluminium bronze.

Collecting and studying coins is called **numismatics**. Rare years or misprinted coins can be worth much more than their face value. The edge of the Fünfliber bears the Latin inscription “Dominus providebit”, which means “The Lord will provide”. Swissmint also issues special coins, for example about Swiss mountains or events.

You need coins, for example, at the kiosk, at the parking meter or for a shopping trolley. Because many people pay by card or TWINT, fewer coins are used today than in the past. The 1-centime piece was abolished in 2007, the 2-centime piece as early as 1978. That is why amounts are rounded to 5 centimes at the till today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The value written on the coin.
Making a coin by pressing it with great force between two dies.
The federal mint in Bern.
The study and collecting of coins.
The Swiss nickname for the 5-franc piece.

gewusst: Swiss coins have had almost the same pictures since the 19th century.
Swiss coins do not say “Switzerland”, but the Latin name “Helvetia” or “Confoederatio Helvetica”.
The name Fünfliber comes from the French word “livre”, an old unit of money.

teile.einleitung: The waiting room is the room in a doctor’s surgery where you wait until it is your turn. You are called from there when the doctor has time.
wichtigste: In the waiting room you wait until you are called.
First you check in at reception.
A medical practice assistant often works at reception.
In the waiting room you behave quietly and considerately.
Anyone who is very ill or has an emergency is seen sooner.

abschnitte.text: When you arrive at a **doctor’s surgery**, you first check in at **reception**. A **medical practice assistant**, MPA for short, often works there. She asks for your name and your health insurance card. Then you sit down in the **waiting room**. There are chairs there, and often magazines or picture books.

abschnitte.titel: Why do you have to wait?
abschnitte.text: The doctor examines one person after another. Some examinations take longer than planned. Anyone who has an **emergency** or is very ill is sometimes seen before the others. That is why it can take a while in the waiting room. A book or a quiet game helps to pass the time.

In the waiting room there are often people who are ill or in pain. That is why you speak quietly and do not run around. Anyone who coughs or sneezes holds the crook of their elbow in front of their mouth. This way **germs** spread less. Sometimes there is a **mask** for people with a cough.

gewusst: In many paediatricians’ surgeries there is a play corner with toys in the waiting room.
Some surgeries have a separate waiting room for people with infectious illnesses.

teile.einleitung: A stock market index combines the prices of many shares into a single number. This lets you see at a glance how the stock exchange is doing overall. The best-known index in Switzerland is the SMI.
wichtigste: A stock market index shows the development of a group of shares.
It combines many prices into one number, measured in points.
The SMI contains the 20 largest Swiss companies on the stock exchange.
If the index rises, prices have gone up overall.
Large companies often count more in the index than small ones.
Well-known foreign indices are the Dow Jones and the DAX.

abschnitte.text: Hundreds of shares are traded on a stock exchange. Each has its own price. To see whether the stock exchange is doing well overall, you need an overview. A **stock market index** combines the prices of selected shares into one number. This number is given in **points**. If it rises, prices have risen on average.

The **SMI** stands for Swiss Market Index. It contains the 20 largest and most traded shares on the Swiss stock exchange. They include companies from pharmaceuticals, food, banking and insurance. The SMI was introduced in 1988. There is also the **SPI**, the Swiss Performance Index. It contains almost all Swiss shares on the stock exchange.

Not every share counts equally in the index. In the SMI, companies with a higher market value have more **weight**. If the share price of a very large company rises, this moves the index more than for a smaller company. The make-up of the index is checked regularly. If a company grows strongly, it can move up into the index, and others drop out.

Every larger country has its own indices. The **Dow Jones** from the USA is one of the oldest in the world. The **DAX** shows Germany’s largest companies. In Japan there is the Nikkei. Today many people save with funds that simply copy an index. In this way, with one purchase you own small parts of many companies.

gewusst: The Dow Jones was already being calculated in the 19th century, back then by hand.
The news often reports by what percentage the SMI rose or fell in a day.

teile.einleitung: A loan is borrowed money that you have to pay back later, usually with interest. With loans, people buy houses, companies build factories and states pay for roads. Loans can be very useful, but anyone who takes on too much debt can get into serious difficulties.
wichtigste: A loan is borrowed money that you have to pay back.
For a loan, the bank usually charges interest as the price for lending.
If you borrow 2000 francs at 10 per cent interest, you pay back 2200 francs after one year.
A loan of 1200 francs in 12 equal instalments gives instalments of 100 francs.
In Switzerland you can generally only take out a consumer loan from the age of 18.
In Switzerland, debt collection proceedings can be used to have unpaid debts officially collected.
With leasing you use a car, for example, in return for monthly payments, but you do not own it.

abschnitte.text: With a **loan**, a bank or another person lends money to someone. The German word Kredit comes from the Latin “credere”, which means to believe or to trust. So whoever lends money has to trust that they will get it back. The person who borrows money is called the **debtor**, the one who gives the money is called the creditor.

Lenders usually charge **interest** for lending. If you borrow 2000 francs at 10 per cent interest a year, you have to pay back 2200 francs after one year. A loan is often paid back in **instalments**, that is, in equal part payments. An interest-free loan of 1200 francs in 12 monthly instalments gives an instalment of 100 francs.

To buy a house or a flat, people take out a **mortgage**, a loan that is secured by the house. A **consumer loan** is used to pay for things such as furniture, holidays or a car. Companies take out loans to buy machines or to cover wages for a while. Overdrawing an account or paying by credit card is also a form of credit.

With **leasing**, you use a car, for example, in return for monthly payments, but you do not own it. At the end of the contract you give the car back or buy it at a fixed price. Leasing is very common for cars in Switzerland. You must insure the vehicle well and return it in good condition.

The **Consumer Credit Act** protects customers. You can generally only take out a consumer loan from the age of 18. Beforehand, the bank must check whether you can afford the loan; this is called a creditworthiness check. In addition, the Federal Council has set a maximum interest rate so that interest cannot be as high as lenders like.

If you do not pay your debts, **debt collection proceedings** can be started against you. **Debt collection** (Betreibung) is an official procedure that creditors use to have their money collected. An entry in the debt collection register can later make it hard to rent a flat. Advice services such as debt counselling help people who have too much debt.

begriffe.erklaerung: The price you pay for borrowed money.
A part payment with which you pay back debt bit by bit.
A loan for a house, with the house serving as security.
An official procedure for collecting unpaid debts.
Using something in return for payments without owning it.

gewusst: Many young adults in Switzerland fall into the debt trap through mobile phone contracts, leasing and tax debts.
More than 4000 years ago in Mesopotamia there were already rules for lending grain and silver with interest.
Compared with the rest of the world, Switzerland has very high mortgage debt per head.

teile.einleitung: A reservation is a restriction in supplementary insurance. If someone already has a particular illness, the insurer can exclude it from the services.
wichtigste: A reservation excludes a particular illness from the services.
Reservations only exist in supplementary insurance.
Reservations are forbidden in basic insurance.
Before the contract is signed, the insurer asks health questions.
You must answer the questions honestly.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who wants to take out **supplementary insurance** first fills in a questionnaire about their health. If the person has already had an illness, this is called a **pre-existing condition**. The insurer can then say: we will accept you, but we will not pay for this illness. This restriction is called a **reservation**. For all other illnesses, the insurance applies quite normally.

In **basic insurance**, every health insurer must accept everyone, and without any reservation. This is required by the Health Insurance Act, **KVG**. Supplementary insurance is voluntary and is governed by the Insurance Contract Act, **VVG**. There the insurer may turn people down or make reservations. That is why it is a good idea to take out supplementary insurance while you are young and healthy.

You must answer the **health questions** fully and truthfully. If you keep an illness quiet, the insurer may in some circumstances cancel the contract. Then you are without protection exactly when you need it. For children, the parents fill in the questionnaire. If you are unsure, it is best to ask the insurer.

gewusst: A reservation is set out in writing in the insurance policy, so that you know exactly what is excluded.

teile.einleitung: Edelweiss Air is a Swiss airline that flies mainly to holiday destinations. Its aircraft take off from Zurich Airport and take travellers to the seaside, to cities or to faraway islands, for example. An edelweiss flower can be seen on the tail of its aircraft.
wichtigste: Edelweiss Air is a holiday airline from Switzerland.
The company was founded in 1995 and is based in Kloten near Zurich Airport.
An edelweiss is shown on the tail of the aircraft.
Since 2008 Edelweiss has belonged to the airline Swiss.
Swiss and Edelweiss belong to the German Lufthansa Group.
Edelweiss flies to destinations in Europe, Africa, Asia and America.

abschnitte.text: **Edelweiss Air** is an airline that specialises in holiday travel. It flies to the Mediterranean and the Canary Islands, but also far away to Canada, Mexico or Thailand. Most flights take off from **Zurich Airport**. According to the company, Edelweiss flies to over 90 destinations in more than 30 countries.

The company is named after the **edelweiss**, a white Alpine flower. The edelweiss is considered a symbol of the Swiss mountains. It can be seen on the tail of all the company’s aircraft. This means travellers can recognise Edelweiss aircraft from far away.

Edelweiss Air was founded in 1995 and began flying in 1996 with a single aircraft. For a long time it belonged to the travel company Kuoni. In 2008 Edelweiss became part of **Swiss**, the largest airline in Switzerland. Swiss in turn has belonged to the German **Lufthansa Group** since 2005.

Edelweiss flies aircraft from the European manufacturer **Airbus**. For destinations in Europe it uses smaller planes from the A320 family. For long-haul routes it uses larger aircraft with two aisles that can fly for many hours without a stop. For some years the long-haul fleet has been renewed with more modern aircraft.

In summer and in the school holidays, Edelweiss flights are often fully booked. That is why many Swiss people associate the airline with a holiday mood. However, flying produces a lot of **CO2** and harms the climate. That is why passengers at Edelweiss can choose to pay for climate protection projects or more sustainable fuel.

begriffe.erklaerung: A company that transports people or goods by aeroplane.
The back part of an aircraft with the vertical fin.
Flights over very long distances, for example across the ocean.
A white, felty flower that grows on limestone soils in the Alps.

gewusst: Edelweiss started in 1996 with just one aircraft, an MD-83.
The edelweiss originally comes from the mountains of Central Asia and only reached the Alps during the ice ages.

teile.einleitung: Before goods end up in the shop, they often pass through wholesale trade. Wholesalers buy large quantities from manufacturers and distribute them further. In this way they connect factories with shops, restaurants and businesses.
wichtigste: Wholesalers buy goods in large quantities from manufacturers.
They sell them on to companies, shops and restaurants.
Selling to private individuals is usually done by retail trade.
Wholesalers store, transport and distribute goods.
Large quantities make cheaper purchase prices possible.

abschnitte.text: A factory makes pasta, for example. It does not want to deliver a few packets to each small shop separately. This is where **wholesale trade** comes in. Wholesalers buy large quantities from the **manufacturer**. Then they distribute the goods to many **retailers**, restaurants or other businesses. This is also called **intermediate trade**.

**Retail trade** sells goods to **end customers**, that is, to private individuals. Examples are supermarkets, kiosks or bookshops. Wholesale trade, on the other hand, mainly supplies companies. In Switzerland there are wholesale markets where only restaurant owners, traders and other businesses are allowed to shop. Goods there often come in large packs.

Wholesalers **store** goods in large warehouses. They organise **transport** to customers and put together different products. A restaurant can therefore order vegetables, drinks and cleaning products from a single supplier. Because wholesalers buy large quantities, they get lower prices. They pass part of this on to their customers.

gewusst: Many goods in Swiss shops come from abroad and enter the country through importers and wholesalers.
A wholesaler often sells thousands of different items.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who has to go to hospital can often help decide which one in Switzerland. But basic insurance does not pay for every hospital and every ward. The cantonal hospital lists are important.
wichtigste: Basic insurance pays for the general ward of a listed hospital.
Every canton keeps a hospital list.
You may also choose a listed hospital in another canton.
Then the insurance pays at most the tariff of your canton of residence.
In an emergency, you go to the nearest suitable hospital.
For the semi-private or private ward you need supplementary insurance.

abschnitte.text: Every **canton** decides which hospitals its population needs. These hospitals are on the **hospital list**. They are called **listed hospitals**. Basic insurance pays for treatment in the **general ward** of such a hospital. The canton also pays a large part of the costs.

You may also choose a listed hospital in another canton. This has been possible since the new **hospital financing** of **2012**. If the treatment there costs more than in your own canton, the insurer and the canton only pay the **tariff of your canton of residence**. You have to pay the rest yourself or through supplementary insurance. This does not apply if there is a medical reason or an emergency.
In an **emergency** there is no time for a long choice. You are taken to the nearest suitable hospital. Basic insurance pays for the necessary treatment. This applies throughout Switzerland.

Anyone who would like to stay in the **semi-private** or **private ward** needs **supplementary insurance**. With it you often have a two-bed or single room. You can usually also choose the doctor who operates. Some supplementary insurance also allows hospitals that are not on a list. This insurance costs extra premiums.

gewusst: The medical treatment in the general ward is just as good as in the private ward.
Before a planned operation, it is worth asking the health insurer what will be paid for.

teile.einleitung: With the Telmed model, when you have a health problem you first call a medical advice service before going to the doctor. Experts on the phone tell you what to do. In return, you pay a lower premium to the health insurer.
wichtigste: Telmed is an alternative insurance model of Swiss basic insurance.
Before a visit to the doctor, you first call a medical advice service.
The advice service can be reached around the clock, every day of the year.
Medical experts decide whether a visit to the doctor is necessary.
In return, there is a lower premium.
In real emergencies, you may go straight to hospital or call 144.
The services of basic insurance stay the same.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who is ill or has hurt themselves first calls their health insurer’s **telemedicine advice service**. On the phone, doctors or nurses ask about the symptoms. Then they give advice, for example to wait at home, go to the pharmacy or make an appointment with a doctor. Sometimes a video consultation is also possible. You must follow the recommendation, otherwise the health insurer can reduce what it pays.

The word **telemedicine** is made up of the Greek “tele” for “far” and the word “medicine”. It means advice or treatment over a distance, in other words by phone, video or app. In Switzerland, for example, Medgate or Medi24 offer such advice. Many health insurers work with these services. The experts there are sometimes also allowed to write prescriptions.

In the Telmed model, the premium is often much lower than in the standard model. You quickly get an assessment without having to leave the house. This is handy at night or at the weekend. Many small problems such as a cold can be solved this way without going to the doctor. This takes pressure off doctors’ surgeries and **emergency departments**.

In a life-threatening **emergency**, you dial the emergency number 144 straight away. With many insurers you may go to the gynaecologist or the eye doctor without calling first. After the call you often receive a case number, which you have to give at the doctor’s surgery. The recommendation usually applies for a certain time or treatment. The exact rules are set out in the **insurance conditions**.

Telmed is one of several **alternative insurance models**. There is also the family doctor model and the HMO practice. Some health insurers combine models, for example an assessment by app followed by the family doctor. You can change the model with effect from 1 January each year. Anyone who rarely goes to the doctor and is happy to talk on the phone often finds the Telmed model practical.

begriffe.erklaerung: Medical advice or treatment by phone, video or app.
Insurance model in which you call first before going to the doctor.
Phone number for the ambulance service in Switzerland.
Reduction on the monthly premium.

gewusst: The telephone advice service is staffed around the clock, even at Christmas and New Year.
Many calls can be resolved without a visit to the doctor, for example with a tip for the home first aid kit.

teile.einleitung: Denner is the largest discount store chain in Switzerland. Its shops have a smaller range than large supermarkets, but low prices. Denner now belongs to Migros, but unlike the Migros branches it also sells alcohol and tobacco.
wichtigste: Denner is the largest discounter in Switzerland.
A discounter is a shop with a smaller range and low prices.
Denner now belongs to Migros.
Denner’s headquarters is in Zurich.
Denner has more than 800 sales outlets all over Switzerland.
Denner’s main competitors are Aldi and Lidl.

abschnitte.text: **Denner** is a chain of shops that sells food, drinks and household goods at low prices. Together with its partner shops, the Denner Satellites, there are more than 800 sales outlets. The shops are usually fairly small and are often right in the middle of villages and neighbourhoods. The company’s headquarters is in Zurich.

A **discounter** offers fewer different products than a large supermarket. In return, it buys huge quantities of each product and so gets low purchase prices. The shops are simply fitted out and there are few staff. This lets the discounter sell the goods on cheaply.

Denner’s roots go back to 1860, when a shop selling colonial goods opened in Zurich. The name comes from the Denner family, who later ran the business. Under the entrepreneur **Karl Schweri**, Denner became a discounter from the 1960s onwards. Schweri fought for shops to be allowed to set their own prices freely and not be bound by manufacturers’ rules.

In 2007 **Migros** took over the majority of Denner and later the whole company. Migros branches traditionally sell no alcohol and no cigarettes. But Denner may do so, and in this way the Migros Group can also earn money in this area. Denner is especially well known for its large range of wines.

The German discounter **Aldi** has been in Switzerland since 2005, and Lidl since 2009. The two chains have opened many shops and compete with Denner. That is why Coop and Migros also lower their prices on many products. For customers, the competition has led to cheaper food.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shop with a small range and low prices.
All the products that a shop sells.
An old name for goods from distant countries, such as coffee, tea, sugar and spices.
Several companies offer similar goods and try to win customers.

gewusst: Denner is one of the largest wine sellers in Switzerland.
The Denner Satellites are often village shops run by independent partners.
Denner has new special offers every week, announced in leaflets and online.

teile.einleitung: Compound interest means that you get interest not only on your savings, but also on the interest that has already been added. As a result, money grows faster and faster over time, like a snowball that gets bigger as it rolls. Those who start saving early benefit most.
wichtigste: With compound interest, the interest is added to the capital and earns interest the following year.
The formula is K_n = K_0 · (1 + p)^n.
At 5 % interest, 1000 francs grow to 1102.50 francs in 2 years.
At 3 %, 10,000 francs grow to around 13,439 francs in 10 years.
According to the rule of 72, money doubles in about 12 years at 6 % interest.
With a nominal rate of 12 % and monthly interest, the effective annual rate is around 12.68 %.
With 2 % inflation, the purchasing power of money halves in about 35 years.

abschnitte.text: With simple interest you get the same amount of interest every year on the original money. With **compound interest**, the interest stays in the account and becomes new **capital**. The following year you then also get interest on this interest. In this way the amount grows a little more each year than the year before.

The final capital is calculated with the formula K_n = K_0 · (1 + p)^n. Here K_0 is the starting capital, p the interest rate as a decimal and n the number of years. With 1000 francs, 5 per cent and 2 years, you calculate 1000 · 1.05 · 1.05 and get 1102.50 francs. With simple interest it would only have been 1100 francs.

With 1000 francs and 10 per cent interest, simple interest gives you 300 francs in interest after 3 years. With compound interest it is 331 francs, so 31 francs more. The longer the time and the higher the interest, the bigger the difference becomes. In mathematics this kind of growth is called **exponential growth**.

With the **rule of 72** you can estimate in your head when money will double. You divide 72 by the interest rate in per cent. At 6 per cent interest it therefore takes about 72 divided by 6, that is 12 years. The rule also works the other way round: with 2 per cent inflation, money has only half its purchasing power after about 35 years.

Sometimes interest is credited not once a year but every month. Then compound interest already takes effect within the year. With a nominal rate of 12 per cent and monthly interest, the **effective annual rate** is around 12.68 per cent. That is why, with loans, it is worth looking at the effective interest rate.

If you start saving when you are young, you have a lot of time in which compound interest can work. In Switzerland, many people use **pillar 3a** for this, a tax-advantaged savings account for retirement. But compound interest also works with debt: if you do not pay off a loan, your debt grows faster and faster. That is why it is important to pay back debts as quickly as possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: The money that you have invested and that earns interest.
Something grows not by the same amount each time, but faster and faster.
The interest you really receive or pay after one year, with everything included.
Prices rise, and you can buy less with the same money.

gewusst: According to an old legend, the inventor of chess asked for one grain of rice on the first square and twice as many on each further square, which in the end comes to more rice than there is in the world.
One franc invested for 100 years at 5 per cent compound interest grows to over 130 francs.
Albert Einstein is said to have called compound interest a great force, but there is no evidence for this quotation.

teile.einleitung: The world economy includes all the countries on Earth that exchange goods, services and money with one another. Your mobile phone, your banana and your trainers often come from far away. Switzerland is a small country, but closely connected with the whole world.
wichtigste: World economy means that countries trade with one another and depend on each other.
David Ricardo developed the theory of comparative advantage.
The World Trade Organization WTO has its headquarters in Geneva.
In 1944 the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were created at Bretton Woods.
In 1960 Switzerland was one of the founders of EFTA.
Since 2014 there has been a free trade agreement between Switzerland and China.
On 1 January 2024 Switzerland abolished customs duties on industrial goods on its own.

abschnitte.text: No country can produce everything its people need by itself. That is why countries buy goods from abroad, the **imports**, and sell their own goods abroad, the **exports**. Huge container ships, aeroplanes and lorries carry the goods around the world. This ever closer interconnection is called **globalisation**.

In 1817 the British economist **David Ricardo** showed that trade is worthwhile even if one country can do everything better. Each country should specialise in what it can do best by comparison. This is called **comparative advantage**. Even before that, Adam Smith had explained that the division of labour increases prosperity.

In 1944 representatives of many countries met in the US town of Bretton Woods. There they created the **International Monetary Fund** (IMF) and the World Bank, which lend money to countries in need. Since 1995 there has been the **World Trade Organization** WTO, based in Geneva, which sets rules for trade. Its predecessor was the GATT agreement of 1947.

Switzerland earns a large part of its prosperity abroad. Important export goods are medicines and chemicals, machines, watches and precision instruments. Its most important trading partner is the European Union, and the USA is a very important single market. Every January, the world’s leading business figures meet at the World Economic Forum WEF in Davos.

In 1960 Switzerland founded the **European Free Trade Association** EFTA together with other countries. Today, besides Switzerland, it includes Liechtenstein, Norway and Iceland. Switzerland has many free trade agreements, including one with China since 2014. On 1 January 2024 it also abolished its customs duties on industrial goods on its own.

World trade makes many goods cheaper and has helped millions of people out of poverty. At the same time, some people lose their jobs when factories move to other countries. Long transport routes harm the environment. When a supply chain is interrupted, as in the coronavirus crisis of 2020, goods are suddenly missing worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A product that a country sells abroad.
A product that a country buys from abroad.
A fee you have to pay when you bring goods across the border.
Trade between countries with no or only a few customs duties.
The worldwide interconnection of economies, cultures and people.

gewusst: About 80 per cent of all goods in world trade travel on a ship at least once.
Switzerland earns about every second franc abroad.
A single large container ship can carry over 20,000 containers.

teile.einleitung: A share is a security that represents a small part of a public limited company. Anyone who owns shares is a part-owner of the company, can share in its profit and can have a say at the general meeting.
wichtigste: A share represents a part of the capital of a public limited company.
Anyone who owns shares is called a shareholder.
Part of the profit can be paid out to the shareholders as a dividend.
Shareholders exercise their voting rights at the general meeting.
With registered shares, the owner is entered in the share register.
The share price can rise or fall, which is why shares involve risk.
In Switzerland, withholding tax of 35 per cent is deducted from dividends (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: When a company needs money for its ideas, it can divide itself into lots of small parts and sell them. Each of these parts is a **share**. A company that is organised like this is called a **public limited company**, AG for short in Switzerland. Anyone who buys a share gives the company money and becomes a part-owner in return. Large Swiss public limited companies include Nestlé, Novartis and UBS.

You can earn money with a share in two ways. Firstly, the company often pays out part of its profit as a **dividend**. If a share costs 75 francs and pays a 3-franc dividend, the **dividend yield** is 4 per cent. Secondly, the share price can rise, so that you can sell the share for more than you paid for it. But the price can also fall, and then you lose money.

Once a year, a public limited company invites shareholders to the **general meeting**. There, the shareholders vote on important questions, for example the amount of the dividend or the election of the board of directors. Usually the rule is: one share, one vote. So anyone who owns lots of shares has more influence. With a **registered share**, the owner is entered in the company’s share register, but not with a bearer share.

**Market capitalisation** shows how much a company is worth on the stock exchange. You multiply the number of shares by the price, for example 50 million shares times 80 francs gives 4 billion francs. The **price-earnings ratio** (P/E ratio) divides the price by the profit per share. If a share costs 120 francs and the company earns 8 francs per share, the P/E ratio is 15. A high P/E ratio means that investors are paying a lot for future profit.

Swiss shares are mainly traded on the **SIX Swiss Exchange** in Zurich. On dividends, the state deducts **withholding tax** of 35 per cent. Anyone who lives in Switzerland and declares the dividend in their tax return gets this amount back. In this way the state makes sure that income from shares is taxed.

Over many years, shares often bring more return than a savings account, but they go up and down a lot. If a company goes bankrupt, the share can become almost worthless. That is why sensible investors spread their money over many different shares, and this is called **diversification**. Parents can open a securities account for children and young people, an account for securities.

begriffe.erklaerung: A company whose capital is divided into many shares.
The part of the profit that a company pays out to its shareholders.
The yearly meeting at which shareholders vote.
An account at a bank in which securities such as shares are held.

gewusst: The Dutch East India Company issued shares from 1602 and is regarded as one of the first public limited companies in the world.
Some shares cost only a few francs, whereas a single share of Lindt & Sprüngli cost around 100,000 francs in 2024.
In the past, shares were beautifully decorated paper certificates, but today they are almost only stored electronically.

teile.einleitung: A commuting accident is an accident on the way to work or home. In Switzerland, the Accident Insurance Act sets out who pays the costs in this case.
wichtigste: A commuting accident happens on the direct route between home and work.
In Switzerland, employees are compulsorily insured against accidents.
This is set out in the Accident Insurance Act, UVG.
Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week is also insured against accidents in their free time.
With fewer than 8 hours a week, an accident on the way to work counts as an occupational accident.

abschnitte.text: A **commuting accident** is an accident on the way between home and the workplace. It might be, for example, a fall from a bike or on a slippery pavement. What matters is that it is the **direct route to work**. A big detour for private errands can change the situation. The accident insurer makes the exact assessment.

The **Accident Insurance Act, UVG**, distinguishes between two kinds. An **occupational accident** happens at work. A **non-occupational accident** happens in your free time, for example during sport. All employees are insured against occupational accidents, and the employer pays the premium. Anyone who works at least **8 hours a week** for the same employer is also insured against non-occupational accidents. Then a commuting accident counts as a non-occupational accident.

Anyone who works fewer than 8 hours a week is not insured against accidents in their free time. So that the journey to work is still protected, an accident on the direct route to work counts as an **occupational accident**. This means the employer’s accident insurance pays. For accidents in their free time, this person needs the **accident cover** of their health insurer. This is important, for example, for young people with a small side job.

gewusst: The largest accident insurer in Switzerland is Suva, based in Lucerne.

teile.einleitung: Every day we spend many hours sleeping. This is not wasted time: during sleep the body recovers, and the brain processes what has been learnt. Children need especially a lot of sleep.
wichtigste: During sleep, the body recovers.
Children need sleep to grow and to concentrate.
Schoolchildren up to about 9 usually need 9 to 12 hours a night.
Teenagers need about 8 to 10 hours, adults less.
Screen light shortly before sleeping keeps you awake.
Fixed bedtimes help you fall asleep.

abschnitte.text: Sleep happens in several **stages**, which repeat during the night. In **deep sleep** the body recovers especially well. In the **dream stage** the eyes move quickly, which is why it is also called REM sleep. During this time we often have vivid dreams. One complete cycle through the stages takes about an hour and a half.

In deep sleep the body produces a lot of **growth hormone**. Hormones are messenger substances that give the body instructions. That is why enough sleep is so important for children. The **immune system**, in other words the defence against illness, is also strengthened during sleep. Anyone who sleeps too little falls ill more easily.

At night, the **brain** sorts out what we have experienced and learnt during the day. Important things are stored in the **memory**. Anyone who has had enough sleep can concentrate better at school. Tired children are often irritable and make more mistakes. That is why people say: a good night’s sleep is half the learning.

The bright light from **screens** tells the body that it is still daytime. As a result, it produces less **melatonin**, a hormone that makes you tired. It is better to switch off the screen before going to sleep. A calm story, a dark room and fixed times help you fall asleep.

Babies sleep for most of the day. Schoolchildren usually need **9 to 12 hours** a night. Teenagers need about 8 to 10 hours. For adults, 7 to 9 hours is usually enough. But every person is a little different.

gewusst: A person spends about a third of their life asleep.
Teenagers often get tired later in the evening because their internal clock shifts.

teile.einleitung: Supplementary insurance adds to the compulsory basic insurance of the health insurer. It is voluntary and pays for services that basic insurance does not cover, or only partly covers.
wichtigste: Supplementary insurance is voluntary and is governed by the Insurance Contract Act, VVG.
Basic insurance is governed by the Health Insurance Act, KVG.
With supplementary insurance, the insurer may ask health questions and turn people down.
Basic and supplementary insurance are separate and can be with different insurers.
For a semi-private or private hospital room you need supplementary hospital insurance.
When changing, you first wait for the new insurer to accept you and only then cancel.
It is worth taking out supplementary insurance while you are young and healthy.

abschnitte.text: **Basic insurance** pays for the same services, set out by law, for everyone. Anyone who wants more can voluntarily take out **supplementary insurance**. There is, for example, supplementary insurance for dental treatment, for glasses, for alternative medicine or for hospital. You pay a separate **premium** for each supplementary insurance. It is a separate **contract** alongside basic insurance.

Basic insurance is governed by the **Health Insurance Act, KVG**. Under it, every insurer must accept everyone. Supplementary insurance is governed by the **Insurance Contract Act, VVG**. That is why different rules apply: the insurer may ask **health questions**, **turn people down** or make a **reservation**. The duration and **notice periods** are also set out in the contract and can differ from the deadline for basic insurance.

In hospital, basic insurance pays for the **general ward**. Anyone who wants a two-bed room (semi-private) or a single room (private) and a choice of hospital doctor needs **supplementary hospital insurance**. Basic insurance usually does not pay for braces either. That is why many parents take out **supplementary dental insurance** for their child early on. This often has to be taken out before any treatment is foreseeable.

Basic and supplementary insurance are separate. You may have them with **different health insurers**. If you cancel the supplementary insurance, the basic insurance stays in place. Anyone who wants to change their supplementary insurance first waits for **acceptance** from the new insurer, because it is allowed to turn people down. Only then do you cancel the old supplementary insurance.

Young, healthy people are usually accepted without any problems and without a reservation. With increasing age, the risk of **pre-existing conditions** rises. Then insurers are more likely to turn people down or exclude certain illnesses. That is why it can be worth taking out supplementary insurance while you are fairly young. But whether it is necessary depends on your own wishes and on money.

gewusst: Many insurers offer to accept newborn babies into supplementary insurance if the parents register them early.
The deadline for cancelling basic insurance to change at the start of the year is 30 November, while for supplementary insurance the contract applies.

teile.einleitung: MSC is the largest container shipping company in the world and is based in Geneva. Its huge ships carry containers full of goods across all the oceans. The surprising thing is that Switzerland has no sea at all and yet is home to this company.
wichtigste: MSC stands for Mediterranean Shipping Company.
MSC’s headquarters is in Geneva.
The company was founded in 1970 by the Italian Gianluigi Aponte.
MSC ships mainly carry containers full of goods.
Since 2022 MSC has been the largest container shipping company in the world.
MSC belongs to the Aponte family and also runs cruise ships.

abschnitte.text: MSC is a **shipping company**, a company that owns and runs ships. It mainly carries **containers**, large metal boxes of a standard size. They contain, for example, clothes, furniture, electronics or food. In 2025, for example, MSC ran well over 800 container ships on all the world’s oceans.

In 1970 the Italian captain **Gianluigi Aponte** bought his first ship. He founded the company in Brussels, but moved its headquarters to Geneva a few years later. Over time the company bought more and more, and bigger and bigger, ships. In 2022 MSC overtook the Danish shipping company Maersk and became the largest container shipping company in the world.

MSC’s largest ships are almost 400 metres long, longer than four football pitches. They can load over 24,000 standard containers. A standard container is called a **TEU** and is about six metres long. Stacked up, the containers on such ships reach as high as a building with several storeys.

Besides its freight business, MSC also has its own cruise company, **MSC Cruises**. Its cruise ships sail, for example, through the Mediterranean, the Caribbean and northern Europe. Some of them are among the largest passenger ships in the world. The group also includes ports, ferries and logistics companies.

abschnitte.titel: A shipping company without a sea
abschnitte.text: Many people are surprised that the largest container shipping company in the world is based in Switzerland. But good connections, experts and stable conditions are also important for companies. Geneva is an important place for **world trade**; many raw materials and trading companies have their headquarters there. The ships themselves are usually registered in other countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A company that owns ships and uses them to transport goods or people.
A steel box of standard size that can easily be moved from ship to train or lorry.
A unit of measurement for a container about six metres long.
Buying and selling goods between the countries of the world.

gewusst: A large container ship can load so many containers that, placed end to end, they would stretch for many kilometres.
Switzerland has no coastline, but it is home to the largest container shipping company in the world.

teile.einleitung: ABB is a large technology group based in Zurich. The company makes things to do with electricity and automation, for example industrial robots, electric motors and charging stations for electric cars. ABB was formed in 1988 from a Swiss and a Swedish company.
wichtigste: ABB is an international technology group with its headquarters in Zurich.
ABB was formed in 1988 from the Swiss company BBC and the Swedish company ASEA.
The abbreviation ABB stands for Asea Brown Boveri.
ABB builds industrial robots, drives, motors and charging stations, among other things.
The company employs over 100,000 people worldwide.
ABB is listed on the Swiss stock exchange SIX and in Stockholm.

abschnitte.text: ABB develops and builds technology for electricity and automation. This includes **electric motors**, drives, switches and control systems for factories. ABB also makes charging stations for electric cars. Many factories, ships, trains and buildings all over the world work with technology from ABB.

In 1891 Charles Brown and Walter Boveri founded the company **Brown, Boveri & Cie.**, BBC for short, in Baden in the canton of Aargau. BBC built generators, turbines and locomotives. In Sweden there had been the electrical company **ASEA** since 1883. In 1988 the two companies merged to form ABB, which at the time was one of the largest company mergers in Europe.

ABB is one of the best-known manufacturers of **industrial robots**. These robot arms weld cars together, pack food or sort parcels. ABB also built YuMi, a robot with two arms that can work closely with people. In 2025 ABB announced that it would sell its robotics division to the Japanese company SoftBank.

ABB is active in over 100 countries and employs over 100,000 people worldwide. In Switzerland ABB has sites in Zurich and Baden, among other places. The company is listed on the stock exchange and is one of the largest Swiss companies. In 2020 ABB sold its power grids business to the Japanese company Hitachi.

ABB puts a strong focus on technology for electric cars, buses and ships with electric drives. The company gives its name to the racing series **ABB FIA Formula E**, in which only electric racing cars compete. Many fast-charging stations on motorways also come from ABB. In this way ABB wants to help reduce the use of petrol and diesel.

begriffe.erklaerung: Machines carry out tasks on their own that people used to do by hand.
A programmable robot arm that works in factories.
Two companies join together to form a new company.
A large company with many subsidiaries in different countries.

gewusst: The company BBC built electric locomotives for the Swiss railways at an early stage.
The company founders Brown and Boveri were both under 30 when they founded BBC.
ABB robots can repeat movements accurately to a fraction of a millimetre.

teile.einleitung: Accident insurance pays the costs when someone has an accident, for example during sport or on the way to work. In Switzerland, all employees are compulsorily insured against accidents through their employer. Children and schoolchildren, on the other hand, are insured against accidents through their health insurer.
wichtigste: Compulsory accident insurance is governed by the Accident Insurance Act (UVG), which came into force in 1984.
All employees in Switzerland are insured against occupational accidents.
Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week for the same employer is also insured against accidents in their free time.
Then, in an accident, the employer’s accident insurance pays.
The largest accident insurer is Suva, based in Lucerne.
Children and people without a job are insured against accidents through their health insurer.
If you cannot work after an accident, accident insurance pays a daily allowance.

abschnitte.text: According to the law, an **accident** is the sudden, unintended harmful effect of an unusual external factor on the body. That sounds complicated. It means, for example, falling off a bike, breaking a leg while skiing or cutting yourself with a knife. Flu or stomach ache, on the other hand, are illnesses and not accidents. Certain injuries such as a torn ligament are treated in the same way as an accident.

Since the **Accident Insurance Act (UVG)** of 1984, all employees have been compulsorily insured. Everyone is insured against **occupational accidents**, including apprentices. Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week for the same employer is also insured against **non-occupational accidents** in their free time. The employer pays the premium for occupational accidents. The premium for accidents in free time is often deducted from wages.

The best-known accident insurer is **Suva**, the Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund. It is based in Lucerne and began its work in 1918. Suva mainly insures companies from industry, construction and trades. Private insurers also offer compulsory accident insurance. Suva is also very active in **accident prevention**, for example with campaigns for safety at work and in free time.

Children, schoolchildren and students without a job are insured against accidents through their **health insurer**. There, the deductible and excess apply just as for an illness. Anyone who is employed can exclude accident cover from their health insurance and so save on the premium. When a job ends, you stay insured through the employer for another 31 days. After that you have to include accident cover with your health insurer again.

Accident insurance covers the treatment costs, for example the doctor, hospital and physiotherapy. If you cannot work after an accident, you receive a **daily allowance** of 80 per cent of the insured wage. If there is lasting damage, it pays a pension or compensation. Unlike with health insurance, there is no deductible and no excess for employees. You must report an accident to your employer or the insurer quickly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Accident Insurance Act, which governs accident insurance in Switzerland.
Accident that happens at work.
Accident in your free time, for example during sport.
Money per day to replace wages when you cannot work.
Largest accident insurer in Switzerland, based in Lucerne.

gewusst: Among employees, more accidents happen in their free time than at work, many of them during sport.
Suva belongs neither to the state nor to shareholders, but is an independent institution under public law.

teile.einleitung: With health insurance you are normally also insured against accidents. But anyone who is already insured against all accidents through their employer does not need this cover twice. Then you can exclude accident cover from your health insurance and save on the premium.
wichtigste: Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week for the same employer is also insured in their free time under the UVG.
Then you can suspend accident cover with your health insurer.
This lowers the premium a little.
Cover for accidents in your free time ends 31 days after your last working day.
After that, accident cover must be included with the health insurer again.
Children and people without a job need the health insurer’s accident cover.

abschnitte.text: **Basic insurance** includes **accident cover**. It pays if someone without other accident insurance has an accident. But employees are insured through their employer under the **UVG**. Anyone who works at least **8 hours a week** for the same employer is also insured in their **free time** in this way. Being insured twice brings no benefit then.

In this case you can **suspend** accident cover with your health insurer. Suspending means stopping temporarily. To do this, you tell the insurer that you are insured through your employer. The **premium** then becomes a little lower. So you save money without losing protection.

abschnitte.titel: After an apprenticeship or a job
abschnitte.text: When a job ends, the protection through the employer also ends. Cover for **non-occupational accidents** still applies for **31 days** after the last working day. If you do not have a new job by then, accident cover must be **included** with the health insurer again. That is why you should let the insurer know in good time. This applies, for example, after the end of an **apprenticeship**.

Sometimes there is a short break between two jobs, for example for a journey. Then you can take out **extended accident cover** with your previous accident insurer. With it, you extend your free-time cover by up to six months. Whether this makes more sense than the health insurer depends on the situation.

gewusst: Anyone who has a gap in their accident cover may have to bear the costs of an accident themselves if the worst happens.
Anyone who works fewer than 8 hours a week still needs accident cover with their health insurer.

teile.einleitung: Rega is the Swiss Air Rescue. It helps with helicopters in accidents and emergencies, especially where no ambulance can reach. You can reach it on the number 1414.
wichtigste: Rega is the Swiss Air Rescue.
Its emergency number is 1414.
With the helicopter it can also reach places in the mountains where no car can go.
With a winch it can lift people out of difficult terrain.
With air ambulance jets it brings sick and injured people back from abroad.
Rega is supported by millions of patrons.

abschnitte.text: **Rega** is the **Swiss Air Rescue**. It was founded in 1952. With its **helicopters** it is ready for action day and night. The helicopters are spread across several bases throughout Switzerland. This means Rega can reach almost any place in the country in a short time.

In the mountains, an **ambulance** often cannot get through. The Rega helicopter can land there too. If that is not possible, it lifts the injured person up with a **winch**. On board are an emergency doctor and other experts. They treat the person on the spot and fly them to hospital.

In an accident in the mountains, you call **1414**. On the phone you say who you are, where you are and what has happened. From abroad you can reach Rega on **+41 333 333 333**. With the **Rega app** you can raise an alarm, and your exact location is sent at the same time. This helps a lot if you do not know exactly where you are.

Rega also has **air ambulance jets**. With them it brings sick or injured people back to Switzerland from abroad. Rega is a non-profit foundation. It is supported by **millions of patrons** who pay a contribution every year. For them, Rega can waive the costs of a mission if no insurance pays.

gewusst: Rega was founded on 27 April 1952.
Many Swiss families are patrons of Rega, even though they hope never to need it.

teile.einleitung: The economy covers all the economic activities of a country: all households, companies, banks and the state. Economics studies how people produce, distribute and use scarce goods. It helps us understand why prices rise, why there is unemployment and how prosperity comes about.
wichtigste: The economy covers the entire economic life of a country.
The classic factors of production are labour, land and capital.
In 1776 Adam Smith published his work “The Wealth of Nations”.
Microeconomics studies individual households and companies, macroeconomics overall quantities such as inflation and unemployment.
Opportunity cost is the lost benefit of the best alternative not chosen.
Gossen’s first law describes the diminishing marginal utility of additional units.
The Swiss Consumer Price Index measures how the prices of a typical basket of goods develop.

abschnitte.text: An **economy** is the entire economic life of a country with all its households, companies, banks and the state. Money, goods and labour flow back and forth between them; this is called the **circular flow of the economy**. Households work in companies and receive wages, which they in turn use to buy goods. An economy’s output is measured with gross domestic product, GDP for short.

**Microeconomics** looks at individual households, companies and markets, for example how the price of apples comes about. **Macroeconomics** studies overall quantities such as economic growth, inflation and unemployment. The two views complement each other. In Switzerland, the Federal Statistical Office and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs SECO provide many figures on this.

Classical economics names three **factors of production**: labour, land and capital. Labour is the work people do, land includes ground and raw materials, and capital means machines, buildings and tools. Today knowledge is often named as an important factor too. Switzerland has hardly any raw materials and therefore relies especially on well-trained people and innovation.

In 1776 the Scottish philosopher **Adam Smith** published “The Wealth of Nations” and is considered the founder of modern economics. He described how the division of labour and free markets create prosperity. In the 20th century, John Maynard Keynes showed that the state can support demand in crises. According to Keynes, a **multiplier** increases government spending many times over; with a propensity to consume of 0.8 it is 5.

Because goods are scarce, people constantly have to choose. If you play football on Saturday, you cannot go to the cinema at the same time; the benefit you miss out on is called **opportunity cost**. Gossen’s first law says that each additional unit of a good brings less benefit. The first glass of water after sport is wonderful, the fifth hardly brings any pleasure; this is called diminishing **marginal utility**.

Measured by GDP per head, Switzerland is one of the richest countries in the world. About three quarters of employees work in the **service sector**, for example in banking, insurance, trade, health and tourism. Important industries are pharmaceuticals, mechanical engineering and watches. The Federal Statistical Office’s **Swiss Consumer Price Index** shows how the prices of a typical basket of goods develop.

begriffe.erklaerung: What you need to produce things: labour, land and capital.
The benefit you give up because you chose something else.
The additional benefit of one more unit of a good.
The study of the economy of a country as a whole.
The value of all goods and services of a country in a year.

gewusst: Adam Smith explained the advantages of the division of labour with a pin factory in which each worker does only one task.
Economics is often also called political economy.
The Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded since 1969.

teile.einleitung: SRG SSR is Switzerland’s public broadcasting company. It makes radio, television and online services in all four national languages. It includes SRF for German-speaking Switzerland, RTS for French-speaking Switzerland, RSI for Italian-speaking Switzerland and RTR for the Romansh speakers.
wichtigste: SRG is Switzerland’s public broadcasting company.
It broadcasts in four national languages.
SRF is the German-language unit and RTS the French-language unit.
RSI broadcasts in Italian and RTR in Romansh.
SRG was founded in 1931 and is based in Bern.
It is financed mainly by the radio and television licence fee.
SRG’s task is to inform all parts of the country equally.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Broadcasting Company** was founded in 1931 to make radio for the whole of Switzerland. From the 1950s **television** was added, and the news programme Tagesschau has existed since 1953. Later came teletext, websites and apps. Today the organisation is officially called the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation.

SRG consists of several **business units**. **SRF** broadcasts in German from Zurich, Basel and Bern. RTS has studios in Geneva and Lausanne, RSI in Comano near Lugano and RTR in Chur. There is also **Swissinfo**, which reports on Switzerland in many languages, mainly for people abroad.

SRG has a legal **mandate**, which is called public service. It is supposed to provide everyone in Switzerland with news, culture, education, sport and entertainment. Small language groups such as the Romansh speakers should also get a good service. That is why part of the money flows from large German-speaking Switzerland to the smaller parts of the country.

Almost every household in Switzerland pays the **radio and television licence fee**, which is collected by the company Serafe. It is about 335 francs a year (as of 2025). Most of it goes to SRG, and a smaller part goes to private local radio stations and regional television. SRG also earns money from advertising on television.

In Switzerland there are repeated votes and debates about the fees. In 2018 voters clearly rejected the **No Billag initiative**, which wanted to abolish the fees. Some people think that a strong public broadcaster is important for democracy. Others think the fees are too high and that SRG should become smaller.

begriffe.erklaerung: Services for the whole population that the state wants to guarantee.
Switzerland’s fourth national language, spoken mainly in the Grisons.
An amount that you are required by law to pay.
A company that makes radio, television, newspapers or online services.

gewusst: RTR makes programmes for less than one per cent of the population, namely the Romansh-speaking people.
SRG is not an ordinary company but is organised as an association.
The Tagesschau has existed since 1953 and is one of the oldest programmes in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The price tells you how much money you have to pay for a product or a service. You find it on the price label in the shop or next to the product in the online shop. With prices you can calculate, compare and save.
wichtigste: The price shows how much a product costs.
The price label on a product shows its price.
An apple for 1 franc means that 3 apples cost 3 francs.
When a product costs less for a short time, this is called a special offer.
If you pay with a larger amount, you get change back: with 5 francs for an ice cream costing 3 francs, that is 2 francs.
Prices come about through supply and demand.
In Switzerland, shops must show the prices of their goods clearly.

abschnitte.text: The **price** is the amount of money you have to pay for something. In the shop it is on a **price label** or on the shelf. In Switzerland prices are given in francs and centimes, for example 2.50 francs. There is also a price for services such as a haircut or a bus journey.

Prices are good for practising sums. If an apple costs 1 franc, 3 apples cost 3 francs, and 2 loaves at 4 francs cost 8 francs. An exercise book for 2 francs and a pencil for 1 franc cost 3 francs together. If you pay for an ice cream costing 3 francs with 5 francs, you get 2 francs **change**.

Prices depend on **supply** and **demand**. If there is little of a product but many people want it, the price rises. If there is a lot of it, the price often falls. That is why strawberries are usually cheaper in summer, when many are ripe, than in winter.

When a product costs less for a short time, this is called a **special offer**. A **discount** is a price reduction, for example 20 per cent less. Shops have special offers so that more customers come. Still, you should only buy what you really need, even if it is cheap.

The same product can cost different amounts in different shops. With food, the **unit price** helps, for example the price per kilogram or per litre. This shows you whether the large or the small pack is cheaper. In Switzerland, the Price Indication Ordinance requires prices to be clearly displayed.

Many goods are more expensive in Switzerland than in neighbouring countries; people talk about Switzerland as a **high-price island**. But wages are also higher. The federal **Price Supervisor** makes sure that companies without competition do not charge excessive prices. Because some people go shopping abroad, people speak of shopping tourism.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small label showing the price of a product.
Money you get back when you have paid too much.
When a product is cheaper for a short time.
A price reduction, often given as a percentage.
The price per kilogram or litre, for comparing packs.

gewusst: Prices often end in 95 or 90 centimes because they then seem cheaper.
In the past, almost every price at markets was negotiated; this is called haggling.
The Price Supervisor is a federal authority that anyone with complaints about prices can contact.
